Part One of the Second Chapter: Refuting Permanence (Nityatva-bhaṅga). Furthermore, there are those who maintain that nirvāṇa is substantially existent, permanent, and blissful, as stated in a sūtra:
"Bhikṣus, you should know that there is a realm of nirvāṇa, which is without birth and without cessation, signless and unconditioned, the ultimate peace and bliss."
This too should be refuted based on the preceding reasoning and scriptural authority.
Furthermore, a verse states:
"Apart from the cause of that which binds and that which is bound, there is no other true liberation."
"Because the conditions for its production are lacking;
even if it were to exist, it would still be called 'non-existent'.
The Treatise says:

It has already been fully explained that all categories of existence (*padārtha*) transcend the domain of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). When engaging in debate, one must necessarily establish through the inference based on the production of effects (*kāryahetu-anumāna*) that there is nothing other than the realm of nirvāṇa that can produce anything.
How can one infer through analogy that there truly exists permanence and bliss?
If it were admitted that [nirvāṇa] could be produced, it would contradict your own treatise.
Since nirvāṇa has no fruit, it contradicts the nature of all conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra); therefore, the essence of nirvāṇa is not substantially existent.
Even if it were granted that [liberation] exists substantially, if it does not perform a superior function within its own basis—the body—how could it be called liberation?
Only if it causes one’s own body to become serene and autonomous, forever free from fetters, can it be termed liberation.
This [unconditioned] has no such function with respect to one's own body; therefore, even if it were to exist, it would be of no benefit to the body. Why then adhere to such a useless thing?
If it were admitted to have a function, it would be identical to the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).
Since it is admitted that it is useless, it is identical to a rabbit's horn.

No person of intelligence would ever concede that an unconditioned phenomenon (*asaṃskṛta*) can be useful while being substantially existent (*dravyasat*) when it is useless; therefore, one knows that the essence of *nirvāṇa* is not substantially existent.

In this context, the afflictions (*kleśa*) and secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*), as well as the various determinate karmas that lead to future rebirths, are collectively termed "bonds" (*bandhana*).
It is by the power of these that sentient beings remain for a long time within the vast prison of birth and death (*saṃsāra*), undergoing intense suffering and failing to attain liberation.

The five aggregates of clinging (*pañcopādānaskandha*) brought about by various fetters are collectively termed "the bound," because the resulting fruit of suffering is tied to the cause of origination and lacks sovereignty.

All noble paths capable of removing these fetters are collectively termed "the cause," because by means of them one permanently severs the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) of the afflictions, no longer draws forth karma, does not invite future suffering, and realizes the fruit of liberation through dissociation (*visamyoga*).

This fruit of liberation does not exist as a separate substantial entity apart from the binder, the bound, and their cause; that is to say, when one attains liberation from the binder, one does not realize liberation as something distinct from the binder.
Because one perceives the distinctions between states as they truly are, that very [state] does not arise; this is called liberation.

It is the same with that which is bound: when one is free from the bonds of affliction and abides in a state of serene and sovereign distinction, it is called liberation; there is no separate dharma whatsoever.
The cause is likewise so: when its functional distinctions are free from all afflictions, it is called liberation.

Apart from the Noble Path, there is no other distinct dharma; therefore, apart from this cause consisting of the fetter and that which is fettered, there is no other truly existent nirvāṇa or liberation.
Furthermore, if nirvāṇa were to exist, it would necessarily have a basis.
As for this basis—whether it be the aggregates (skandhas) or a self (ātman)—neither can be found at the time of parinirvāṇa.
Therefore, it is said in verse:
"At the time of ultimate nirvāṇa, there are no aggregates and no self;
if one does not perceive a nirvāṇa-attainer, upon what basis could there be nirvāṇa?"
The Commentary states:

Abiding in the state of parinirvāṇa without remainder, the preceding aggregates are eternally extinguished and subsequent aggregates do not arise; therein, there is no continuity of any aggregates whatsoever.
Since no one is seen to enter parinirvāṇa, on what basis can one speak of a truly existent nirvāṇa?
If at that time one were to allow for the designation of a truly existent *pudgala*, one would fall into the error of the view that the Tathāgata definitely exists after his passing.
If, at that time, a person (pudgala) were not posited as existing, the same fault as before would follow.
Since one who attains parinirvāṇa cannot be found, it is certain that there is no real nirvāṇa.

Because one has never seen anyone in the world who is free from greed and yet possesses greed and so forth, even if one were to postulate a basis for nirvāṇa, then because nirvāṇa would have a basis, its nature should be impermanent, just like greed and the rest.

Furthermore, if the essence of nirvāṇa were existent, it would possess characteristics that could be perceived through conditions; it should, like form and other such phenomena, not transcend birth and death.
As it is said: "World-Honored One!..."
If one seeks nirvana as having a real, substantial essence, one will not transcend birth and death. Why is this?
That which is called "nirvana" is the eternal cessation of all marks and the departure from all discursive agitation.

The meaning of this sūtra is that because one is forever free from all worldly distractions and false views, and because the characteristics of the grasped (grāhya) and the grasper (grāhaka) initiated by them are eternally extinguished, one realizes nirvāṇa.
Therefore, nirvāṇa is definitively not a basis or object for any form of clinging to existence (*bhavagrāha*).

Some say that two phrases indicate their respective order: nirvāṇa eternally extinguishes the various signs that serve as objects, and it is eternally free from all discursive movement of the subject that perceives them.
Since *nirvāṇa* transcends all manifold characteristics and mental agitation, one cannot apprehend *nirvāṇa* as an existent entity.
Nevertheless, when the sūtras speak of the "realm of *nirvāṇa*" (*nirvāṇadhātu*) and so forth, it is for the purpose of refuting the view of those who deny the existence of *nirvāṇa*.

There are those who maintain that birth and death are without beginning and without end, and that a realm of parinirvāṇa definitively does not exist; therefore, the Buddha taught that there is a realm of parinirvāṇa wherein the blazing fires of afflictions and manifold sufferings are eternally extinguished—a state that is without arising, without cessation, signless, unconditioned, and ultimately peaceful and blissful.

This establishes the principle that the fire of birth and death is not a constant succession and has no time of permanent extinction, because it arises from various conditions and is subject to affliction, just like the blazing fires in the mountains and forests of the world.

This means that although the suffering of birth and death has been continuous and uninterrupted since beginningless time, arising in dependence upon various conditions, when one encounters a virtuous friend, hears the Dharma, and practices it such that the untainted noble path manifests before one, all afflictions are extinguished and no further karma is produced; thus, subsequent suffering does not continue, which is called *nirvāṇa*. It is, for example, like the extinction of fire when the fuel in the world is exhausted.
However, this nirvāṇa is realized through the noble path; it is ultimate quiescence, free from all natures and characteristics, and forever cuts off all conceptual proliferation and discursive play.
Thus, the various teachings proclaimed in the sūtras are all skillful means intended to eliminate false views and attachments.
All those who possess wisdom should correctly realize this and not claim that nirvāṇa is existent, non-existent, or otherwise.
If one gives rise to various conceptual discriminations regarding saṃsāra, it is easy to employ skillful means to eliminate them.

If one gives rise to various conceptual discriminations regarding nirvāṇa, that affliction is deep-seated and difficult to cure; therefore, one should not cling to such notions as existence or non-existence.
Furthermore, the Sāṃkhya outsiders speak thus:

"When cause and effect are dispersed and destroyed, and all longing has ceased, there remains only the conscious self (puruṣa) in isolation from its bonds; at that time, it is called nirvāṇa and liberation."
To refute that attachment, a verse is spoken:
"If I were at that time to abandon all virtues, what intention could there be apart from craving?
The commentary says:
One discriminates and experiences according to the objects that appear; you call this "volition" (*cetanā*), yet it is grasped as a self.

This necessarily does not occur apart from the conjunction of the sense faculties and their objects. Thus, these two things do not exist apart from desire; in order to fulfill that desire, the sense faculties and objects conjoin, and volition experiences according to the objects that appear.
At the time of parinirvāṇa, all longing has ceased; since cause and effect have been dispersed and destroyed, how could there be volition?

Since there is no volition, neither is there a self. How then can you say that only the self associated with volition remains dissociated [from defilements], and that this state is called nirvāṇa-liberation?
If you further claim that at the time of parinirvāṇa, although there is no volition, the self still exists, this too is not so;
therefore, a verse is spoken:
"If there were a self without volition, It would be the same as non-existence."
The treatise says:
According to your school’s tenet, the self is conceived as having volition (*cetanā*) as its essential nature and characteristic.
At the time of parinirvāṇa, since volition no longer exists, both its nature and characteristics are extinguished and nothing remains. Upon what, then, could one rely to say that a self exists?

If it is argued that although the function of volition is absent at that time, the self-substance as seed still persists—just as the visual faculty functions by seeing forms, yet the substance of the eye remains even when its function has ceased.
This is also not the case.
Such a thing could only exist if there were a basis for it. Why is this so?
The differentiation of functional capacity is called a "seed.
Such a seed must necessarily depend upon something else; since there is no basis [for it], how could a seed exist?

The specific functional capacity within consciousness—induced by the differentiation of functional capacities of the formations (*saṃskāra*) of previous lives—which is capable of producing a specific visual consciousness, is designated as the "eye."
In this way, the visual faculty necessarily relies upon the ālayavijñāna and the four great elements.

In the state of nirvāṇa without remainder, causes and effects are dispersed and destroyed; all aspirations and deliberations are utterly extinguished, leaving no basis whatsoever. To then calculate that there is a self-substance which serves as the seed is logically untenable.

Furthermore, if one maintains that the self is itself the seed from which the specific activity of volition arises, then this self must be subsumed under the category of the "preeminent," because it possesses a superior capacity for giving rise to all phenomena.

Furthermore, if one maintains that the self is the substratum of the seeds, and that by means of this as a cause the fruit of volition (*cetanā*) is produced, then one loses the tenet of one's own school that volition is itself the self, and one also loses [the view] that the self is volition; for its nature would then be indolent and passive, being merely an experiencer (*vedaka*) rather than an agent (*kartṛ*).
If the self you grasp is not identical to volition, you must now describe the characteristics of such a self.
If the self were established even without its characteristics being described, then all false attachments would likewise be established.
Furthermore, it is said in verse:
"If there were a self-essence remaining without remainder, Then volition would certainly be able to arise;
But when there is neither self nor volition, Then all states of existence cease to be."
The Commentary states:

If, in the realm of nirvana without remainder, the seeds of a self were not permanently uprooted, then one would necessarily give rise to the thought that manifests: "I am no different [from before]," just as in the previous state.
If volition were to arise [in this state], then everything would be present; how, then, could it be called liberation from the bonds of birth and death?
If you argue that although the seed of the self exists therein, volition cannot arise because the necessary conditions are lacking, [we reply: ...
This is also not the case, because since the self has no distinction [from other things], it should be as in the previous state where all requisites are present without deficiency.

Furthermore, according to your own tenet, the essence of the self is omnipresent and is therefore constantly associated with the requisites of others; since there is no separate location, it is just like one's own possessions.
How can it be said that the requisites for the assembly are deficient?

If you say that because each requisite belongs to oneself, even though one is constantly associated with the requisites of others, they are nonetheless considered deficient because they do not belong to oneself—then [this argument is flawed].
This is also not the case, because since their locations are not distinct, they are always associated; why then would [the seeds] not belong to [the self] already?
Such a tenet will be refuted extensively later.

If it is said that in this state there is ultimate quiescence—wherein fundamentally there was no self and now there is no volition, such that all seeds, having nothing to rely upon, are eternally extinguished and do not give rise to future existence, just as sprouts and so forth do not arise without external seeds—[then we reply:]...

This is precisely what is called ultimate liberation: it is neither empty nor existent, neither annihilated nor eternal, neither suffering nor pleasure, neither self nor non-self, neither defiled nor pure; it cuts off all conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*). To stop the false view that denies the existence of *nirvāṇa*, it is therefore said that there truly exist permanence, bliss, self, and purity.
These words of expedient means should not be clung to as definitive.
Since one neither clings to existence nor repudiates non-existence, this is called right knowledge and liberation.
Furthermore, the Vaiśeṣika outsiders speak as follows:

If one can forever uproot the very source of suffering, pleasure, and so forth, and having relinquished all things, remains alone in solitary independence, performing no actions and dwelling eternally in peace and bliss, this is called Nirvana.
Thus, nirvāṇa must certainly be admitted.
If it were merely the cessation of suffering without a self, it would be a state of annihilation; what, then, could be called nirvāṇa?
Furthermore, this nirvāṇa is characterized by liberation from all fetters and sovereign freedom, which the wise delight in.
If the self were entirely non-existent in essence, what would there be to rejoice in?
This is mere empty talk devoid of actual meaning; to refute that attachment, the next verse says:
"If there were a self apart from suffering, Then nirvāṇa would certainly not exist."
"Therefore, within nirvāṇa, we all shall be eternally extinguished.
The commentary says:

You maintain that all phenomena such as suffering and pleasure are attributes of the self (*ātman*), and that they constantly follow their own substratum, the self, until it is extinguished. How then can these be separated from the self in this state?
Since I am not distinct [from them], I should be associated with them as I was in my prior state.

Furthermore, within the state of nirvana without remainder (nirupadhiśeṣa), this pleasure and so forth should not be permanently separated from their own substratum, the self, because they are qualities of the self, just like number and other such attributes.

Just as you maintain that a single quality pervades all qualities because they are qualities of the self and are therefore eternally conjoined with it, so too must suffering and the other qualities be present; how then could they ever be separated?

Thus, this self, being constrained by the logic of the realm of nirvana without remainder, would also remain associated with suffering and its other qualities; consequently, nirvana would definitively not exist, for the self would be perpetually bound and never liberated.

In birth and death, there is only the accumulation of manifold sufferings; through the power of causes and conditions, one wanders in saṃsāra from time without beginning. Deluded by ignorance, one falsely gives rise to the grasping of a self, thinking, "I am constantly scorched by the fire of suffering. Fearing the loss of this self, one does not seek liberation; even if one seeks liberation, one cannot realize it because of the false attachment to a self, which causes all sufferings to blaze intensely.

When those who possess wisdom rely upon a true and virtuous friend and, having understood these matters without inversion, apply themselves with diligent skillful means as if their heads were on fire in order to extinguish the blazing great suffering, they repeatedly pour upon it the water of noble wisdom; when the blazing fuel is thus forever extinguished, there is tranquility and bliss, which is called *nirvāṇa*.
When this entire mass of suffering of birth and death is thus utterly extinguished and the bliss of nirvāṇa is attained, what person of wisdom would not rejoice?
What wise person, afflicted by a grave illness and fearing the severance of their life, would take pleasure in that sickness?
Only fools are capable of such a thing.

Just as those sentient beings in the hells, though scorched by various fierce flames and oppressed by great suffering without a moment’s respite, still harbor deep attachment to their own bodies; this is entirely due to the power of their own evil karma, being possessed by the demons of ignorance and false views, and failing to uproot the fundamental affliction of the view of self, which causes those beings to fear annihilation.

When the wise observe that the continuity of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) is empty and devoid of a self, and that this mere mass of great suffering is forever severed and extinguished, what is there to fear?

Therefore, if one can abandon the view of a self, one will certainly rejoice in the eternal extinction of *nirvāṇa*, and by means of this, one is also able to relinquish the view of annihilationism (*ucchedadṛṣṭi*).
To perceive the self as being annihilated is called the view of annihilationism (*ucchedadṛṣṭi*); it is not merely the cessation of suffering that is termed the view of annihilationism.
Therefore, the Sūtra says:
"Because one views the self and the world as being eternally cut off and destroyed, it is called the view of annihilationism."

Regarding the term "the world," it refers to the grasping at my objects and the grasping at "I" and "mine" as having a truly existent essence; upon hearing that these are severed, one then gives rise to the view of annihilationism.
If there were no such grasping, there would be no view of annihilationism.

Based solely upon the objects of the grasped "self" and "mine," the two views of eternalism and nihilism arise as perversions; the Unsurpassed Great Teacher established these as "views of extreme adherence. From these false views, birth and death are struck forth, and the blazing fire of great suffering is made to increase and expand, oppressing immeasurable sentient beings who lack wisdom.
Therefore, the World-Honored One praises eternal cessation, the supreme peace and bliss of detachment and tranquility, so that those who are to be converted may take deep delight in it.
Thus, nirvāṇa is neither non-existent nor existent; it is realized by sublime wisdom and is termed the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
Furthermore, because it is the most excellent among all objects, and because there is no further object to be sought beyond it, it is called the "ultimate object" (*paramārtha*).
Moreover, some say:

permanent phenomena definitely exist, for the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*)—being unborn, unceasing, and truly existent—is able to serve as the objective condition (*ālambana*) that gives rise to noble wisdom (*āryajñāna*).
This is also not the case, because it is not the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
If the ultimate truth were substantially existent (*dravyasat*), it would have to arise from a multitude of conditions, just like form (*rūpa*) and other phenomena.
If it does not arise from conditions, its essence must be non-substantially existent, just like a rabbit's horn.
Furthermore, there is no similar example (sapakṣa), so the reason (hetu) is unestablished.
Even if one were to grant that the reason is established, it would not be eternal.
Moreover, if the essence of ultimate truth (paramārthasatya) were an existent entity, it would—like a jar or other such things—not be the object of noble wisdom (āryajñāna).
If true noble wisdom were to take conditioned phenomena as its object, it would be like other forms of cognition and would not be true noble wisdom.

It would not sever the afflictions nor realize the ultimate truth of nirvana; it would be neither empty nor existent, neither permanent nor impermanent. If one seeks therein for even the slightest inherent nature, it is certainly impossible to find.
To clarify this meaning, the following verse says:
"Better to seek within the mundane world than to seek in the ultimate truth;
for that which is rare in the mundane world is entirely absent in the ultimate truth."
The commentary states:
There are, briefly, three kinds of phenomena in the world:
first, phenomena known through direct perception, such as form, sound, and so forth;
Second are phenomena that are experienced as they manifest, such as jars, clothing, and so forth.
These two types of phenomena are commonly known by the world to exist and do not require formal proof.
Third are phenomena that possess functional activity, such as the eyes, ears, and so forth.
Through their respective functions, they are known to exist.
These three phenomena are the objects of engagement and comprehension within the conventional world (*saṃvṛti*).
Furthermore, there are three kinds of non-existence in the world: absolute non-existence, and the non-existence of the prior and posterior limits of the three realms of existence (*bhava*).
To exclude this non-existence, it is said that "something exists"; furthermore, to distinguish it from the various phenomena established by false views, it is said that "something exists.

Thus, whether the three realms of existence or non-existence are conventional, they are all not real when spoken of in terms of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*). This is because the ultimate truth is neither existent nor nonexistent, and cannot be reached by conceptualization or language.

It would be easier to find even a slight degree of intrinsic nature within the deceptive phenomena of the world than it would be to ultimately find intrinsic nature within the true reality of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*). Since even that slight degree of intrinsic nature found in the world does not exist there [in the ultimate], how much less could any other intrinsic nature exist?

If that is so, one would rather prefer such a small measure of the worldly realm than such a total absence of the ultimate truth; for although the world possesses various calamities and faults, there are still some dharmas therein that can be experienced and utilized.
In the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), there is not even the slightest phenomenon; what, then, could be experienced?

Otherwise, if suffering existed or did not exist in the ultimate sense of the world, it would be subject to either delight or aversion. What wise person, knowing that water does not cure the suffering of a severe illness, would seek to drink more of it?

Alas! The world is deluded and inverted; it delights in and praises the cycle of birth and death where manifold sufferings blaze forth, yet it feels aversion toward and disparages the ultimate truth of tranquil peace and bliss. Why trouble oneself to listen to such foolish words?

Therefore, the wise should diligently apply themselves to the contemplation of the emptiness of all phenomena; regarding the suffering of birth and death, they should eliminate wrong aspirations, and regarding the bliss of the ultimate truth, they should cultivate right aspirations.

Thus, being fully endowed with the three doors of liberation, although they dwell for a long time within the great ocean of birth and death, they are not defiled by the faults of birth and death; remaining serenely liberated, they bring benefit and happiness to sentient beings.

By virtue of this thorough mastery of the meaning of the sūtra passages and their skillful means in realizing the emptiness of phenomena, those who have attained realization are not burned even when situated amidst fierce flames, and though they manifest birth and death, they remain eternally liberated.

2. Chapter on Refuting the Self (*Ātma-pratiṣedha-varga*). *The Commentary on the Extensive Hundred Stanzas of the Mahāyāna*, Part One: Chapter Two, Refuting the Self (1). Furthermore, the Vaiśeṣika non-Buddhists speak as follows:

"The previous statement that in the state of parinirvāṇa without remainder there are neither aggregates (*skandha*) nor a self (*ātman*), and that one speaks of nirvāṇa based upon something [else], is illogical, because the self definitely exists."
If there were no self, upon what basis would the view of a self arise?
If the view of a self did not exist, the grasping at the view of "mine" could not exist either.

If ordinary beings and others had not, from time immemorial, given rise to such views of self and mine, they should—like those who have eternally extinguished the view of a personal identity (satkāyadṛṣṭi)—not undergo the manifold sufferings of birth and death within the three realms.

Furthermore, one should not say that the view of self arises conditioned by the mind, the faculties, and the body, because the mind, the faculties, and the body are conventionally described in the world as "belonging to me.

Moreover, there must be a definitive distinction between the self and what belongs to the self, because they are expressed by the terms "possessor" and "possessed," just as in the case of Devadatta and the carriage he rides.

Furthermore, because the view of self (*ātmadṛṣṭi*) does not exist with respect to the bodies of others, if one were to allow that the view of self arises taking the mind, the sense faculties, and the body as its object, it would follow—just like the views held by Devadatta or Yajñadatta—that it would likewise arise taking the bodies of others as its object.

Nor should it be said that because there are differences between one's own mind and the minds of others, the view of self (*ātmadṛṣṭi*) does not take as its object the root-mind and so forth that have existed since beginningless time; for it is admitted that the view of self arises by taking as its object [the mind] as it exists at each moment, which differs from one moment to the next in its preceding and succeeding states.
Furthermore, this view of self does not take the present mind as its object, for that would contradict what is perceived by worldly experience.
Nor can it take past or future minds and so forth as its object, because they lack substantial existence; thus, like flowers in the sky, they do not give rise to the view of self.

Since it is observed that a self exists neither in the past nor in the future, and because two minds do not coexist within a single body, one cannot say that the view of a self arises conditioned by the present mind itself.

Furthermore, the mind arises and perishes differently from moment to moment; if there were no self, how could there be such things as memory, recognition, learning, recitation, or the awareness of enmity and favor?

Moreover, the mind, the sense faculties, and so forth, certainly cannot be the objects of the view of a self, because characteristics such as male or female are absent therein, just as they are absent in objects like jars or basins.
"Therefore, it is certain that a real self exists; conditioned by this, the view of a self arises, and on this basis, one claims, 'I am a great man.
Although such statements exist, they are empty words devoid of actual meaning."

Why is this so? If the self were to exist, it would have to arise from conditions like form and other phenomena; since that which arises must inevitably return to cessation, it would not be permanent.
If it were not born of conditions, it would lack any superior essence or function, like a rabbit’s horn; how then could it be called a "self"?

Furthermore, although you establish that the self exists and is permanent, you ultimately fail to provide either a logical reason (*hetu*) or an illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*). What is to be established cannot be proven without a reason and an example.
If it were possible for a thesis (*pakṣa*) to be established by mere assertion alone, then everything one might propose would necessarily be established.

Even if one were to employ skillful means to falsely establish a reason and an example—namely, that the self whose existence is being posited is impermanent because everything that has a cause is impermanent;

and that the self whose existence is being posited is certainly not substantially real because the nature of a permanent self is an object of knowledge and an object of discourse, like a jar or a basin.
Furthermore, if the self as it is established were truly existent, it should not be the object of the perverted view of self.
If seeing it as it truly is were considered a perversion, then all noble wisdom would necessarily be perverse.
Since all noble wisdom perceives objects in accordance with their true nature and is thus not inverted, the view of self (*ātman-dṛṣṭi*) should likewise not be inverted.
If that were so, the view of self would be like noble wisdom and could not be the root of saṃsāra from time immemorial.

If this view of self were known as it truly is, yet had been inducing birth and death since beginningless time, then noble wisdom would likewise induce all births and deaths, and one would ultimately never attain nirvana.

Therefore, ordinary beings, being deluded and inverted, falsely grasp at a self within the five aggregates of clinging—which are devoid of a self—and consequently grasp at what belongs to a self (*mamakāra*).

Because this false grasping at the views of "self" and "mine" does not accord with the actual state of reality and constitutes an inversion, it is able to draw forth the manifold sufferings of birth and death within the three realms.

If one gives rise to noble wisdom and vision regarding the five aggregates of clinging as being without self, thoroughly penetrates the absence of self and what belongs to self, eternally severs birth and death, and realizes nirvana, then for this reason one must certainly accept and believe in non-self.

Furthermore, regarding your statement that because the mind, the faculties, and the body are spoken of by the world as "mine," the view of self (*ātmadṛṣṭi*) should not arise taking them as its object: I too should not be the object of the view of self, for the world also speaks of "what belongs to me" and "I have such-and-such characteristics. Therefore, it is not correct to claim that something cannot be the object of the view of self simply because it is spoken of by the world as "mine."
The relationship between "I" and "mine" is not fixed when compared with one another; there may be distinct entities, or there may be no distinct entities.

Furthermore, as for your argument that "I" and "mine" must necessarily be different because they are expressed by the terms "possessor" and "possessed," like Devadatta and so forth—this reason is inconclusive.
The world also says that such food and drink possess fragrances and flavors that are particularly distinct from the ordinary; how could there be food and drink apart from fragrance and flavor?

Although the views of "self" (*ātman*) and "what belongs to self" (*ātmīya*) both take the aggregates (*skandha*) as their object, one may alternatively grasp a single aggregate as the self and the remaining aggregates as what belongs to it, or again, grasp the internal aggregates collectively as the self and the external aggregates as what belongs to it. Therefore, the thesis you have established suffers from the fault of being redundant (*sādhya-sama*).

Furthermore, regarding your statement that because the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*) does not exist with respect to another's body, the mind and so forth are not the objects of the view of self—I too should not be the object of the view of self, since the view of self does not exist with respect to "another-self."

If one does not give rise to the view of self when taking another person as an object, yet gives rise to the view of self when taking oneself as an object, then even if one does not give rise to the view of self when taking another's body as an object, what prevents the view of self from taking one's own mind and so forth as its object?

Sentient beings lacking wisdom do not understand the principle of equality—the emptiness and selflessness [of phenomena]. They merely habitually cultivate the views of "self" and "mine" regarding all conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*) from time immemorial; thus, within the continuity of their own and others' aggregates (*skandha*), they grasp at themselves as "self" and that which is distinct from themselves as "other," even though therein exists no substantial nature of a self whatsoever.

Furthermore, as for what you have said—that one should not claim there is a distinction between one's own mind and the minds of others, and that the view of self (*ātmadṛṣṭi*) does not take as its object the root-mind and so forth from beginningless time—which are distinct in each preceding and succeeding moment—yet you nevertheless allow that the view of self arises by taking them all together as its object; this too is incorrect.
One's own continuity of cause and effect across preceding and succeeding moments is severed from that of another;
for according to your own tenet, the self-essence is a single unity without difference between before and after, while distinct selves are mutually separate.
When I perceive the self as my own object, the power of that perception is exhausted once it does not extend to another self.
It is the same with the self: although its own states differ from moment to moment throughout its beginningless past, the continuity of cause and effect remains uninterrupted.
Just as a lamp or a river is conventionally designated as a single continuum, sentient beings lacking wisdom perceive it as a single self and thereby give rise to the view of a self;
however, because another's body is severed from one's own causes and effects, the view of a self does not take it as its object.
Furthermore, you conceive of a self that is similar for both oneself and others, omnipresent, eternal, and unconditioned; for what reason, then, would there be the view of a self?
It must be conditioned by this and not by that.

If you conceive of a self as being subject to conditions or as having distinctions of "this" and "that" based on its arising, it should—like form and other phenomena—be impermanent by nature. Therefore, one should know that the continuity of causes and effects within conditioned phenomena is distinct; it is precisely because of these differences that the view of a self manifests such distinctions.
Furthermore, the objections you have raised—such as that the view of self does not take the present mind as its object—are all unreasonable.

Why is this? Because the view of self arises based on a conventional designation of a single "self" in relation to the continuity of causes and effects within one's own body across preceding and succeeding moments; thus, there is no fault of taking the present mind as its object.
Furthermore, within a single body there are many mental complexes (*citta-kalāpa*), yet those linked by cause and effect are designated as one sentient being.
What fault is there in conceiving a self by giving rise to the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*) with respect to one mental complex while taking another mental complex as its object?

Regarding what you conceive as a real self: if the view of self perceives the self as it truly is, like right view, it would not be a false view; if it does not perceive the self, like wrong view, it would not be the view of self.

Furthermore, as for your statement that because the mind and its associates arise and perish differently in every moment, there could be no such things as recollection, recognition, learning, chanting, or the remembrance of kindness and enmity if there were no self—this too is not correct.

Within the bodies of sentient beings, each possesses its own ālayavijñāna. This consciousness continues as a single stream, maintaining the seeds of all phenomena so that they are not lost; it acts as both cause and effect for all phenomena, and through the power of perfuming (vāsanā), it enables such functions as memory, cognition, learning, recitation, and the awareness of kindness or enmity.
Regarding the self you conceive as permanent and unchanging, it should remain as it was in its subsequent state; such a thing cannot be.
What exists should always exist, and what does not exist should always be non-existent, because the essence of the self is unitary.

One cannot say that the "self" undergoes transformation while its activity does not depart from its essence; for if the self were likewise subject to change, then this self—just like form and other phenomena—would have both essence and activity undergoing transformation, and would thus be impermanent.

If it is claimed that the mind and so forth all belong to a self, and that because such transformations as these occur within the mind and so forth, the self to which they belong also receives those names;
then the mind and so forth should arise from the self, since they are capable of producing effects, and thus the self would be impermanent.
If the self has no function of producing or sustaining the mind, how can it be said that the mind belongs to the self?
Since the self is eternal, it cannot maintain the seeds of the mind and so forth; how, then, could there be such phenomena as memory and cognition?

Furthermore, as for your statement that this mind, the sense faculties, and so forth are definitely not the objects of the view of a self because the characteristics of male, female, and so on are absent therein—just as in the case of a jar and the like.

This reason is unestablished, because the physical forms characterized by male, female, and so forth are presently perceived; furthermore, the self as it is conceived would likewise not be the object of the view of self, since characteristics such as male and female do not exist within that [conceived] self. Thus, the reason you have established is indeterminate.
To clarify this meaning, the following verse says:
"The internal self is truly neither male, Nor female, nor neuter;
It is only due to ignorance That one calls the self a 'man'."
The Commentary states:

Because there are distinctions in the physical characteristics upon which they depend, conventional discourse designates them as male, female, or neither; yet these specific characteristics of the body do not exist within the internal self, because the essence of the conceived self is held to be a single unity.

Furthermore, the characteristics of "male" and so forth arise and undergo transformation; we also observe that within this very life there is change, wherein one abandons a distinct characteristic and assumes another.
Since the self (*ātman*) you maintain is eternal and immutable, it neither abandons nor assumes anything, and therefore lacks such characteristics.

Nor can it be said that although the characteristics of male, female, and so forth are not the substance of the self, they are attributes of the self, and that the self is designated as "male" and so on because it is conjoined with these attributes. Why is this so?
Because they are not mentioned among the qualities such as pleasure (*sukha*) and so forth, my unique qualities (*āveṇika-guṇa*) are, in brief, of nine kinds:

first, suffering (*duḥkha*); second, pleasure (*sukha*); third, attachment (*rāga*); fourth, aversion (*dveṣa*); fifth, diligence (*vīrya*); sixth, the dharma (*dharma*); seventh, the non-dharma (*adharma*); eighth, conduct (*caryā*); and ninth, knowledge (*jñāna*).
The characteristics of male and female and so forth are not included among the nine qualities; how, then, can it be said that these are qualities of the self?

Furthermore, qualities such as pleasure pervade all their substrates, whereas the substrata of the characteristics of male and female do not so pervade; how, then, can it be asserted that these are qualities of the self?

Furthermore, it cannot be said that the commonality and difference of male and female are subsumed by the self, for based on that very commonality and difference, one may also say that the self is male or female. Why is this so?

Regarding the nature of identity and difference: the substratum is determined to be permanent and all-pervading. Since the self (*ātman*) is permanent, it should never relinquish its characteristics as male, female, and so forth; thus, these three characteristics should exist at all times.

Furthermore, since the characteristics of "male" and so forth pervade all [notions of] the self and the body, how can they be subsumed under the category of "self-identity and difference" (*sāmānyaviśeṣa*) alone?

Moreover, the substrata of self-identity and difference are distinct; even if one were to grant that they are subsumed under the category of self-identity and difference pertaining solely to the self, how could a single self possess three types of identity and difference?
One does not perceive a single basis possessing multiple identities and differences.

Nor can it be said that, as with a single *pāṭala* tree which possesses three identities and differences—namely, its nature as a *pāṭala*, its nature as a tree, and its ultimate reality (*tattva*)—so too is it with the self:
within the single substance of the self, there are three identities and differences, namely, masculinity, femininity, and the neuter gender.

Why is this so? The nature of *palāśa* pervades all *palāśa* trees; the nature of "tree" pervades all trees; and the nature of "substance" pervades all substances. Among these three bases, there is a mutual difference in their breadth and narrowness.
In my [view], the three natures mentioned above are all merely the pervasive self; since their substratum is not distinct, how could they serve as metaphors?

Therefore, it is based solely on the conventional characteristics arising from beginningless habituation to false conceptualization that, within the mundane path, they are spoken of as "male" and so forth; it is not that there exists a real self possessing the characteristics of being male and so forth.
It is solely due to ignorance, arrogance, negligence, and false conceptualization that fools claim for themselves, "I am a man," or likewise claim for themselves, "I am a woman" or "neither.
Because it is abbreviated in the verse, only "man" is mentioned here.

Since the characteristics of male, female, and so forth exist within the body, yet the self-entity as conceived by you lacks such characteristics as male and so forth, your logical reason (hetu) suffers from the fallacies of being unestablished (asiddha) and inconclusive (anaikāntika).

If you further argue that although both the self and the body possess the characteristics of male, female, and so forth, the self is real while the body is merely conventional, this is also incorrect.
If the characteristics of male and so forth exist in both places, how can one know that one is conventional and the other is real?

One should formulate the following formal argument (*prayoga*): "The cognition I perceive is definitely not directed toward a real self (*ātman*), because it is intermingled with the characteristics of male, female, and so forth, just like the mind that arises directed toward the body and is intermingled with the characteristics of male and so forth."
Furthermore, the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*) and so forth do not take a real self as their object, because they possess an objective referent (*ālambana*), just like other states of mind.
Moreover, the object of the view of self is not a real self, because it is the object of a mind that perceives characteristics such as masculinity, just like the body and so forth.
Therefore, what you have said is empty and devoid of real meaning.
Furthermore, the Lokāyatikas speak thus:
"All phenomena and the self have the great elements as their nature; apart from the four great elements, there is no other distinct entity."

That is to say, the four great elements combine to form the self, as well as the various internal and external phenomena such as body and mind; these exist in the present life but do not exist in prior or subsequent lives.
Phenomena categorized as sentient beings are like bubbles and the like; they all arise from the various conditions of the present, neither coming from a previous life nor going to a future life.

With the conjunction and establishment of distinctions within the body-faculty as conditions, the minds of "male," "female," and so forth are initiated; these serve as the basis for experience and conjoin with the self, causing the appearance of male and other such characteristics within my own substance.
Based on this object of "self," the view of a self arises again, asserting that "I" am male, female, or neither.
Now one should question him:

"When you say that the transformation of the combination of the great elements constitutes the body-faculty and so forth, thus establishing the intrinsic nature of the internal great elements, is that [nature] male and so forth?"
"Is it not male and so forth?
He replied: "It is not the internal or external primary elements (*mahābhūta*), because their nature is without distinction.
Although the nature of the primary elements is no different internally or externally, there exists a differentiation in the established characteristics of shape."

Thus, all such forms known in the world, including the distinctions of intrinsic nature among males and so forth, arise solely from the conceptualization of one's own mind; they do not exist as such natures within any real entity.
If that is so, the verse says:
"If among the primary elements (mahābhūta) there are no males, females, or those who are neither;
how can the characteristics of male and so forth arise from these primary elements?"
The Commentary says:
If the intrinsic nature of the four great elements has no male, female, or non-dual [gender],
how can the characteristics of male and so forth arise?
On what basis do the minds of male and female arise?
Although the substratum of experience is conjoined with the self, how does it cause the appearance of male and other characteristics in me?
If the self possesses no characteristics of male and so forth, why does the view of self (ātma-dṛṣṭi) conceive of the self as being male, female, or neither?

If a thing lacks an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), then even when combined with another, it can never be made to transform into another characteristic, nor can it be made to give rise to a mind characterized by another; this is like a pure white object which, though combined with other colors, does not assume another characteristic nor produce another state of mind. One might argue that clear crystal (*sphaṭika*) and the like could serve as an analogy, since when combined with other colors they cease to be what they were and arise anew; however, this cannot be used as an analogy.

Therefore, it is certain that there is no real self (*ātman*) whose nature consists of the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) and which persists for a long duration, serving as the object of the view of self (*ātmadṛṣṭi*) characterized by such features as masculinity.
Furthermore, the proponents of the *Vyākaraṇa* heretics say:
"All phenomena and the self are all conjoined with the three characteristics."
By means of these three characteristics, one is able to give rise to three kinds of mental sounds.
What are the three characteristics? First is the male characteristic, which can produce all phenomena;
second is the female characteristic, which can extinguish all phenomena.
If it is claimed that the three [factors] are not of two natures and can maintain their own positions,
this is also incorrect.
Since the entities of all phenomena and the self do not possess the nature of the three characteristics, how could they give rise to the three types of mental states and sounds?

Furthermore, it cannot be said that they transform into the three characteristics by combining with something else, because the fault previously mentioned—that they would not be inseparable—would apply.

If the entities of the dharmas and the self do not themselves possess the three characteristics, yet transform into the three characteristics through combination with them, then since those three characteristics themselves lack any further three characteristics with which to combine, these three characteristics should not be "three characteristics," and they should be unable to give rise to the three kinds of mental states and sounds.

Furthermore, if these three characteristics, when conjoined with non-characteristics, could cause those non-characteristics to transform into characteristics, then when all phenomena and the self are conjoined with characteristics, they should cause the three characteristics to transform into non-characteristics. In that case, the three kinds of mental states and sounds would ultimately be unable to arise.

Furthermore, as for the functional distinctions of these three characteristics, they are mutually contradictory and must necessarily not coexist; how then could a single entity possess all three designations?
For example, regarding an object such as a horn, it is commonly known in the world that it is designated by the three terms "male," "female," and "neither," which are not two [but three].

Furthermore, if the functional capacities of the three characteristics within a single entity could coexist despite being mutually contradictory, then all entities should possess all three characteristics, and one should not perceive differences among sounds as they actually appear.

Furthermore, if these three characteristics were substantially existent, they could only depend upon that which exists and not upon that which does not exist; in that case, the three terms would fail to be all-encompassing. How then can we observe the various linguistic expressions found in different dialects?
There are phenomena where existence is absent and phenomena where non-existence is present; since these are directly perceived objects, they cannot be denied.
If there were three sounds despite the absence of the three characteristics, then this would have to be the case everywhere.
Furthermore, it is logically untenable to correlate these three characteristics with arising, abiding, and ceasing.
This is because when a man dies and a woman is born, these are not the deaths and births of two distinct entities, as is clearly observed in the world.
Moreover, these three characteristics possess no separate substantial reality, as will be extensively demonstrated later.

Therefore, one merely follows conventional linguistic usage to speak of the distinctions among the three genders—male and so forth—but there do not exist separately as real entities these three characteristics.

The non-Buddhists (bāhyaka) cling to the existence of these three characteristics, which they rely upon as the objective referent of the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*) regarding a real self; this is inverted cognition (*viparyāsa-jñāna*).
The followers of the Inner Way (ādhyātmika) do not cling to them, and thus they are free from inversion.

You should not, when engaging in correct discernment with one who is free from error, establish as an authoritative standard a perverted cognition that takes the view of self as its object and realizes a truly existent self.
Furthermore, regarding this view of self: is it that one clings to a self by following the characteristics of a self, or does one cling to a self by following one's own internal cognition?
If it were by following the characteristics of a self, it should be called right view.
If it were to follow self-awareness, it should not take the self as its object.
Furthermore, regarding the first case, the verse says:
"You, the self, and others are not the self; Therefore, the self has no fixed characteristic."
The treatise says:

If the self-characteristic of the self within your own body exists identically within all other bodies, and you give rise to the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*) in accordance with that self-characteristic, why does this single perception not take all [selves] as its object?
Since there is no single perception that takes all selves as its object, we know that the view of self does not follow the characteristic of a self.
If the self-characteristic within your own body were different from the self-characteristic within other bodies, then that which you consider a self would be non-self for others,
and that which others consider a self would be non-self for you.

Thus, this characteristic of a self is not determinate; since there is no determinate characteristic, there is no determinate nature. When nature and characteristics are indeterminate, they are neither real nor permanent. How, then, can one cling to a self as being truly existent and eternally abiding?

Furthermore, one may formulate the following formal argument: The view of self regarding one's own body does not arise in accordance with the specific characteristics (svalakṣaṇa) of a self, because it does not take as its object the production of another self’s specific characteristics, just like other cognitions that take various objects as their conditions.
Furthermore, one's own self should not serve as the object-condition for the arising of the view of a self, because you admit that it is a self, just like the self in another’s body.

Moreover, all views of a self certainly do not take a self as their object, because the objects of self and other mutually possess existence and non-existence, just like the cognitions that apprehend blue, yellow, and so forth.
Furthermore, the object of the view of "self" or "non-self" does not exist at all, because it is not subsumed under any other existing phenomena, just like the horns of a rabbit and the like.
Moreover, the self is not of the nature of a real self, because it is an object of knowledge, just like all other phenomena.

Therefore, my vision does not take a real self as its object; all those things conceived as a self lack any real nature or characteristic. They are not objects of perception for any wise person, yet fools alone constantly and deeply delight in them, just as the objects of a diseased eye are certainly not truly existent.
Therefore, one cannot use the object of the view of self to prove that this self truly exists and is permanent.
As for the second [position], the verse says:
"Is it not the case that, regarding what is impermanent, one falsely discriminates it as a self?"
The Commentary states:

If one who adheres to a self based on their own perception were to do so, would they not merely be taking the impermanent body and so forth as their object, and through false discrimination, grasping them as a real self?

Why is this so? We see directly in the world that, based merely on the body and other such factors, one falsely discriminates according to the distinctions of successive states and conditions, conceiving: "I am fat," "I am thin," "I am superior," "I am inferior," "I am bright," "I am dark," "I am suffering," or "I am happy."
It is possible for things such as the body to be impermanent; however, a permanent and real self possesses no such distinctions.

By this inference, one knows that all views of a self lack a real self as their objective referent; they take only false things such as the body as their objects, arising in accordance with the awakening-intelligence of one's own deluded conceptualization, just like the inverted grasping of a rope in the dark as a snake.

Furthermore, just as in the world people engage in false conceptualization, grasping at the existence of things such as sky-flowers or a second moon, they must first have seen some small instance in the world before they can subsequently grasp that such things exist.

My view that there is a self is likewise so: first, one takes as an object the phenomena of the five aggregates of clinging which arise and perish, and only subsequently does one determinately grasp at a real self.
It is also like the false objects in a dream, which are constructed through conceptualization based on what was previously seen.

The view of a self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*) regarding objects is likewise: first one takes the aggregates (*skandha*) as an object, and subsequently, through their conjunction, one engages in false conceptualization.
Furthermore, there are briefly two types of the view of a self:
first, the innate (*sahaja*), and second, the discriminative (*vikalpita*).

The innate view of self has existed since beginningless time; by the power of internal causes, it is always present with the body. It arises spontaneously without depending on false teachings or erroneous discrimination, and is therefore called "innate."
This, moreover, is of two kinds:

the first is the constant continuity, which resides in the seventh consciousness; taking the eighth consciousness as its object, it gives rise to the appearance of its own mind, which it then clings to as "self," and this is termed the view of self (ātma-dṛṣṭi).

The second is intermittent; it resides in the sixth consciousness and, taking the five appropriated aggregates as its object—either collectively or individually—it gives rise to the mental image of itself and clings to it as a self, which is termed the view of self (ātmadṛṣṭi).
These two types of self-view are both innate and subtle, making them difficult to sever; only through the repeated cultivation of the superior contemplation of non-self can they be eliminated.

As for the conceptualized self-view, because it arises due to the power of external conditions in the present world and does not coexist with the body, it must await false teachings and false discrimination before it can arise; therefore, it is called "conceptualized."
This also has two types:

first, taking the characteristics of the aggregates as taught by false teachings as an object, one gives rise to a mental image within one's own mind and discriminates it as a self; this is called the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*).

Second, taking the characteristics of a self as taught by false teachings as an object, one gives rise to a mental image within one's own mind and discriminates it as a self; this is called the view of self.

These two types of conceptualized view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*) are coarse and easily severed; they are eliminated as soon as the initial manifestation of the noble truths (*ārya-satya-abhisamaya*) occurs.

Regarding all such views of self described above: while the aggregates (*skandha*) as external objects may sometimes exist or not exist, the aggregates as internal objects always exist. Therefore, all views of self are false attachments that take the conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) of the impermanent aggregates as their objective referent and falsely conceive of them as a self.
Because the modes of the various aggregates arise from conditions, they exist as illusory phenomena;
because the self grasped through delusion does not arise from conditions, it definitely does not exist.
Therefore, the Sūtra says:
“Bhikṣus, you should know that all views of a self held by the śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas of the world arise entirely in dependence upon the five aggregates of clinging.

Furthermore, one should now inquire: for those who are like the blind, devoid of the principle of non-self, what loss have they suffered that they must insistently conceptualize and stubbornly cling to a self?
If all phenomena were empty and devoid of self, both saṃsāra and nirvāṇa would be lost. Why is this so?

Because it is due to the existence of a self that those lacking wisdom take pleasure in and cling to saṃsāra; they first create wholesome and unwholesome karmas that can summon results, and subsequently experience the desirable or undesirable fruits produced by them.

All those who possess wisdom and rejoice in Nirvana first contemplate the torment and oppression of the fires of suffering within birth and death, thereby giving rise to a mind of weary detachment; only thereafter do they abandon evil, diligently cultivate all that is wholesome, and attain true liberation.

All of this is accomplished by means of the self; the self is the agent and the self is the experiencer. Being oppressed by suffering, the self gives rise to the mind of renunciation, abandons evil, cultivates good, and realizes nirvāṇa.
If that were so, the verse says:
"The self would be identical to the body, undergoing change with every birth;
therefore, the principle that there is a self apart from the body which is eternally abiding is untenable."
The Commentary states:

If I were to first perform various types of karmic actions and only later experience various types of retributive fruits, then this self-entity would necessarily undergo transformation; for there must be a transformation in the cause, since there is a distinction in the fruit.
It is illogical that a result could be manifold while its cause remains unchanging; nor is it possible for such a cause to be non-constant.

That is to say, regarding the various births within the different realms and destinies—such as the hells—that you assert to be a "self," if this self were capable of producing various karmic fruits, then it should undergo transformation and change along with the body's successive births. It cannot be that the person Devadatta, whose body does not undergo such transformation, first performs both wholesome and unwholesome deeds and later experiences the two results of suffering and pleasure.

Therefore, my substance is identical to the body upon which it relies; because it can create and experience [suffering], it undergoes transformation from life to life. Since there is transformation, there is birth and cessation. How could that which is associated with birth and cessation be permanent?

Furthermore, the self as it is conceived does not exist apart from the body and other factors comprised within the category of sentient beings; because its essence is impermanent, it is like the body upon which it depends.

Therefore, the assertion that the self is permanent, exists apart from the body, and acts as both agent and experiencer throughout the cycle of birth and death is entirely unreasonable, for apart from the body and such, it possesses no distinct function.
Furthermore, how is it that this "I" can perform various karmas?

If it is claimed that it can perform them because it is conjoined with the body—on the grounds that this internal self possesses the quality of effort (*vīrya*), and by virtue of this quality, it unites with the body to initiate various actions.

Although this meritorious karma depends upon the physical body, it belongs to the self; just as when a stone or metal object is thrown against a tree branch, it causes the branch to shake due to its association with weight.
It may be argued that although this quality of virtue depends upon the branches of a tree, it actually belongs to the metal or stone;
however, this is not so, for such an action of movement can only exist in relation to a tangible object.
For you and me, it is not so; how could the union of the body be able to produce various karmas? Why is this?
The verse says:
“If a phenomenon is without contact, it is without movement;
therefore, the bodily action is not something created by a life-principle.
The commentary says:
All things capable of initiating movement and action are invariably not separated from contact with a tangible object.
Since I am without tangibility, even though I am conjoined with the body, how could I act as the cause for the activity of movement?
As for the time when [the wind] is grasped as it is held [to exist], there is no tactile contact; although it may be conjoined with the body, it cannot perform an action.

It is only the mind and mental factors that can produce wind, and only when the wind is conjoined with the body can an action be performed. Therefore, the reason (hetu) established is not subject to the fallacy of being inconclusive (anaikāntika).
This explains the proximate cause, not the indirect one.
Furthermore, that which can combine must possess spatial dimensions (*digbhāga*); the contact between two objects without any interval is called "combination.
Since the self (*ātman*) as you conceive it lacks spatial dimensions, how could it combine with the body to produce karma?
One cannot falsely claim that because I possess spatial dimensions, I must therefore possess a real capacity for arising and performing functions;
otherwise, one would have to admit that by metaphorically calling water "fire," there must truly be a burning action of actual fire.

The various phenomena are conventionally designated by the person who speaks them; it is not because of any distinction in the speaker that the nature of the phenomena being taught undergoes transformation.
That the nature of phenomena is fixed has already been fully discussed above.
In the root verse, the absence of "contact" (*sprṣṭi*) indicates the absence of spatial parts (*digbhāga*).
The absence of "movement" (*calana*) indicates the absence of the sense of conjunction (*saṃyoga*).
Furthermore, only that which possesses movement itself is capable of moving another.

Just as gold, stone, and the like must themselves possess motion before they can act as causes to move the branches of a tree, since I am devoid of motion and lack physical form or obstruction, how could I act as a cause to move that upon which I depend?

Just as gold, stone, and the like in a state of non-motion do not encounter resistance—demonstrating their lack of physical form or obstruction—and because they lack physical form or obstruction they themselves lack motion, so too one who is without agitation demonstrates that he is not a cause of motion.
If this so-called "immovable self" (ātman) lacks even the power to move a single hair, how much less could it create karma to be called an "agent"?
Since it does not create karma, there can be no fruit; if it does not experience the fruit, how can it be called an "experiencer"?

Furthermore, as for what you have said—that one who is oppressed by suffering gives rise to the mind of renunciation, abandons evil and cultivates good, and thereby attains liberation—this too is not so.
Why is this? The verse says:
"Since the self is eternally incapable of being harmed, why trouble myself with cultivating the causes for its protection?"
"Who fears eating a vajra, that they would grasp a staff to defend against all pests?
The commentary says:

Since the "self" you postulate is devoid of change, its essence is eternally abiding like empty space and cannot be harmed by any calamities or sufferings; why then trouble yourself with the diligent cultivation of causes for protection?
This body is subject to decay, oppressed by suffering, and defiled by sin; it must necessarily be guarded.
What wise person, knowing that a diamond-like object cannot be destroyed, would fear its being consumed and lead a following with weapons to defend it against woodworms?
Only a fool would act for the sake of such things as these; objects that are subject to decay and destruction should be guarded with care.
If you think that because life can be harmed, I too should be harmed accordingly—[you are mistaken].
This is also not the case; since the self is eternal, it should not be subject to harm.

Furthermore, your reckoning that life is a conjunction of three things—namely, body, self, and mind—has already been refuted, because the self and the body cannot be conjoined as they lack spatial dimensions.

According to your conception, the various qualities such as form lack the meaning of combination; furthermore, that which is combined has no distinct intrinsic nature, but exists merely as spatial parts arising without interval.
Since there is no separate entity, what could possibly be harmed?
If this [self] were subject to harm, it would necessarily follow its basis; yet since the basis is eternal, how could it be harmed?
Furthermore, even if life were taken, why should that cause me any affliction?

Since you conceive of the self as eternal and unimpeded—like the great void which cannot be harmed by cold, heat, wind, rain, frost, or hail—how could such a nature of the self be afflicted by suffering?

Furthermore, the nature of the self as you conceive it is immutable and undergoes no change from beginning to end; even if it were freed from all evils, what would be added to it such that it could be called "liberated"?
Is it not the case that wholesome dharmas increase at this stage?
If the nature of the self is eternal, what benefit is there in the increase of virtue?

Since the essence of the self as you conceive it is eternal and undergoes no change, other phenomena may arise, yet they neither increase nor diminish it; thus, liberation would be of no use to such a self.
Therefore, to cling to the self as permanent and unchanging results in the loss of both saṃsāra and nirvāṇa;
if there is emptiness and no-self, both matters are established.
