2. The Remainder of the Second Chapter, "Refuting the Self. Furthermore, some say:

"If there were no self, then since the mind and other factors perish immediately after arising, the cognition that recollects past lives—remembering that 'such-and-such was my name'—would be this very same self; yet this [recollection] should not exist."
Why is this? Because the past and the present are different.
The world does not perceive a past body as being the "I" of the present; therefore, there must certainly exist a permanent referent for the notion that arises when one says, "That is I."

This is also not the case. I have already explained previously that although cause and effect are distinct, they are conventionally treated as one within a continuum; based on this conventional unity, one may say that "what was in the past is what exists now.
Furthermore, it is said in verse:
"If one has recollection of a former birth, One would then claim that the self is permanent."
"Having already seen the traces of the past, the body too should likewise abide eternally.
The Treatise says:

If the recollection of former births relies upon similar characteristics, and one sees the past as resembling the present—taking the present to be the past—one then claims that there is a self which is both unitary and eternal.

Since one perceives the present body as resembling its prior state, and because the scars appear similar to those of the past, one might claim that the past is the present; by this logic, the body should also be admitted to be permanent and unitary.

This demonstrates that for commonly known distinct objects, even though they are conventionally designated as non-different based on a continuum, one cannot therefore infer the existence of a self that is unitary and permanent simply because there is no perceived difference in their characteristics.

Furthermore, when one recollects matters such as the suffering and pleasure of a past body, one realizes that what was "now" is now "past," and thus impermanent; by this analogy, one should also know that although the "self" (ātman) is said to be no different between the present and the past, it is nonetheless not permanent.

Furthermore, although there is a difference in essence between the present and the past, because the wisdom of the past apprehended its object, it possessed a superior capacity to infuse the foundational consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*). Consequently, when conditions arise, a power of recollection manifests in association with it, appearing as an image resembling the object of the past; this is what is called "recalling events of former lives."

Although there is no self that is unitary or eternal, there exists the cognition that recollects events from past lives. This is evident in the world when, for example, one consumes elixirs of the immortals: after consuming them for a long time, although the substance of the medicine no longer remains, it leaves behind an induced, superior efficacy which later matures to eliminate disease and prolong life; yet, in this process, there is no self.
This case is also like that: if there were only mindfulness, who would be the mindful one?
Nor can it be said that mindfulness itself is the mindful one, because both alternatives are free from fault.
Even if a self were to exist, who would be the one to think?
It cannot be said that the self is the thinker, because the self as it is grasped does not possess the characteristic of cognition (*jñāna*).

If it is argued that although the essence of the self is not cognitive by nature, it can still possess thought because it is conjoined with volition (*cetanā*), then at the time this self is conjoined with volition, there must be taking and rejecting in relation to itself and others.
If there is grasping or rejecting, it is impermanent;
if there is no grasping or rejecting, it is no different from what preceded it, and thus even when conjoined with thought, there is no thinking.
Therefore, this self is not a thinker.
Furthermore, it is said in verse:
"If the self were to unite with volition and thereby become the thinker, then volition itself would not be volition; therefore, the self is not permanent."
The Commentary states:

If the self as it is conceived were not by nature volition, yet becomes volitional through conjunction with volition—just as a crystal is not blue by nature, yet appears blue through conjunction with something blue.
In that case, because this volition would be conjoined with a non-volitional self, it should become non-volitional.
If one argues that although volition is conjoined with a non-volitional self, it does not abandon its own nature and thus does not become non-volitional; [we reply:]...
I, too, should be like this: although conjoined with volition, it does not abandon its own nature nor does it become the act of thinking.

When a crystal gem is joined with blue or other colors, a distinct entity arises throughout its entire substance, and thus a different color is perceived; it is not that the original nature itself transforms into another characteristic.

Because the substance of crystal is clear and moist, when it comes into contact with other colors, a distinct form arises throughout its entire body; this form, which resembles the original, is called the "substratum" (bimba), yet in reality, the fundamental nature of the crystal does not transform into those other colors.

Furthermore, since the crystal at the beginning and the crystal at the end are distinct entities due to the difference in their characteristics—just as with blue, yellow, and so forth—the self should likewise be so; how then could it be eternal?
Moreover, it would consequently lack the nature of a real self, and by this, [the doctrine of a permanent self] is refuted.
That treatise presents alternative explanations, stating that some say:

"The nature of crystal is pure and does not obstruct the eyes; when it comes into contact with other colors, each remains in its own distinct location, neither abandoning its original characteristics nor assuming the characteristics of others."
Whether one attends to it or not, one again perceives its original appearance as well as the colors adjacent to it.
Furthermore, some say:

"The nature of crystal is transparent like a clear mirror; when other colors come into contact with it, their reflections appear within it. The observer’s eyes become confused and they claim that the crystal has become those other colors, yet in reality, this jewel remains unchanged as before."
All of these are irrational, as they contradict inference (*anumāna*).
If it is seen by the eye to be like lightning or a lamp, how could its essence and characteristics remain unchanged throughout its prior and subsequent states?

Furthermore, since the existence or non-existence of the characteristics of the conceived self (*ātman*) before and after the arising of thought is not determinate, it would follow that the self is identical to thought, which arises and perishes moment by moment.

Furthermore, if you claim that volition (cetanā) becomes [the experiencer] through conjunction with volition, then it should likewise become pleasure or pain through conjunction with pleasure and pain.

If this were not the case, then even when conjoined with pleasure and pain, it would not relinquish its prior state; like space or rain falling on fire, it would undergo no change and thus could not be the experiencer.
Therefore, it is said in verse:
“I am conjoined with pleasure and so forth; In various ways, I am like pleasure and so forth.
Because I am like pleasure and so forth, I am neither one nor permanent.”
The treatise states:

Since the intrinsic natures and characteristics of pleasure and so forth are mutually contradictory, if a manifold self were to unite with them, it would necessarily assume a manifold nature, just as pleasure and the others do.

Therefore, this self-nature (*ātmatva*) should be like pleasure and so forth: it would be distinct for each body, neither unitary nor permanent, and like pleasure and so forth, it would not be the true nature of the self.

Consequently, it is illogical to claim that there exists a separate self-entity apart from cognition (*cetanā*), which, by being conjoined with cognition, shares its characteristics and is thus called the "rememberer" (*smāraka*).

Mindfulness (smṛti) is that which, at the very moment its characteristic mark arises, resembles the object being recollected; although it lacks a sovereign agent, it appears to possess an activity and is thus conventionally designated as "mindful. Its distinct discernment and recognition is what is termed mindfulness.
There is no fault in dividing the meaning of a single dharma into two.
Furthermore, the Sāṃkhya non-Buddhists speak thus:
"Volition is the self, and its nature is eternal. Thus, this self of volition exists as a distinct substance and characteristic apart from the mind and mental factors, and it is difficult to discern.

Why is this so? The essential nature and characteristics of the self (*ātman*) are not objects of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), because its specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) is not commonly known by the world;
nor are they objects of inference (*anumāna*), because the characteristic of "thinking" resides solely in the self and is not shared with anything else.

Now, as for inference (*anumāna*), it is the knowledge of a common characteristic (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) through analogy; that is, by means of a general resemblance between the effect and so forth and the cause and so forth, one infers that the latter generally exists. However, because the "self" (*ātman*) postulated [by the opponent] is unique (*asādhāraṇa*), there is no similar instance (*sapakṣa*).
Since neither a similar instance nor a dissimilar instance exists— because there is nothing to serve as a counterpart—
it follows that the principle of a self is in reality non-existent.
Even if one were to concede the existence of a self whose nature is volition (*cetanā*), one must then pose this inquiry:
In this way, is this nature of the self established through the power of another,
or is it established through its own power?
If it were established through the power of another, it would be impermanent, like visual consciousness and so forth.
If volition were established through its own power, it would not depend on conditions, like space and so forth.
To clarify this meaning, another verse is spoken:
"If one claims that the self and volition are permanent, This is a false attachment brought about by the assistance of conditions."
"If one says that fire is permanent, then it would not depend on fuel and so forth.
The treatise says:

Just as a phenomenon that has already arisen abides in its own specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), it never again relies upon causes or auxiliary conditions; for once it has arisen, it cannot arise yet again.

I, too, should be thus; since the essence of volition (*cetanā*) is eternal and its own characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) abides securely without depending on anything else for its establishment, why would it further require the assistance of transforming external conditions to transform that volitional self, so that it might experience and utilize various objects of enjoyment?
If it were not subject to transformation in dependence upon others, then there would be no auxiliary conditions for its being experienced.
If it were subject to transformation, it would necessarily be impermanent.

Just as fire in the world is impermanent by nature: if one pours ghee or oil over the fuel, grass, and so forth, and throws them into the fire, the flames increase and blaze; if this is not done, the intensity of the fire diminishes. Furthermore, if the fuel and such were absent, fire would not exist.
Since fire depends upon fuel and such conditions, how could it be permanent?
Since the self likewise relies upon conditions, how could it possibly be eternal?
If you should further say:

In my treatise it is said that although the essence of such a conceived self is eternal, it is manifested through the conjunction of the sense faculties and their objects, just as jars, basins, and the like are revealed by light.

Why is this so? It is because the faculty of thought cannot observe by itself; it must depend upon the transformation of causes and conditions corresponding with one another to become manifest. Therefore, although it relies upon conditions, the self remains eternally abiding.
Such a defense only increases the fault.
Why is this? One does not perceive that things such as jars, though manifested by conditions, possess an eternal essence.

Although *tathatā* and *nirvāṇa* may be clearly manifested, this is based on conventional truth (*saṃvṛti*) and not according to ultimate truth (*paramārtha*). Within ultimate truth, there are no conceptual proliferations (*prapañca*) such as distinctions between permanence and impermanence or clarity and lack of clarity; for [these] are manifested by the objects of thought and the grasping self. Therefore, their nature must be impermanent, just like a jar or similar objects.
If you further argue that although the "I" lacks volition during the state of concealment, it nonetheless possesses functional capacity, and that such capacity is not distinct from volition—
then since there is no volition, how can there be functional capacity?
Furthermore, the function of volition must necessarily depend upon the substance of volition; since that substance does not exist, what could the function depend upon?

Moreover, when [the self] is latent, it takes volition as its nature; since volition does not exist, the self is therefore non-existent. How, then, can you say that while the self of volition is absent during the latent state, it nonetheless possesses functional capacity?

If you claim that when [the self] is hidden it is not a thinker, you must now explain what the characteristics of this self are. If the self were established without its characteristics being explained, then all false attachments would likewise be established.
Such logical investigations have already been fully explained above.
Furthermore, according to your own tenet, the various potencies and that which possesses these potencies are of one nature.
If this were so, then the possessor of the potency would not be the substratum of the potency, because their nature is one and the same.
Furthermore, because there is no capacity [to act] at this stage, one cannot say that the capacity relies upon the capacity itself; for it is logically contradictory for something to act upon itself.
Nor can it be said that the capacity has no basis, lest it follow that even the Supreme One (the *parama-śreṣṭha*) would likewise lack a basis and thus be without fault.

Why is this so? If the functional capacity of volition were to exist independently without any basis, then the functional capacity of transformation would likewise have to exist independently; why, then, would the *parama* (the Supreme) be required?
Furthermore, according to what you maintain, the functional capacity of the "thinking self" (manas) varies in infinite ways depending on its respective objects of experience.
Since you admit that it can be manifold, how can its essence be one?
For your school definitively maintains that the essence and the capacities are one.
In the world, there is not a single dharma whose essence does not simultaneously produce multiple effects. The phrase "not at different times" clarifies that they occur at one and the same time.
If a single dharma-essence could produce multiple effects at different times, its essence would necessarily be distinct [for each effect].
How is it that you maintain that a single self possesses multiple capacities over time and gives rise to manifold reflections?
Furthermore, why does this self, which is characterized by reflection, not simultaneously give rise to all the reflections that result in experience?
If it is claimed that volition must necessarily undergo transformation before it can arise, this is also not the case.
Why is it that the most excellent [consciousness], which possesses all functional capacities, does not instantaneously give rise to all transformations?

Because its supreme capacity is unimpeded, even if one were to grant that the supreme [principle] simultaneously gives rise to all transformative functions at a single moment, then this very supreme principle would necessarily undergo cessation; for its entire substance would be transformed, thereby losing its original nature.
Just as the Supreme Essence is so, so too must I be; for their natures are both eternal and endowed with all capacities.
Thus, your position that when [the self] is in a state of concealment it possesses all functional capacities yet lacks consciousness entails many faults from which you can ultimately not escape.
Furthermore, there are others who offer this defense as an expedient means:
"I am the thinker; thought is my function, not something that perishes when its activity ceases.

It is observed that while the functions of the eyes and so forth perish, their substance remains even in the absence of the activity of illuminating forms and the like. Therefore, although the function of thinking is absent during the state of concealment, the thinker exists; thus, the substance of the self is not non-existent."
This is also not the case. If the self associated with the latent state were distinct from volition (*cetanā*), it would again incur the same fault as before.
One might ask: "Is there not a lack of distinction between the activity and the agent, since their substance is not different?"
Your argument is much like that of a deluded elephant bathing: intending to avoid a minor fault, you instead incur a grave defilement.
Since there is no difference between my thinking and the functioning of my body, when the thinking ceases, the body of the self should likewise cease.
If you then consider that the self is definitely impermanent, you contradict your own tenet; how can this be called "rescuing the argument"?

Furthermore, regarding what you said—that we currently perceive that although the eyes and so forth lack the function of illuminating forms and the like, they nonetheless possess a substantial entity, and the self is likewise so—it is not correct.
This is also not the case; therefore, the next verse says:
"Just as with an object that has reached cessation, action does not exist therein.
The commentary states:

Just as it is capable of illuminating and cognizing the functions of form and so forth, up until their cessation, this consciousness constantly follows along to discern its own respective objects; by virtue of these functions, it is the very essence of consciousness.

If activity were to cease, the substance of consciousness would be non-existent; for the various faculties, such as the eye, would lack this function from the moment their continuity is severed until the end, because their intrinsic natures are distinct. Why is this so?
The intrinsic nature of the eye and so forth is not that of illumination and the like; therefore, when they cease, this [self] does not follow in cessation.

Since the eye and so forth have the nature of translucent matter (*rūpa-prasāda*) produced by them, and since your "self" has no distinct substance apart from thought, it is impossible for its substance to remain alone while thought ceases. Have you not stated that the self is characterized by thought? How then can you say that it has no substance apart from thought?
Although you have stated this previously, it is not reasonable. Why is that?
Because the volition and its function do not cease simultaneously; therefore, they must possess distinct entities.
My essence is not volition;
the faults [of this position] are as previously stated.
Since there is no distinct entity for its function, the previous objection recurs.

Furthermore, one reflects that the thinker and the act of thinking are established in mutual dependence; they are constituted only when both are present, for it is impossible for either to be lacking.
Whether the thinker and the act of thinking are identical or distinct, they inevitably incur the two faults previously mentioned.
Having thus explained it, there is another interpretation:

Just as the eyes and other [faculties] of another, up until their cessation, always possess an activity capable of producing distinct entities, you do not admit that such is the case for the activity of the "I" (ātman) as you conceive it.
The function of color and other objects upon which distinct entities depend is precisely the capacity of the eye and other faculties to produce consciousness with respect to their respective objects.

Although the various self-characteristics (svalakṣaṇa) manifested by the sense organs such as the eye—corresponding to the consciousnesses they produce—have no separate substantial entity apart from the causal consciousness, they nonetheless possess their own specific characteristics apart from the resultant consciousness.

You maintain that there is a self capable of producing volition, yet you do not allow for a distinct intrinsic nature apart from volition; therefore, this cannot be cited as a valid corroborative example.
Thus, the verse says:
"Therefore, the existence of a self without volition is logically untenable."
The Commentary states:
As for having distinct characteristics, because they are not of the same substance, one may say that when one ceases, the other remains.

However, since the function of volition (*cetanā*) and the agent of volition have no distinct characteristics, when volition ceases, the agent of volition must also cease. Therefore, your thesis that there exists a self devoid of volition cannot possibly be established through logical reasoning.
Furthermore, there are those who maintain that apart from thought (*cetanā*), there exists a real self (*ātman*) whose substance is all-pervading, yet only a single part of it generates thought.

They claim that first, one part of the self is conjoined with cognition (*jñāna*), which initiates a superior mental formation capable of producing thought; subsequently, another part of the self is conjoined with the mind (*manas*) to produce thought. Therefore, they argue, the aforementioned faults do not apply.
This is not reasonable; therefore, a verse is spoken:
“The mental sphere arises in one direction, Yet the thought is perceived in another place.
The commentary says:
If their locations were different, cause and effect could not be established.
We have never seen seeds and sprouts, for example, existing at a great distance from one another while still forming a causal relationship.

You maintain that a distinct, superior volition (*cetanā*) and mental formation (*saṃskāra*) first exist at a distance, conjoined with a self and wisdom, and through activities such as reciting scriptures and practicing crafts, they become skillful and leave an impression (*vāsanā*) within that self.
If, later, in another location and provided there are no obstructions, my self (ātman) conjoins with the mind to produce a present volition (cetanā),
then it is clear that cause and effect exist in different places.
Would this fault not be avoided on the grounds that the essence of the self conjoined with volition is not distinct [from the self]?

If that were so, then since all formations (*saṃskāra*) and other causes and effects would be conjoined with the self (*ātman*), their locations would necessarily be identical; thus, you would lose your own thesis that the essence of the self is omnipresent. [Furthermore,] one part [of the self] would be conjoined with cognition to give rise to volitional formations (*cetanā-saṃskāra*), while another part would be conjoined with the mind (*manas*) to produce manifest volition (*vijñapti-cetanā*).

If you further argue that it is like a bar of molten iron: although one end of the bar is first in contact with fire while the other end is not, because they constitute a single substance, the entire bar gradually melts away.
The same applies to the formations (*saṃskāra*) and cognition (*vijñāna*); although their places of arising differ, because the essence of the self (*ātman*) is one, cause and effect are established.
This is also not the case; therefore, the following verse says:
"Just as an iron bar melts away, the essence of the self should likewise undergo transformation and destruction."
The Commentary says:

It is like a bar of molten iron; one end of the bar first comes into contact with fire and immediately melts, and subsequently, as the heat spreads through it, the remaining parts away from the fire also melt.

In this way, the essence of the self first combines with cognition in one part to transform and produce the fruit of volition; subsequently, through the mutual communication of their powers, it combines with the mind in another location to transform and produce the fruit of volition.
If this were so, the essence of the self would necessarily be impermanent; how then can you falsely establish that the self is permanent?
Furthermore, your position that the self is designated as "the thinker" based solely on its limited capacity to produce volition (*cetanā*) is also incorrect. Therefore, the subsequent verse states:
"The volition is small like the measure of a thought, While the self is vast like space;
One should observe only its own specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), And then one will not perceive the volition."
The Commentary states:

You maintain that a portion of the self’s essence (ātman) conjoins with the mind and is thus able to produce volition (*cetanā*), and is therefore called the "volitional self"; whereas other portions of the self’s essence do not conjoin with the mind and, because they do not produce volition, are not called the "volitional self. Since the mind possesses resistance (*sapratigha*) and is subtle like an atom (*paramāṇu*), while the nature of the self is pervasive and vast like the realm of space, it follows that only a small portion of the self conjoins with the mind to give rise to volition, while its infinite remaining portions are devoid of thought. Therefore, one should regard the self according to its majority; one should not, based on a minor portion, view it as being the "volitional self."

Regarding the provisional establishment of names and conventions for its own essence: either it expresses the essence by relying on multiple characteristics, or it manifests its characteristics through being defiled by others. Since neither of these two cases applies to me as described above, I should not be designated by the name "thinker."

If you further argue that volition (*cetanā*) does not possess the characteristics of a self (*ātman*), and that volition is a quality (*guṇa*) while the self is a substance (*dravya*), and that these three natures—substance, quality, and action (*karman*)—are not mutually confused; [we reply:]...
Why is this impossible?
It is because you are unable to set aside conceptual thought and separately manifest the self-characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the self; therefore, it is impossible.

If you cannot separately manifest the self-characteristic of the self, you can ultimately never establish that the self possesses substantial reality. Since its self-characteristic is ultimately inexpressible, the "self" you have established is, in fact, no-self.

Furthermore, if you establish that the self is not volitional, you lose the defining characteristic of the self; because it is non-volitional, it would be like dharmas such as form, which are neither self nor volitional.

Moreover, since volition comes first, the various karmas produced by it would not belong to the self, which results in a contradiction, as they would then be incompatible with the volitions of both oneself and others.
I have no intentionality regarding that which is sought, and the causal factors do not meet by design; it would be like the case of the crow, the *eḍakā* plant, and the *udumbara* fruit.
Due to such numerous faults as these, I would be dispersed and destroyed, and could never achieve success.

Furthermore, there are others who, in a desperate attempt to avoid such a web of errors, do not allow that even a fraction of the self's essence gives rise to activity; instead, they maintain that the qualities which depend upon it pervade the entire self as their substratum.
This too is incorrect.

If virtue were pervasive throughout the self (*ātman*), then the conjunction of the sense faculties (*indriya*) and so forth would be useless, because pleasure and other sensations would exist even where the faculties are absent.

If you argue that this is not the case—that pleasure and so forth arise pervasively through the conjunction of one part of the self with the faculties, just as the power of a wick and other factors in a single location initiates the light of a lamp which pervades many places—[we reply: [this is untenable].
If that is so, the verse says:
"If my virtues were all-pervasive, why would others not receive them?
The commentary says:
If the self (*ātman*) and its attributes were both omnipresent, then the pleasure and other states of one person should be present in all selves; why then would the other selves not experience them?

It is better to admit that when a portion of the self conjoins with the mind, it is precisely in that location that suffering, pleasure, and so forth arise, which the self can then perceive; thus, there is no such fault.
If you further argue: "Whatever belongs to me belongs only to me; I alone can experience the pleasure and so forth of one person.
Although these qualities pervade all *ātman*s, they belong only to one and are not connected to others; how then could I cause another to experience my own suffering or pleasure?"
In the world, it is commonly observed that all material wealth can only be enjoyed by its owner and not used by others.
This may be the case where there is a distinction between individuals;
however, since they are living together as one, why should it be problematic for them to enjoy it in common?

If objects located in the same place do not belong to oneself, although one lacks the autonomy to take them up or set them aside for personal use, who could possibly prevent one from seeing, touching, or utilizing them?
We observe in the world that regarding objects not belonging to oneself, if they are in the same location, there is no obstruction to seeing or touching them.

Since suffering, pleasure, and so forth are now devoid of form and substance, they can only be seen and touched, and cannot be grasped or discarded; therefore, your argument does not constitute a valid defense.

If you claim that another self cannot experience the suffering and pleasure of others due to the presence of obscuration—just as in the world, although things may coexist, one with unobstructed vision can see them, whereas one whose vision is obstructed perceives nothing—[this remains unproven].

I am also like this: because I have no obscuration regarding my own pleasure and pain, I am able to experience the pleasure and pain of others; yet, although we dwell together, because they possess obscurations, they cannot experience them.
If that is so, does the obscuration of darkness occur only partially?
He says no, because it occurs pervasively.
Is this obscuration located in a different place from that self?
Again, it is said: "No, because there is no distinction in their locus.
If that were so, the verse says:
"Since it is stated that the obstructors are pervasive, they should not obstruct only one [of the two]."
The treatise says:
Within a single location of darkness, there are infinite selves. Since the location is not distinct, if one self is obstructed by it, why would the others not be?

Who could believe that the characteristic of darkness is non-distinct while the characteristics of the selves are identical, such that the location of the obstructor and the obstructed is likewise non-distinct?

The same principle applies to the pleasure and other sensations one experiences: there would then be no distinction between those with obstructions and those without, nor between those that are experienced and those that are not; everything would be identical.
Furthermore, we do not observe any external darkness in the world such as the internal distinctions of darkness you have postulated.

Although the previous argument held that virtue does not pervade its substratum, the claim that my own substance (*ātman*) is all-pervasive and thus capable of receiving [pleasure] by being conjoined with the virtues of others is subject to the same fault.

For do I not say that pleasure and the like must occupy the same location as the mind (*manas*) in order to be experienced? Therefore, there is no fault of experiencing the pleasure and so forth of others.
You outsiders speak according to your own subjective opinions; words spoken according to such opinions cannot accord with correct principle.
It is not the case that where an object can be illuminated within the light of a lamp, yet this very lamp-light fails to illuminate it.
I, too, should be thus; why then do you not accept it?
If you further argue that although the entire substance of the self is all-pervasive, one's own pleasure and so forth are not shared with others.

Why is this? Because qualities such as pleasure arise through the power of karma; this karmic power receives its fruit based on what is dharma and what is adharma. Thus, this principle is established.
Such expedients are of no benefit to the principle; their faults are identical to those previously mentioned, and thus they fail to establish a valid defense.

When such a proponent employs logical reasoning for investigation, having been preceded by false views, the thesis that a self is permanent, omnipresent, the agent, and the experiencer cannot be established.
Furthermore, some say that the three qualities—sattva, rajas, and tamas—are non-conscious agents, while the self is non-active yet capable of experiencing.
To refute this argument, the following verse states:
"If virtue were not volition, how could it create anything?
It would be like madness; being accompanied by delusion, nothing would be accomplished."
The commentary states:
If the essence of the three qualities (*guṇas*) as you conceive them were devoid of thought, how could they act as a self (*ātman*) to create the myriad things?
If they were originally without thought yet produced something, in what way would they differ from madness and chaos?
Even if he were like one who is insane, what fault would there be?

If he were like one who is insane, he would be unable to create for me the objects required for my use; for we have never seen a foolish or mad servant or craftsman able to provide a master with things according to his wishes.
Furthermore, if those virtuous ones were unskilled in the tasks they undertake, they would be like fools who are unable to accomplish their work, such as carving or painting.
If one possesses skillful means, why cannot one enjoy [the fruit] immediately for oneself?
To clarify this meaning, the verse further states:
"If one possesses virtue and is skilled at understanding, In constructing houses and other such things..."
Yet they do not know how to enjoy them; how could anything be more unreasonable than this!
The Commentary says:

If one were to say that these virtuous ones are like skilled artisans, who are able to perform difficult tasks with great proficiency and accomplish whatever is required, whether internal or external, without fail; yet—
Yet, one fails to properly comprehend the objects of enjoyment that are easily perceived;
how irrational this is!

Aside from merely guarding one’s own ignorance, who would ally themselves with such a view? These three qualities are likewise skillful regarding the objects of enjoyment, for they constitute its very essence, just as they are skillful in all their various functions.
This demonstrates that since both the agent and the experiencer are established based on the three *guṇas*, it is unnecessary to postulate a separate self (*ātman*) as the experiencer.

If one were to argue that although the *pradhāna* (primordial nature) is not sentient by essence, it nevertheless fashions the myriad things through the power of conditions in order to allow the sentient self to enjoy them at will—just as grasses and trees, though lacking sentience, produce various flowers and fruits through the force of karma for human enjoyment—[the response follows].
If that were so, the activity of the Primal Nature (prakṛti), being devoid of volition, would be like a flower or fruit that does not cease even after its enjoyment has been completed.
However, for those things that produce fruits through volition, the fruit comes to an end once its enjoyment is sufficient.
Prakṛti is not conscious, like external grass and trees;
furthermore, it is eternal and indestructible. [The opponent argues: "Once I have finished enjoying it, my activity ceases"—this logic is incorrect.

If one says that the three *guṇas* are by nature intelligent and that whatever they perform is without lack of skill, while I, as the divine lord (*puruṣa*), am capable of excellent reflection, causing them to act and freely experiencing the results—claiming that those three *guṇas* understand the *puruṣa*, and only when there is a need do they give rise to cognition and wisdom, subsequently initiating activity to transform and create the myriad things, and thus I reflect upon my own sovereign enjoyment—[this is untenable].
Your statement merely restates your own school's tenet and is of no use whatsoever in the context of this debate.
Furthermore, according to your own position, the self possesses volition, and the qualities possess cognition and wisdom.

Thus, it is difficult to discern the distinction between the nature and characteristics of these two types [of consciousness], both of which are capable of experiencing and cognizing their respective objects; therefore, one should not falsely discriminate with an awakened intelligence, conceiving that the faculty of volition (*cetanā*) as a quality resides within a self.
Furthermore, the *guṇas* would lose their own specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) of cognition and wisdom, because they lack volition, just like form (*rūpa*) and other such entities.
As for your claim that the three *guṇas* cognize the *puruṣa*, and that consciousness (*buddhi*), volition, and activity arise only when there is a need from the *puruṣa*: [this is untenable].

This is not the case; within the state of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), there is no activity of cognitive discernment (*buddhi*). Who, then, could know that my mind has a need? If cognitive discernment had already arisen at that time, why wait for it to know my intention before arising?
If, at that time, discerning intelligence (*buddhi*) has not yet arisen, how could the three qualities (*guṇas*) first arise within the Great One (*mahat*)?
If the essence of the Great One were to arise spontaneously without discerning intelligence, then all things should likewise arise spontaneously.
Therefore, this cognitive awareness has no function whatsoever regarding either the effect of transformation or the cause of intrinsic nature.
Others further establish an inference as a defense, stating:
"Cognitive awareness is not volition, because it is impermanent."
All things that are impermanent are devoid of volition, just like form (*rūpa*) and so forth.
To say this is to contradict one's own position.

It is through mental deliberation and discrimination that the name "awakened wisdom" (*buddhi*) is obtained; if there were no deliberation, it would not be awakened wisdom. How, then, can you claim that awakened wisdom is devoid of volition?

Furthermore, it has already been stated previously that awakening-wisdom (*buddhi*) and mental deliberation (*manasikāra*) both cognize their own objects as being identical in nature and characteristics; how then could awakening-wisdom be devoid of mental deliberation?
Therefore, your statement contains the fault of self-contradiction.

Furthermore, there is the fallacy that the cause of impermanence cannot be established; for regarding the meaning of arising and ceasing, this is not admitted by our own school, and as for the interpretation based on the meaning of concealment and manifestation, it is not established in other schools.
If you say that the meaning of "cause" should not be differentiated but should be stated only in general terms, [the same fault remains].
This is also not the case.
If the individual and the collective are both established, one may speak of them in terms of the collective;
just as when individual instances are seen, the collective is manifested as their cause.
Since the individual [parts] cannot be established, upon what could the whole be based?
Furthermore, it is based on activity that one speaks of concealment and manifestation; it is by relying on this that the meaning of "impermanence" is established as a reason.
You establish that my "thinking" (ātma-manas) also possesses activity, and thus your reason suffers from the fallacy of being inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).
Furthermore, your attempt to establish that the essence of cognition (buddhi) is distinct from the self (ātman), or that the self is distinct from cognition, cannot be established.
Such categories are not commonly accepted; therefore, your proposed position lacks a valid basis for proof.
Therefore, the claim that "I" am the thinker who experiences and the three *guṇas* are the agents who act does not establish its meaning.

Furthermore, there are those who maintain that the essence of the self (*ātman*) is eternal, all-pervading, and unobstructed, and that it is capable of creating all things, thus designating it as the "agent."
This is also not the case, because it contradicts the logical meaning.
If you maintain that the self possesses the activity of motion and is thus called an "agent," then there would be the fallacies of impermanence, material obstruction, and non-pervasiveness.
It is observed that only that which is impermanent, non-pervasive, and obstructed possesses the capacity for motion;
for a capacity for motion has never been seen in that which is permanent, pervasive, and unobstructed.
If the self as you conceive it were devoid of activity, how could it be designated as an agent?
Therefore, one must necessarily admit that it possesses activity.
If that were so, one would have to admit that the essence of the self is impermanent, obstructive, and non-pervasive.
To clarify this meaning, the following verse says:
"Where there is activity, there is impermanence; where there is empty penetration, there is no activity."

The treatise says: The power of the wind element (*vāyu-dhātu*) is capable of producing motion; that is to say, by means of the wind element, conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) flow and circulate, arising in successive locations without interruption. According to conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), this is called "motion," and based on this motion, one speaks of an "agent. This [agent] necessarily does not transcend the nature of being obstructed and impermanent; that which is obstructed and impermanent is not omnipresent.
Your own school also admits that atoms possess movement; since they are obstructive and non-pervasive, this has already been refuted previously.
To maintain that they are permanent is to manifest their impermanence; therefore, the inference is free from the fallacy of inconclusiveness (*anaikāntika*).

If it is argued that because our school does not admit that the internal self-substance possesses the cause of motion, the reason [of the opponent] is unestablished, this is also not the case, for we must necessarily admit it.
If there were no motion, how could it be called an "agent"?

Although you do not admit that the term "action" (karma) refers to movement while maintaining that there is an agent, you must say that [the agent] depends on movement—just as one speaks of the coming and going of a flame—and furthermore, you must necessarily admit that the self possesses activity.
If one were to entirely deny that the self possesses any activity, then the self would be non-existent, just like a rabbit's horns.
To clarify this point, the following verse states:
"Lacking activity, it is identical to non-existence."
The commentary states:

If, as you maintain, the self possesses an activity that can function as an agent and serves as the basis for its designation, then if it lacks such activity, it would be equivalent to non-existence; upon what, then, could one say that the self is an agent?
Since it lacks functional activity, it should not be called "existent. If you argue that the term "existent" does not depend on functional activity,
but rather depends on having the same nature and being associated with that [nature], then...
This is also not the case.

Worldly wise ones establish names and conventions based on entities that possess utility; if there is no utility, then there is no entity. Without utility and without an entity, upon what could a name be established?
Why do you speak of a "self" that acts?
If you do not understand the basis upon which such speech relies, you should simply observe the discipline of silence; why must you insist on asserting that there is a self that acts?
There are those who say that an entity possessing functional utility is what is conventionally accepted by worldly wisdom, and you must certainly conform to this.
If you insist that the self lacks functional activity, then it should be regarded as an absolute non-entity, just as is commonly agreed upon.
By this inference, the self is simply non-existent; why, then, do you not delight in the principle of emptiness and selflessness?
To clarify this meaning, the following verse says:
"Why do you not rejoice in selflessness?"
The commentary states:
Just as past phenomena lack the functional capacity to produce other phenomena and thus possess no intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*),
so too must it be for the self (*ātman*) by virtue of this same principle.

Since there is no function such as burning or moving that is commonly accepted by the world, nor any function such as coming and going that you yourself accept, it follows that [fire] would lack an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).

In this way, the nature of the self (*ātman*) is entirely non-existent; this not only accords with reason but also accords with your own mind. Why, then, do you not joyfully seek the principle of emptiness and selflessness?
The reason for this lack of faith is simply that the power of false attachments arising from ignorance is so strong.
If you argue that although the self has no distinct function, it is nonetheless called the "agent" because it serves as the object for the arising of the mind that conceives a self, [we reply:]...
This too is flawed; it has already been extensively refuted previously, yet it is brought forward again.
Furthermore, the self cannot be the object of the view of a self, because it lacks functional activity, just like a rabbit's horn.

These [notions] such as the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*) do not likewise take a self as their object, because they possess an objective referent (*ālambana*), just like the mind that takes form (*rūpa*) as its object.

If a real self truly existed that could give rise to the view of self, how could this self—like a skillful magical artifice—manifest various appearances according to one's wishes, deceiving the world and causing the arising of various distinctions of the view of self?
To clarify this meaning, the following verse says:
"Either one contemplates the self as all-pervasive, or sees its measure as equal to the body,
or clings to it as being like an atom."
The commentary states:

A certain class of non-Buddhists (tīrthika) maintains that because the self experiences pleasure and pain while pervading all places, it is without physical form and lacks movement; thus, it cannot travel through birth and death in accordance with the body. Therefore, they know that the internal self pervades everything.
A certain class of non-Buddhists speaks thus:

"If the self were all-pervasive like space, it should not experience various forms of suffering and pleasure according to the body; it should be like the realm of space, without coming or going, its nature serene and not an agent or an experiencer."

Therefore, my nature should be like form and so forth; it is indeterminate in its dimensions according to the body upon which it relies, and although it lacks physical obstruction, it has a basis of reliance and undergoes various sufferings and pleasures in accordance with the body through transformation.

Although it contracts and expands according to its physical form, my essential nature is neither born nor extinguished; it is like a drop of oil upon water, which follows the breadth or narrowness of the water, contracting and expanding as it may, yet without increase or decrease.
A certain class of non-Buddhists further asserts:
"If the nature of the self conforms to the dimensions of its form, then it must possess parts and undergo transformation, just as the body does.

Furthermore, you maintain that the self follows its supporting body—like water following an embankment or oil following water; thus, this self, like that water or oil, would be subject to change and multiplicity, and therefore would be neither eternal nor unitary."
To cite this as an analogy and claim that the self-substance is eternal and unitary contradicts reason.

Therefore, the self-substance abides within the body with an extremely minute dimension, like a single atom; it cannot be analyzed, its substance is eternal and unchanging, and it is capable of initiating thought and movement of the body, as well as performing actions and experiencing results.
This is also not the case,
for it contradicts reason.

Since a multitude of atoms aggregate to form an extremely large body, while the self residing within it is of a very minute dimension, how could this minute self cause the large body to move such that every part of its entire form is seen to act simultaneously?

If you think that although my measure is small, it moves back and forth within the body, striking and activating it, gradually circling like a whirling firebrand, and because of its extreme speed, one says they move simultaneously.
If that were so, as the substance of the self circulates through the body, it would necessarily undergo arising and ceasing and consist of manifold parts.
For anything that migrates from one place to another must inevitably involve arising and ceasing and must necessarily possess manifold parts.
Since you claim that the self undergoes transition and its destination is not constant, how could it be a single, permanent entity—any more than the light of a lamp?
That which is permanent must be motionless; that which moves is not permanent.
For the self to be both moving and permanent deeply contradicts correct reasoning.
Furthermore, since the self as you conceive it has both abiding and moving, how can it be said to be permanent and unitary?
If, when moving, the self does not relinquish its nature of abiding, then it should be like its state of abiding and thus would have no movement.
If, when moving, the self were to abandon its stationary nature and a distinct entity were produced, how could it be permanent and unitary?
Such categories of self-clinging are infinite; yet when examined through reasoning, none of them are established.
To clarify this meaning, the following verse states:
"The wise realize that [it] does not exist.
The commentary says:

If there were a real self whose nature and characteristics were all identical, such that it served as the condition for the arising of the view of self, then this view of self should not exist with its various distinctions that are mutually contradictory.

From this we know that there is no permanent, substantial self; rather, it is solely due to the maturation of the functional capacity of long-practiced false views of a self, which have been perfumed within consciousness. Just as the body changes differently according to karmic conditions, so too does the view of a self vary according to its respective causes and conditions.
There is only the manifestation of manifold mental characteristics, yet within them there is not a single substantial entity of a self.
Therefore, the noble ones accumulate the causes for non-erroneous realization and diligently seek through skillful means to realize that the self does not exist.
Furthermore, those who claim that "I" can realize liberation merely follow the deluded mind and ultimately contradict correct reasoning. Why is this so?
Therefore, the following verse says:
“The eternal dharma cannot be afflicted; how then could one abandon affliction to attain liberation?
Therefore, to conceive of a self as eternal and claim to realize liberation is irrational.
The commentary states:

If one reckons that the self is permanent and undergoes no change, then even when encountering various sufferings such as frost and hail, it would be like the great void, entirely incapable of being harmed.

In that case, a wise person should not, observing how all worldly beings are oppressed by manifold sufferings, resolve to cultivate weary detachment and apply right effort through skillful means to realize liberation.
This demonstrates that because the self is eternal and cannot be afflicted, it should not perceive even when encountering manifold sufferings.
If there is no perception, there is no disenchantment; if there is no disenchantment, there is no correct exertion; and if there is no correct exertion, there is no liberation.

Alas! The heterodox practitioners are deluded, chaotic, and ignorant; they are like someone who, fearing that frost, hail, violent winds, torrential rains, water, fire, and other such calamities might damage space, exerts great effort to protect it.
Since you already cling to a self, yet remain free from affliction and profoundly serene, why trouble yourself with such hardship to falsely seek liberation?
Who with a heart could look upon this deluded madness and self-inflicted suffering without feeling deep compassion?
The scriptures of the non-Buddhists all state:
"Attachment to a self is saṃsāra; detachment from a self is nirvāṇa.
Since they praise the relinquishing of the self to inspire delight in liberation, how can they stubbornly maintain that a real self exists?
To clarify this meaning, it is further stated in verse:
"If the self truly possessed an intrinsic nature, one should not praise the relinquishing of the self.
The commentary says:

If the self truly existed, then the view of a self arising in dependence [upon it] would be real; one should not, therefore, urge its abandonment for the sake of realizing the true self. Instead, one should more earnestly urge the cultivation of the view of a self to make it firm. Why, then, urge the abandonment of the real view of a self and instead cultivate the false view of non-self?

Furthermore, various non-Buddhists, whether following the instructions of their teachers or through their own independent reflection, give rise to various views of a self (*ātman*). They engage in diverse disputes and arguments that contradict one another; how can they maintain that these are true views?
One might perhaps harbor doubts regarding the conflicting disputes over a single self, but how can one maintain that it is real?
If the view of self does not correspond to a real self, you should not claim that it can realize nirvāṇa.
If one who does not perceive nirvāṇa as it truly is were to know the true path to liberation, this statement would have to be false.
To clarify this point, the following verse says:
"One who definitely knows the truth Would find the path to liberation to be false."
The Commentary states:
If the existence of a self were real, then the view that there is no self or what belongs to a self—the means for liberation—would necessarily be false.
Furthermore, the view that there is a self and what belongs to a self, which contradicts *nirvāṇa* and accords with *saṃsāra*, would [paradoxically] have to be real.
If inverted views accord with nirvāṇa and non-inverted views accord with saṃsāra, how can your treatise state that one who definitively knows reality is able to proceed toward liberation?

From this, it is known with certainty that the view of emptiness and non-self is not false, as one attains nirvāṇa through it; thus, the views of "self" and "mine" are abandoned at the time of nirvāṇa, and like other views, they must be considered erroneous inversions.

Furthermore, your treatise asserts that the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*) is non-erroneous during the stages of hearing and reflection, but upon reaching the stage of cultivation, once this view of self is abandoned, it becomes erroneous again.
This is because the characteristic of "self" is briefly of two kinds:

first, existence; second, non-existence. Existence accords with *saṃsāra*, while non-existence accords with *nirvāṇa*; therefore, when one enters the state of a noble one (*ārya*), the view of self is abandoned.
This deluded discourse of yours is ridiculed by the world; when scrutinized, it is found to be non-existent—how then could it truly exist?
It is like seeing a rope in the darkness at first glance and calling it a snake, only to realize upon careful observation that it is not real.

The non-Buddhists are likewise; within the darkness of ignorance, they perceive this impermanent body as having a permanent self. If they attain noble wisdom and contemplate this body with discernment, they will realize its emptiness and selflessness, thereby attaining liberation.
To know that the view of a self is real at first but false later is to speak with certainty while claiming the object exists; such a person has faith but lacks wisdom.
Since you admit that the view of a self is real initially but false subsequently, you must likewise admit that there is no self at the time one attains nirvana.
If it were non-existent later, it should also have been non-existent previously.
To clarify this meaning, the following verse states:
"If it does not exist within liberation, It should likewise not have existed previously."
The Commentary states:

The meaning here is to clarify that just as there is no characteristic of a self in the state of liberation, it should likewise not exist prior to liberation, because its nature is without distinction.

Furthermore, since there is no self at the time of liberation when the body and so forth have ceased, there should likewise be no self in the state prior to liberation, as there is no difference in their characteristics.

Various non-Buddhists, however, are shrouded by the sleep of ignorance which blinds the eye of wisdom; failing to understand the subtle distinctions within the continuum of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), they falsely cling to a self that is unitary and eternal.

One cannot claim to have realized the ultimate truth by means of a confused vision devoid of wisdom; rather, one realizes the ultimate truth only by relying on a pure and unadulterated vision of wisdom.
To clarify this meaning, the following verse says:
"What is seen at the time it is unadulterated— that should be known as its true nature."
The Commentary states:
Just as water possesses its own characteristic even when mixed with fire, one knows that heat at the time of being mixed with fire is not the essence of water;

so too should it be understood for the body and other aggregates. Since they are empty and selfless at the time of attaining liberation, there is likewise no self in the state where they are mixed with the view of a self.

Alternatively, one should know that my own nature is likewise so: since there are no characteristics in the state of non-confusion, there are also no characteristics in the state of confused views of self; therefore, one should know that what is seen in a state of non-confusion accords with the true nature of phenomena, whereas confused views do not.
Furthermore, various non-Buddhists all raise this objection:
"If all phenomena are empty and without self, how is it that this mind, its faculties, and the body do not cease?
All impermanent conditioned formations that are empty and without self must undergo total annihilation, just like a lamp, a fire, or a sound."
This is also not the case; therefore, the subsequent verse says:
"If all that is impermanent were to be annihilated, why would grass and the like not be so?
The commentary states:
Although grass and other such things are without self and impermanent, they nevertheless possess a continuity of causes and conditions that does not cease.
One should know that the mind, the faculties, the body, and so forth are likewise; therefore, the reason you have established suffers from the fallacy of being inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).
Furthermore, your establishment of reasons and examples to prove that the mind, the faculties, and the body are all subject to annihilation is not yet fully understood.
Do you mean by "annihilation" that a single moment arises and ceases without interval, never again to continue in succession?
Is that which has continued in an uninterrupted succession over a long period of time necessarily called "ceased" only when it finally comes to an end?
If you say the former, it lacks the commonality [of the example], for lamps and the like arise continuously for a long duration in accordance with their causes.
If you say it is the second [alternative], I also grant that; for in *nirvāṇa* without remainder, both saṃsāra and [the self] are severed.
To refute the preceding reason, he further states a verse:
"If this principle were true, then ignorance would likewise not exist."
The treatise says:
Since the intrinsic nature of ignorance is neither self nor permanent, it should likewise cease spontaneously, just as a lamp is extinguished.
If this were the case, the afflictive obscurations such as craving produced by ignorance would also cease spontaneously.
If that were so, then one would be bound by birth and death yet naturally liberated without effort.

These two half-verses both demonstrate that the aforementioned reason is subject to the fallacy of being inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), with the distinction lying in whether the factors are internal or external.
Furthermore, certain non-Buddhists (tīrthika) maintain this view:
"Although phenomena such as form (rūpa) are impermanent, they continue in an uninterrupted succession because they depend upon a self (ātman).
This is also incorrect, as it contradicts liberation (vimukti).
If phenomena such as form were produced in dependence upon a self, then since the self is eternal and remains unchanged before and after, one would ultimately never realize liberation.
If it is argued that although all phenomena arise in dependence upon a self, this fault does not occur because they are assisted by conditions; [this is untenable].
If that were so, all phenomena would arise solely from those various conditions; what further use would there be for a self?
The productive conditions and the resulting fruit would simply follow one another in mutual conformity, existing together or ceasing together.
Since the self is eternal, it exists at all times.
The fruit is not so; how could it arise by depending upon that [self]?
My function is understood through the power of conditions that are difficult to discern; why then do you take my side and disbelieve in the existence of multiple conditions?
To clarify this meaning, the following verse states:
"Directly perceiving that formations such as form arise, abide, and cease from conditions,
One knows that your postulated self, though it exists, is useless."
The Commentary states:
When conditioned phenomena such as form arise, abide, and cease, they are seen to proceed from conditions and do not depend upon a self.
Since you maintain that the essence of the self is not produced by conditions, it follows that it possesses no functional activity, as has already been explained above.

Furthermore, because the characteristics of arising, abiding, and ceasing of phenomena such as form differ in both category and timing, how could they depend upon a single, permanent self as their condition?
This is just as the conditions for burning, cooking, and so forth are distinct from one another.

The categories of matured qualities (*vipākaja*) also possess distinctions; such distinctions do not depend on a single condition. Rather, they arise from the transformation of various functional capacities—distinct types of linguistic and habitual imprints (*nāma-vāsanā*) regarding form and other phenomena since beginningless time, as well as the diverse karmic actions previously performed that lead to various realms of existence—which, upon encountering specific conditions, ripen and give rise to the distinct manifestations of form and so forth, and of birth and so forth.

As for what is called "conditions": semen, blood, and so forth are the conditions for its arising; food, clothing, meditative concentration, and so forth are the conditions for its abiding; poisons, calamities, misfortunes, and the disorder of the four elements are the conditions for its cessation.
Regarding the various notions of a self, it has no such distinct function; yet the deluded outsiders insistently establish it as existing.
To clarify this meaning, another verse is spoken:
"Just as sprouts and so forth arise from conditions, And seeds and so forth are produced by conditions;”
"Therefore, all impermanent phenomena arise from that which is impermanent.
The Commentary says:

Just as external seeds and the like arise based on the specific functional capacities of their own causes and conditions, they further depend on the assistance of other conditions to exert their power and transform into their respective fruits, such as sprouts of their own kind.

One should know that the internal body, mind, and so forth are likewise: the continuity of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), whether of the same or different types, produces distinct results according to the conditions encountered. This demonstrates that because the substance of the internal body and mind is impermanent, they must arise from their own kind of impermanent causes, just as external sprouts and the like do.
I have no capacity to produce activity within body or mind because I am not produced through conditions, just like the hair of a tortoise and so forth.
Furthermore, this is to demonstrate that although all phenomena lack a self, they are nonetheless not subject to the two faults of annihilationism or eternalism.
Therefore, at the end of this chapter, a verse is further spoken:
"Because phenomena arise from conditions, their substance is not annihilated;
Because phenomena cease from conditions, their substance is also not eternal."
The treatise states:

All phenomena, evolving from beginningless time, arise as outflowing fruits (*niṣyanda-phala*) based on homogeneous causes (*sabhāga-hetu*); as subsequent effects arise in succession, they continue preceding causes without interruption, and it is for this reason that there is no break in the stream.
If the preceding cause ceases and the subsequent effect does not arise, there would be an interval between them that could be called "annihilation.
However, because the power of the preceding cause is extinguished by the arising of its antidote, such that the subsequent effect does not continue, it is therefore not eternal.
If a phenomenon remains motionless and does not abandon its prior characteristics, its essence being immutable, it may be called "permanent.
Furthermore, because the preceding cause ceases, it is not permanent; because the subsequent effect continues to arise, it is not annihilated.
Furthermore, because it arises, it is not eternal; because it can produce effects, it is not annihilated.
Moreover, because each moment is distinct, it is not eternal; because there is a continuous succession of similar moments, it is not annihilated.
Furthermore, because phenomena do not exist, they are not eternal; yet because they are not non-existent, they are not annihilated.
For existence implies eternity, while non-existence implies annihilation.

Thus, O Son of the Buddha, one remains far removed from the two extremes and awakens to the subtle principle of the Middle Way within dependent origination, correctly contemplating that all things are neither existent nor non-existent.
Since phenomena are by nature empty, how could a self possibly exist?
The view of a transitory collection (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), along with its latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) and all that arises from them, is forever extinguished herein.

Furthermore, observing that all conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*) are equal in their emptiness, both "self" and "other" vanish and the notion of self and other ceases. Toward all sentient beings to be converted, one gives rise to objectless compassion (*apratigha-maitrī*) and pours down the rain of the sublime Dharma; until the end of the future and the limits of space, the supreme function of benefiting and gladdening sentient beings is inexhaustible.

This courageous one is sustained by the contemplation of emptiness; thus, though all manner of intense sufferings burn fiercely, none can touch him. He perceives the great cycle of birth and death as being like an empty house, wherein numerous anxieties and sufferings are drawn forth by false conceptualization—resembling a raging fire with surging, violent flames that incinerates immeasurable sentient beings lacking wisdom. With a heart entwined by compassionate vows, he feels no fear or hesitation, casting himself into the depths to rescue them at the cost of his own life.

This Great Wisdom contemplates emptiness without error; having eliminated the notion of self and being free from the two types of craving associated with the grasping at "mine," it no longer views with attachment the phenomena that serve as the basis for afflictions such as greed. Thus, for the benefit of others, it constantly remains within the cycle of birth and death without being defiled by it—this is itself Great Nirvāṇa.
Though dwelling within the boundless ocean of suffering in the realm of worldly toil, they constantly experience supreme bliss that surpasses even the two types of nirvāṇa.
*Mahāyāna-śata-śāstra-vyākhyā*, Fascicle Three.
