Furthermore, one must first examine within oneself and know that the substance of abiding exists before one can explain to others the characteristic of abiding.
However, there is no expedient means by which one can examine and abide in its essence to know for certain that it has the capacity to abide in phenomena. Why is this?
Therefore, the next verse says:
"Just as there is no single consciousness that can cognize two objects,
so too there is no single object that can be known by two consciousnesses.
The commentary says:

The various objects perceived must be known to exist through the prior observation and subsequent examination by the perceiving consciousness; if two cognitions of the same class belonging to one body were to observe and subsequently examine a single manifest object, and if they were to ascertain that the characteristics of the object do not differ from what was previously perceived, only then could it be said that the present phenomenon abides.

Since there is no single body that possesses two simultaneous cognitions of the same class—one observing and the other examining the present object—how can you know that the present phenomenon has a duration of even a moment, upon which you establish the concept of "time"?

You must not say that the preceding moment of mental consciousness observes future phenomena and the succeeding moment of mental consciousness examines present phenomena, thereby knowing there is an abiding essence, because phenomena in the future world do not yet exist.

Nor can it be said that the mental consciousness of the preceding moment contemplates present phenomena while the mental consciousness of the succeeding moment examines past phenomena, thereby knowing there is an abiding essence; for the phenomena of the past have already ceased.
Even if one were to concede that past and future phenomena exist, they cannot be said to "abide" as time shifts and eras change.

Furthermore, it cannot be maintained that material phenomena (*rūpa*) and other such factors abide for a long duration in the present, while mental phenomena (*citta*) and others are impermanent and rapid; therefore, two moments of mind directed toward the same present object could first observe and subsequently examine it to know its abiding. This is untenable.
Since they are equally conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), why are they not equal? Why do form (*rūpa*) and other phenomena not abide for a long duration?
Because they are conditioned, just like the mind (*citta*) and so forth.
Others maintain that form has duration while the mind does not; this too should be refuted by using the mind as an analogy.

Two consciousnesses of the same class within a single sentient being's body certainly do not simultaneously take a single present phenomenon as their common object, because they are consciousnesses of the same class belonging to the preceding and succeeding moments of one body, just like two minds—one perceiving blue and the other yellow—that occur in succession.

Nor can it be said that the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), which observes the five sensory consciousnesses, is able to discern their persistence; for you do not admit that two consciousnesses arise simultaneously, since by the time the mental consciousness arises, its object has already ceased.
Even if it were granted that multiple consciousnesses arise simultaneously within a single body, each perceiving a distinct object, they would not be capable of deliberate discernment.

Although it is granted that the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) cognizes the objects of the five sensory consciousnesses, each [consciousness] transforms its own object and is subsumed under direct perception (*pratyakṣa*); thus, they both experience new objects rather than engaging in repeated, deliberate discernment.
For this reason it is said: there is no single object that can be known by two consciousnesses.
Furthermore, there is also no single consciousness that thoroughly knows two objects, as both [objects] possess real substantiality.
Why is this? If one applies the mind with careful discernment, one knows that when the preceding object exists, the subsequent object has not yet arisen;
and one knows that when the subsequent object exists, the preceding object has already ceased.
Since there is not even the capacity to carefully examine a single truly existent entity, how much less can one know two present objects?
Although both may be cognized, because they are both newly experienced, this does not constitute a repeated careful examination.

A consciousness that takes another object as its condition cannot definitively ascertain that other object as truly existent, because it bears the aspect of that [other] object, just like two distinct minds each taking their own respective objects.

Furthermore, an investigative mind cannot definitively ascertain the true existence of external objects, because it bears the aspect of something else, just like a mind newly cognizing a present object.
Furthermore, the Sāṃkhya proponents assert the following:

If one establishes that the essence of wisdom consists of distinct cognitions arising in each successive moment to know various phenomena, then it would be impossible for there to be prior seeking followed by realization, prior reception followed by recollection, or prior doubt followed by resolution.
Why is this so? Because we do not see Devadatta first seek to receive doubt and later have Yajñadatta able to provide the testimony that resolves it.
From this, one should know that there is only a single wisdom that is constantly able to illuminate and comprehend all objects.

Therefore, one might formulate a formal argument (*pramāṇa*) as follows: "The wisdom that cognizes blue and so forth is necessarily not separate from the wisdom that cognizes yellow and so forth, because it is of the nature of wisdom, just like the wisdom that cognizes yellow and so forth.
Consequently, [the claim that] a single wisdom cognizes all objects is also incorrect; for the transformation of eternal phenomena has already been refuted previously and should not be reasserted.
Furthermore, how do you know that this single wisdom, whose essence is permanent, knows all objects?

One cannot say that this wisdom knows all objects without examining the characteristics of the objects to be known; nor can it be said that this very wisdom is able to examine itself, for such a thing has never been observed among phenomena such as form (*rūpa*).
This wisdom must necessarily have another distinct wisdom capable of knowing it, because it is an object of knowledge, just like form and other such phenomena.
Furthermore, the natures of wisdoms regarding blue and so forth are each distinct, because their objects of knowledge differ, just as the wisdoms of oneself and others are distinct.

The intention here is to clarify that there is no single cognition capable of re-examining two objects as being substantially real; it does not mean that a single cognition cannot know multiple phenomena, lest one conclude that a single moment of mind cannot comprehend multiple objects.

Furthermore, it is not that the essence of wisdom cannot examine itself; rather, we do not say that the essence of wisdom cannot illuminate itself. Do not claim that mental states and mental factors cannot be self-verified, for if that were so, one would not be able to recollect them at a later time.

If it is argued that illumination of objects is a function (*vṛtti*) rather than the essence (*svabhāva*), and that because the essence is not itself an act of illumination it does not vary according to objects, whereas the illuminating function varies with conditions and is thus immeasurable—then because there are many such functions, the aforementioned fault does not apply.
This is also not the case; if its essence were not illumination, it should—like form and other such things—not be designated as "wisdom" (*prajñā*).

If you argue that this fault does not apply because the function of illumination is not separate from the essence, this too is not the case: if the function is not separate from the essence, then illumination should become one with it, precisely because it is not separate from the essence, just like the essence of wisdom itself.
If the essence were not distinct from its function, then wisdom would necessarily become manifold, because it is not distinct from its function—just like the function of illumination.
In this case, the function would follow the essence as being one, which contradicts the aforementioned inference.
If the essence conforms to its functions, it contradicts what you yourself have established.

If the functions were non-different from the essence, then there would be no distinction among such functions as general cognition (*samantālambana*), specific cognition (*viśeṣālambana*), aspiration, realization, reception, recollection, doubt, and certainty.

If the substance [of wisdom] possesses distinctions according to its functions, then the wisdom you have established should be distinct in every moment; furthermore, there would be no such thing as first seeking and later realizing, first receiving and later recollecting, or first doubting and later resolving. Thus, your own words turn back to harm yourself.

Furthermore, if you argue that although the essence of wisdom is one, there is no fault because its functions transform into various kinds according to conditions, this is also not the case; since the function of wisdom transforms into many according to conditions, its nature should likewise not be one, just as in the case of pleasure and so forth.

In the world, one does not perceive any entity such as form that is eternally one in essence yet becomes many in its function; for within conventional matters, while one may provisionally establish the distinction between essence and function, it is possible to designate an entity as one and its functions as many.
Within the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), such a principle does not exist; how could a single entity truly possess both unity and multiplicity?
Furthermore, as for your claim that the essence of wisdom (*prajñā*) is distinct in each moment—just like the wisdom belonging to different bodies—that is incorrect.
If it is argued that there can be no such thing as first seeking and later realizing, then the logical reason (*hetu*) is unestablished;
for our own school does not admit this, as the essential natures (*svabhāva*) of the two types of wisdom—the prior and the subsequent—are distinct.

Furthermore, even if one grants that the function of illumination differs from moment to moment, the fact remains that there are occurrences of first seeking and later realizing; therefore, the reason proposed suffers from the fallacy of being inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).
Furthermore, pleasure and so forth are objects of distinct cognitions (*buddhi*), and both parties agree that these serve as valid examples (*dṛṣṭānta*).

From this inference, one knows that consciousnesses apprehending distinct objects must differ in essence because they are apprehended by distinct cognitions; that is to say, consciousnesses of blue and so forth differ in essence because they are apprehended by distinct cognitions, just like pleasure and so forth.

Is it not the case that when pleasure and so forth undergo transformation, they combine with form and other phenomena such that their characteristics do not differ, and at that time they are further the objects of a single cognition? Thus, the proposed similar instance (sapakṣa) lacks the probans (sādhana), which is not a genuine fault.

When I say that being the object of distinct cognitions is the cause for establishing their distinct natures, I am not saying that they are *only* objects of distinct cognitions; what fault is there in this?

Furthermore, since pleasure and the others differ in their essential natures, one must necessarily admit that they are objects of distinct cognitions. Therefore, it is certain that there is no single cognition whose nature is eternal and which knows all objects.
Therefore, it is established by reason that no single consciousness can definitively cognize two objects as both possessing real substantial entities.
This digression arose from the need to explain the verse; now, let us temporarily cease this and proceed to correctly analyze the subject under discussion.
Furthermore, one should now interrogate the proponent of abiding:
Does this essence of abiding abide in a phenomenon by depending on another act of abiding, or is it not so?
If that were so, what would be the fault?
If the abiding dharma depends on another abiding [factor] in order to abide, then it should not be called "the abider," just like the state of being abided-in.
If the abiding dharma does not depend on another abiding [factor], then the same applies to that which is abided-in; it too should not depend on anything else.
To clarify this meaning, the subsequent verse says:
"If time were to exist apart from abiding, then abiding would not constitute time.
The commentary states:
An intrinsic nature cannot assist or bring about its own nature; therefore, there is no mutual dependence between similar categories occurring at the same time.
All conditioned phenomena must depend on the assistance of dissimilar categories to be established, such as wisdom and the mind, or earth and water.

Likewise, if one maintains that abiding has a separate abiding, then this abiding would lose its essential nature as abiding because it would depend upon another abiding, just like the dharma that is being abided in.
In the verse, the term "time" (*kāla*) is a synonym for abiding; thus, it should properly be said that abiding has another abiding, whereby abiding does not constitute abiding.

This is because it has been established as such. For this reason, arising and the other [characteristics] likewise lack a homogeneous cause; therefore, the formal argument (*pramāṇa*) that has been set forth is free from the fallacy of being inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).
Furthermore, the subsequent verse says:
"If time did not exist as abiding, then subsequent cessation would not exist.
The commentary states:
"Time" refers to abiding.
If other abiding factors were non-existent, then just as a dharma that is to be abided in cannot abide by itself, how could it abide others when it does not abide itself?
If this were so, it should not be called "capable of abiding."
Since abiding itself is non-existent, how could conditioned phenomena abide even for a single moment?
If initial abiding is already non-existent, how could subsequent cessation exist?
This is because the initial abiding and the subsequent cessation are established in mutual dependence.

Furthermore, if this abiding were able to abide by itself without depending on another abiding, then phenomena (*dharma*) should likewise be able to abide through their own power without depending on another abiding.
Since abiding (*sthiti*) is non-existent, cessation (*nirodha*) likewise does not exist; how then can you maintain that there is initial abiding followed by subsequent cessation?

Furthermore, since abiding and cessation act as mutual auxiliaries to produce their effects, if the characteristic of abiding is empty, then cessation and the others do not exist either. In that case, all phenomena would have no subsequent cessation.
If there is no subsequent cessation, what is meant by impermanence?
Furthermore, are all conditioned phenomena identical to or different from the characteristic of impermanence?
If this were so, what would be the fault?
If one says they are different, they should not be impermanent.
If one says they are identical, there should be no abiding.
To clarify this meaning, the verse continues:
“Dharmas are distinct from impermanence; dharmas are not themselves impermanence.
The commentary states:

When various dharmas such as form (*rūpa*) are called “impermanent,” they are designated as impermanent because they are conjoined with the characteristic of impermanence. However, since form, sensation (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), and so forth each have distinct characteristics and differ in their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), they are not themselves impermanence.
If that were so, since form and the other aggregates differ from impermanence, their essence—like that of space and so forth—should not be impermanent.

If you say that although form and the others have distinctions, they share "impermanence" as a common characteristic (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*), then if this common characteristic is separate from form and the others, and form and the others are distinct from it, the same fault as before recurs.

If it is said that form and the other aggregates are not distinct in essence from their common characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*), then because form and the others would lack any unique nature, they would lose their own specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*).

If it is said that all phenomena each possess two characteristics—namely, the specific and the common—which are inseparable, then since these two types are respectively universal and particular and their characteristics differ, they ought not to be a single entity.
Just as the characteristic of impermanence is not identical to form and so forth, so too form and so forth are not identical to impermanence.
Since their characteristics are distinct, although they are conjoined together, their essences are different, just like color and taste.

If it is argued that form and so forth are not actually impermanent, but are only conventionally designated as "impermanent" because they are conjoined with impermanence—just as a person holding a staff is called "the staff"—then there is no fault of form and so forth being non-impermanent.

If that were so, for one who cultivates the contemplation of impermanence, they would be superimposing impermanence upon form and other phenomena—which are not themselves impermanent—by means of their own mind; thus, this contemplation of impermanence would become a perversion (*viparyāsa*). If that were the case, it would be incapable of severing the afflictions (*kleśa*); therefore, impermanence must be identical to form and the other phenomena.

If form and so forth were themselves [the ultimate], they would lose their own-characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*); thus, these phenomena—both their own-characteristics and common-characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*)—are provisionally established through mutual dependence within the conventional path (*saṃvṛtimārga*). One must not dogmatically cling to them as being either identical or different; in the context of the ultimate principle (*paramārthanyāya*), they cannot be discussed at all.
Having already explained the fault that impermanence would be distinct from the phenomenon, the following verse is spoken again to demonstrate the fault that they would be identical:
"If the phenomenon and impermanence were one, The phenomenon should have no duration."
The treatise says:
Impermanence and the nature of abiding are mutually contradictory in their characteristics.
How can a single dharma possess these two kinds [of natures]?
Just as suffering and pleasure are mutually contradictory in their nature and characteristics and thus cannot even be associated, how much less could they be of one and the same substance!
If phenomena such as form were identical with impermanence, they would necessarily lack even the slightest sense of abiding; how then could one establish a real duration based upon that abiding?
Furthermore, there are those who say:
"As it was stated above, since all phenomena are impermanent, how could there be any duration?
This is not reasonable. Why is that?"

Although the intrinsic natures (svabhāva) of all phenomena are simultaneous, their functions differ according to temporal sequence; for example, while the four great elements (mahābhūta) act as co-existent causes (sahabhū-hetu) and their substance must necessarily be simultaneous, their functions occur in succession.

Thus, although these three characteristics exist simultaneously in their substance, their functions occur at different times: first the characteristic of arising performs its function, followed by abiding, and finally cessation.
Although impermanence exists during the time the characteristic of abiding performs its function, it lacks a predominant function, because the function of abiding is predominant at that time.

It has already been explained that the characteristics of arising (*utpāda*), abiding (*sthiti*), and ceasing (*nirodha*) have completed their functions regarding the basis (*āśraya*). You might argue that impermanence (*anityatā*) subsequently exerts a superior function to destroy the basis upon which these characteristics depend.

This, however, is not the case; for the intrinsic natures and functions of the characteristics of arising, abiding, and ceasing are mutually contradictory, just as suffering (*duḥkha*) and pleasure (*sukha*) cannot coexist. How, then, could they possess a single substance while their functions occur sequentially?
If you admit that things with mutually contradictory intrinsic natures can arise simultaneously, why do you not admit that their functions are simultaneous as well?
Since the functions are not concurrent, their substantial entities must likewise be so; thus, the analogy of the four great elements is logically untenable.
If their functions do not occur at the same time, their essences should likewise be so.
Furthermore, if both abiding and impermanence exist simultaneously within the essence, their functions should not differ in terms of temporal sequence.
If it is argued that because abiding is stronger and impermanence is weaker, abiding arises first in its function while impermanence arises later, this is also incorrect.
Therefore, the subsequent verse says:
"Since impermanence is initially weak, the power of abiding must necessarily be strong;
for what reason, then, do these two later appear as a perversion?"
The Commentary states:

Since their substance is simultaneous while their functions occur sequentially, one cannot say that the power of these two characteristics is equal; it must necessarily be the case that stability is superior and impermanence is inferior.

If that were so, for what reason would one later observe that the power of impermanence (*anityatā*) becomes superior, subduing the power of duration (*sthiti*) and destroying both its basis and its own characteristics?

At a later time, the power of duration ought to restrain impermanence, since it was stronger at the initial stage; yet, during this interval, there is no distinct means by which the efficacy of the characteristic of duration could be diminished, nor the efficacy of impermanence made to increase.

If it is argued that because the function of the characteristic of duration has already been completed, its power is diminished at this time, whereas the characteristic of impermanence, having not yet performed its function, its power is intensified at this time.
This is also not the case, for it contradicts reason.

Since stability (*sthiti*) and impermanence (*anityatā*) are of one and the same substance (*ekadravya*) in terms of their prior and subsequent states, by what cause do their functional powers differ in terms of decline and flourishing?
Furthermore, at that time when the characteristic of stability is present, its substance is neither deficient nor diminished; by what cause, then, does its functional power suddenly undergo decay?
Furthermore, as for the function of the characteristic of duration (*sthiti-lakṣaṇa*), at what point should it cease?
If you say that the function of duration lasts for only a single moment (*kṣaṇa*), for what reason is this duration considered so certain?
If the power of the characteristic of duration is limited to merely enabling a phenomenon to endure for one moment, then what further use would there be for impermanence (*anityatā*)?
Once the power of abiding has been exhausted, the various phenomena that were abiding naturally cease to abide; what need is there for extinction?

Thus, the essence of the characteristic of abiding is identical in its beginning and end, and the activities it performs likewise remain unchanged. That it sometimes gives rise to function and sometimes does not is a difficult point to comprehend; the wise should reflect upon this.

Furthermore, it is commonly known that at a later time, the power of impermanence (*anityatā*) is superior and is able to destroy the characteristic of duration (*sthiti-lakṣaṇa*); by this same principle, one should also believe that the power of impermanence was already superior in the preceding stage and was able to subdue the characteristic of duration.
If that were so, the characteristic of duration (*sthiti-lakṣaṇa*) would always be useless; why then do you insist on such a useless duration?
Therefore, the wise should believe in non-duration.
Since there is no duration, upon what could time be established?

Furthermore, to maintain that impermanence is initially weak and subsequently powerful, and to maintain that the characteristic of duration is initially powerful and subsequently weak, is in both cases contrary to reason.
Therefore, the verse says:
"If the power of impermanence, Pervading the essence of all phenomena, Is initially weak;..."
"There would either be no abiding at all, or everything would be eternal.
The treatise says:

If the power of the characteristic of impermanence is weak at the initial moment and cannot destroy the dharma, then the dharma abides naturally; for what reason do you insist upon this useless abiding?
In that case, the characteristic of abiding would fundamentally not exist, because it would be useless, just like a rabbit's horn.

If one were to say that at the initial moment the power of the characteristic of abiding is superior and can suppress impermanence, then it should remain superior at all times, for its essence does not differ.
If that were so, conditioned phenomena would never cease and should thus be permanent, which would contradict the scriptural teaching that all conditioned formations are impermanent.
Furthermore, one must now challenge those who maintain that the characteristic of duration coexists [with other characteristics]:
do all conditioned phenomena necessarily arise simultaneously with the characteristic of impermanence?
Does impermanence begin to arise at the time it performs its function?
First, this is not the case; therefore, the subsequent verse says:
"If impermanence were always present, then abiding would necessarily be non-existent."
The Commentary states:
It has already been fully established that conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) are subject to impermanence and cannot remain even for a moment.

This characteristic of impermanence harms conditioned phenomena, just like an extremely violent enemy or creditor who constantly follows, pursues, and presses them, not allowing them to stay still for even an instant.
Therefore, if one asserts that all conditioned phenomena are eternally impermanent, then they would never abide;
yet this latter view is also untenable. Thus, the verse says:
"Or if that phenomenon were first eternal, And later became non-eternal."
The Commentary states:

If impermanence were to begin at the end of a moment, then this characteristic of impermanence would not exist in the preceding state; at that time, that phenomenon would become permanent, because it would lack impermanence. However, this is not what is meant by "permanent," as in the case of space and other such things.

If there were some distinct entity possessing the nature of impermanence, yet it were designated as "permanent" merely by being devoid of the characteristics of impermanence, then by this logic, form and other phenomena would lose their conditioned nature.

If one argues that this fault does not apply because they must necessarily perish at a later time, this is also incorrect; for such a thing has never been observed among unconditioned phenomena. Just as with space and the like, which are initially free from impermanence, they can never subsequently undergo destruction or disintegration.
Conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) should likewise be so; how then could they necessarily perish at a later time?
Furthermore, since the initial state of form and so forth is no different from the subsequent state, it should be subject to impermanence just as the later stage is.
Furthermore, in order to summarize the preceding meaning, it is said again in verse:
"If a phenomenon is co-existent with impermanence, yet one says it has duration;
then its association with impermanence is false, or its association with duration is empty."
The treatise says:

If conditioned phenomena are accompanied by the characteristic of impermanence, yet one claims that conditioned phenomena possess the characteristic of stability, these two characteristics are contradictory in nature; thus, one must necessarily be false and the other true.
Why is this so? If one says that the characteristic of duration possesses a superior functional power, such that it maintains conditioned phenomena (saṃskṛta-dharma) so they do not perish for a time;
yet once the power of duration is exhausted, all conditioned phenomena naturally disintegrate and perish.
If that is so, what is the function of the characteristic of cessation?

Alternatively, it may be that the subsequent moment of duration possesses a superior power, as in the preceding state, which suppresses impermanence and renders it powerless to cause the destruction of its supporting basis.
If that is so, for what reason do you maintain the characteristic of impermanence?

If you say that although impermanence possesses the power and function to destroy all phenomena, at the initial moment of a phenomenon its force is weak and inferior and thus cannot act as a powerful adversary; therefore, the characteristic of impermanence temporarily relinquishes its hold, allowing the phenomenon to abide for a brief time.
If that is so, what is the purpose of the characteristic of duration (*sthiti-lakṣaṇa*)?
Alternatively, the preceding moment of impermanence should be like its subsequent state, causing the basis upon which cessation depends not to endure for even a moment.
If this is the case, for what reason do you maintain that there is a characteristic of duration?
Furthermore, some may say:

"As for the previous statement that there is no abiding, what is its essence? This argument is incorrect; although the essence of abiding does not exist, there is non-abiding, and the intrinsic nature of all phenomena cannot be denied."

One should speak thus: conditioned phenomena arise and perish in a continuous succession; at the moment of their uninterrupted cessation, there is not even for a single kṣaṇa a substantial entity that abides. Why is this so?
The power and function of impermanence, which flows and shifts without abiding, is established as "cessation.
If the essence of phenomena (*dharma*) does not exist, upon what would cessation depend?
If one were to say that there is a characteristic of impermanence external to phenomena that serves as the cause for their cessation, that too would be subject to this same difficulty.
I do not negate that all phenomena are non-existent; rather, I say that the substantial entities upon which you rely as being real and permanent cannot be found. Why is this so?
The claim that an abiding entity depends upon time has already been extensively refuted.
The claim that arising and ceasing depend upon time is likewise unreasonable. Why is this so?
That which was originally non-existent and now exists is conventionally designated as "arising"; that which was originally existent and now no longer exists is conventionally designated as "ceasing.
Since such arising and ceasing are not substantially real, how can one rely upon them to maintain that there is a substantially real time?
Furthermore, how is it known that arising and ceasing are provisional?

That which was originally non-existent and now exists is called "arising"; that which was originally existent and now no longer exists is called "ceasing. Both arising and ceasing are formed by the conjunction of two factors, like a house or a forest; how could they be called real?
Furthermore, since arising and ceasing are each composed of two parts, being half-existent and half-nonexistent, how can they be definitively established as existent?
Moreover, that which lacks the factor of "arising" cannot be called "arising," because its essence does not exist, just like the hair of a tortoise and so forth.
That which currently possesses parts is not called "arising," because its substance is not non-existent, as in the case of *nirvāṇa* and so forth.
Furthermore, that which originally possessed parts is not called "ceasing," because its substance is not non-existent, as in the case of space and so forth.
That which currently lacks parts cannot be called "ceasing," because its substance does not exist, like the horns of a rabbit.
Since each individual part neither arises nor ceases, how could their two-fold combination possibly arise or cease?
While such a principle may be applicable to phenomena that are merely conventional designations, within the realm of ultimate reality, no such meaning exists.

Furthermore, regarding each of the two phases of arising and ceasing, there was originally no future and there is now no past; since the two limits of the past and future have already ceased and not yet arisen, their substance being non-existent, they are not actual arising and ceasing.
Now, if there were both the "originally existent" and the "simultaneously present," how could arising and ceasing exist concurrently in a single moment?

It is impossible for two moments to exist within the present, such that the former is called "arising" and the latter is called "ceasing. Since their times are distinct, how could they belong to the same world-period (*adhvan*)?
If this were necessarily the case, the world would fall into confusion: at the time of arising, cessation has not yet occurred and should thus be called "future";
at the time of cessation, arising has already ceased and should thus be called "past."

Furthermore, the cessation that causes phenomena to cease prevents them from entering the past; since cessation exists in the present, it is said to have "arising. Once a phenomenon has arisen, it is caused to enter the present; thus, arising should be said to be "non-existent" in the future.
Furthermore, that which originally did not exist is called the future; that which exists at present is called the present;
that which existed previously is called the present; and that which no longer exists now is called the past.
How can two distinct time periods be combined into a single moment, such that one could say this moment exists as a determinate reality?
By investigating in this manner, it is evident that arising and ceasing are not real; therefore, one should not establish the existence of a real time based upon them.

If conditioned phenomena lack real arising and ceasing, how can it be as stated above that they are transmuted by impermanence—arising momentarily and then immediately ceasing—and how could there be any duration?
Since impermanence itself does not exist, how could it possibly transmute phenomena?
All that I have said above is intended to refute attachment; it is speech conforming to the perspectives of others and does not represent my own view.
Since they cling to impermanence while simultaneously clinging to persistence, I provisionally accept impermanence in order to refute that notion of persistence.
Now, since "abiding" does not exist, "impermanence" is also refuted; you should not claim that I definitively assert impermanence.

Like a skilled physician who administers medicine according to the illness, all that I have said is tailored to what is appropriate for each case; therefore, one should not dogmatically cling to my words.

If phenomena such as form were to truly possess duration, one could clearly recognize them as being conditioned; since they lack duration and yet are not unconditioned, they should not be grasped as being substantially real.
Since phenomena such as form do not exist as fixed realities, how can you establish "time" based upon them?
This may be acceptable from a conventional perspective, but it is not the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
Furthermore, some have said this:

If one were to posit a separate entity of "stability" (sthiti) apart from conditioned phenomena (saṃskṛta-dharma) that could cause phenomena to abide, such a view has already been shown to be erroneous. However, since conditioned phenomena themselves can produce subsequent moments from preceding moments, what fault is there in designating this process as "stability"?
This is also not the case.
Since conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) in their final moment do not produce a subsequent fruit, they would lack the characteristic of duration (*sthiti-lakṣaṇa*).
If they lack the characteristic of duration, they should be designated as unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
If that were so, then all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) prior to this [moment] would likewise not be conditioned, as they are of the same nature.

Furthermore, if it is argued that the characteristic of duration (*sthiti-lakṣaṇa*) consists in each subsequent moment of a conditioned phenomenon continuing from its predecessor, this is also incorrect. If the arising of the subsequent moment were to serve as the characteristic of duration for the preceding moment, then "arising" itself would be non-existent; and if that were the case, conditioned phenomena would lack the four characteristics.

If, at the time of subsequent arising, one looks back toward the preceding state as "abiding," then within that same position both "arising" and "abiding" would coexist; this would mean that what is called "arising" is itself the characteristic of "abiding," such that although the names differ, their functions would not be distinct.
Since these four characteristics thus have no distinct functions, why establish such useless characteristics?

Since the final moment has no subsequent thought-moment arising in succession to it, there should be no characteristic of duration; therefore, even the characteristic of the dharma’s own duration does not exist.
Furthermore, some say:

that which causes conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) to produce a subsequent fruit at the moment they are about to perish is the function of the characteristic of duration (*sthiti-lakṣaṇa*); by virtue of this function, although conditioned phenomena do not remain even for an instant, they possess the characteristic of duration.
This is also not the case.
If the final moment does not produce a subsequent effect, it would follow that it lacks the characteristic of abiding; the fault here is the same as previously stated.
If you argue that it is indeed capable of producing a subsequent [effect] at that time, yet the subsequent effect does not arise because other conditions are lacking, [we reply: ...
Since that final effect will ultimately never arise, how can one know that the preceding [moment] possessed the capacity to produce it?

If you argue that because the preceding moments were seen to possess a similar capacity, one may infer by analogy that the final moment also possesses such a capacity, this is also not the case, for we observe that they are different.

In the preceding moments, the various formations (saṃskāras) give rise to subsequent fruits; yet in the final moments, the subsequent fruits do not continue. Since the attainment of the fruit is distinct, how could they be the same as causes?
If they were the same as causes, they should all possess their fruits simultaneously; if that were so, the final moment would be untenable.
Furthermore, you should not use the preceding and succeeding formations (saṃskāra) as analogies for one another on the grounds that they are of the same kind, thereby concluding that all are causes;
do not say that because there is no fruit later, it must be the same as before, or that because there is a fruit before, it must be the same as after.

Furthermore, the aforementioned conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are not invariably able to produce a subsequent fruit at the moment they are about to perish; for instance, the final moment of consciousness in states such as the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) cannot produce a subsequent outflowing fruit (*niṣyandaphala*). Moreover, it should not be said that [the final mind] is a "conditioned phenomenon" (*saṃskāra*) in relation to what follows, acting as a homogeneous cause (*sabhāgahetu*), because their categories are distinct.

If an Arhat, upon entering the state of nirvana without remainder, were to have a mind that serves as a condition for the arising of another's consciousness or a body devoid of consciousness, then it would be called a "homogeneous cause" (sabhāga-hetu) taking an "equal-and-immediate fruit" (niṣyanda-phala). If this were so, there would be no possibility of permanent extinction (parinirvāṇa).

If it is argued that there is no fault because the final mind either conditions another consciousness or a body devoid of consciousness, and thus is not a causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*), this is also incorrect.

The final moment of mind upon entering the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*) and so forth is likewise not a causal condition for subsequent matter (*rūpa*) or formations (*saṃskāra*); how then can it be said that they arise through the power of the characteristic of duration (*sthiti-lakṣaṇa*)?

If you claim that when matter (*rūpa*) and formations (*saṃskāra*) are compared to a subsequent mind, they are outflow fruits (*niṣyandaphala*) because they share the same nature, and that the subsequent mind acts as their homogeneous cause (*sabhāgahetu*)—being thus called a "power of abiding" due to being a causal condition (*hetupratyaya*)—then consider the mind entering *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* in relation to the consciousness of another body or a body devoid of consciousness: according to your own school, these also possess the quality of sharing the same nature; why, then, are they not considered its homogeneous cause?
Now, as for "causes and conditions" (*pratyaya*), they refer to the capacity to produce a fruit through the perfuming of its own kind, and not to other dharmas.
Therefore, your establishment of the characteristic of duration (*sthiti-lakṣaṇa*) is untenable, because not all dharmas arise from their own kind.
Furthermore, since conditions (*pratyaya*) are conventionally established as mere designations, how can one rely upon them to establish a real characteristic of abiding?

Moreover, you yourself admit that all five causes both take up and give forth results; why then do you claim that only the single function of taking up a result by a similar cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) constitutes the power of the characteristic of abiding?
Furthermore, since the future does not possess a real substantial entity, how could it serve as a homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) in relation to that [present]?
The past and future are not subsumed under the present world nor under the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*); like a rabbit's horn and the like, they lack the nature of real existence.
Therefore, because the effect does not yet exist at the time of the cause, it is like a rabbit's horn, which cannot be its real cause;
because the cause has already ceased to exist when the effect is present, it is like a tortoise's hair, which cannot be its real effect.
Since cause and effect do not even possess a truly existent essence, how could the characteristics of dependence, establishment, and duration possibly exist in reality?
Since the characteristic of duration does not exist, upon what could time depend?
Therefore, it is certain that there is no real essence of time.
Furthermore, how can it be definitively known that all phenomena possess an intrinsic nature, such that one clings to the existence of a real time based upon that nature?
If it is argued that the existence of phenomena is known through direct perception, this is also not the case, because what is perceived is not real.
Why is this so? Therefore, the subsequent verse says:
"Seeing that there is nothing to be seen, one turns the mind away from conditions based on delusive objects."
Therefore, it is only a mere fiction; that which is called "arising" exists only as a mental recollection.
The treatise says:
All that is perceived is produced by consciousness; apart from consciousness, there is not a single dharma that is real.

This means that from beginningless time, one has repeatedly practiced various views; accordingly, following the views thus practiced, following the conditions encountered, and following the specific maturation of one's own seeds, these [seeds] transform and appear as the various marks of phenomena (dharma-lakṣaṇa).
Just as things seen in a dream and the like are all illusory manifestations and entirely devoid of even a single reality;
since everything is produced by the mind and consciousness, how can one definitively know that phenomena possess an intrinsic substance?
If external objects do not exist, internal consciousness must exist, just as in dreams and the like where there is mind despite the absence of objects.
Why, then, does such false attachment arise?
Since objects are non-existent, how can consciousness exist?

The fact that the substance of consciousness definitely exists is likewise unknowable, because a self-substance cannot know itself, and you do not admit that multiple consciousnesses arise simultaneously.

Even if one were to admit the simultaneous arising of various consciousnesses, there would still be no sense of direct mutual conditioning (*pratyaya*); how, then, could one know that the substance of consciousness definitely exists?

If that were so, the Mahāyāna would be like a dream or the speech of a mute; it would negate all phenomena as being entirely void, and thus be unable to distinguish and explain the specific natures of all mundane and supramundane phenomena.

Furthermore, unlike those who are mute in their dreams—who can still discern various objects of experience but cannot speak due to the lack of the causal conditions for speech—this [state] is unable to discern phenomena nor can it speak; how great is this suffering!

We are unable to follow such provisional teachings established by this Great Vehicle, for all phenomena can be directly perceived and thus cannot be denied as non-existent, since they are directly perceived.
How extraordinary and pitiable are these foolish people of meager merit, who are unable to believe in or understand the meaning of the Mahāyāna Dharma!
If there were a seer, something seen, and an act of seeing, then since the seer does not exist, who could see what is seen?
Because those who are able to see cannot themselves examine and know that they possess an intrinsic nature, nor can they examine others;

at the time of such investigation, both the seer and the seen are non-existent and cannot be scrutinized. Therefore, one should not cling to the notion that presently perceived phenomena definitely possess an intrinsic nature, for when the mind turns back [in analysis], all objects of cognition are merely provisional.

Why is this so? When recollection arises, there are in reality no various objects such as seeing and the like; rather, they arise simply as various objective appearances—such as seeing and so forth—which are transformations of one's own mind according to causes and conditions.
Because that which is recollected is not real, there arises only what is called a false recollection.
It is named "mindfulness" (smṛti) because it is the turning of the mind toward the essential characteristics of various phenomena as they were previously experienced, thereby recollecting them.
Since the objects previously experienced that are being recollected do not exist at the time of recollection, the one who recollects likewise does not exist.
What is called "recollection" is merely a conventional designation established in accordance with the habitual practice of various inverted views.

Due to this mindfulness, sentient beings in the world falsely give rise to various conceptualizations and disputes, vying with one another to cling to the distinct intrinsic natures of all phenomena; thus they sink into the mire of evil views, unable to extricate themselves.
If there is nothing seen and nothing heard, then everything is utterly non-existent; why then do you now bind stones together to make a raft?
What purpose, furthermore, would any practice or vow serve?
One should not raise objections regarding that which is provisionally designated in accordance with what is seen and heard in conventional reality;
for within the ultimate principle, neither of these two is admitted, as all conceptualization and discursive proliferation have ceased.
The Tathāgatas have no dharma to be taught, nor is there even the slightest dharma to be attained; therefore, a sūtra says:
"When the Tathāgata was formerly with Dīpaṃkara Buddha, there was not the slightest dharma that could be taught or grasped."
"If that were so, diligent effort would be in vain, and one would have to abandon the Tathāgata’s sublime teaching of the deathless nectar.
However, in order to employ skillful means to eliminate the adherence to inverted views, the presentation of these two matters is entirely without fault."
Since it has been stated that all objects seen and the seer are non-existent, how can there be no fault?
Although there is no real object seen or seer, foolish worldlings, through their perversion, claim they exist.
In order to eliminate their views of overweening pride, it is without fault to provisionally designate [the Buddha] in accordance with worldly convention.
If one can practice according to this holy teaching, one may be called a true disciple of the Buddha in accordance with worldly usage.

Worldly fools give rise to views based on the inverted appearances of objects that manifest according to their own minds; since the Buddha is not within their sphere of experience and is of no use to them, how can they be called disciples of the Tathāgata?
There is no fault in this, for that seeing-mind arises with the Buddha’s vows and practices as its dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*).

That is to say, when the Blessed One was formerly on the path of a causal bodhisattva, he initiated boundless efforts, vows, and practices out of a desire to bring benefit and happiness to all sentient beings. By means of these, he realized non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*); through the power of this wisdom, he initiates immeasurable activities for the benefit and happiness of sentient beings, which are inexhaustible.

All classes of sentient beings, by means of the Buddha’s vows and practices, take the sublime wisdom thus attained as their dominant condition; they then manifest within their own minds the forms of the Buddhas and the teachings they proclaim—forms that accord with the most excellent paths of birth in the world and the definitive, transcendent path beyond the world.

Based on the appearances of their own minds, they give rise to overweening pride, claiming: "I have seen the Buddha and heard the sound of his preaching the Dharma; I have followed it with faith and practiced both mundane and supramundane deeds. For this reason, they are called disciples of the Tathāgata.

If that were so, then non-conceptual, non-erroneous vision and wisdom would have to arise from inverted vows and practices; for they arise because one perceives that all sentient beings possess benefit and happiness due to one's original vows and practices.
If this were granted, what contradiction would there be?
Is it not contradictory for cause and effect to be of different categories?

Furthermore, if each individual cause were to produce everything, yet produces a result of a different category according to the power and function of the cause—since both [parties] grant this, what contradiction is there?
Just as the arising of the untainted from the tainted does not mean that faculties produce faculties or consciousness produces consciousness—
it being impossible to see how that which produces one kind could cause each and every thing to produce everything— so it is here.
It should not be considered difficult for them to share the same views and knowledge, for both parties would equally incur the fault of what is undesirable.
Furthermore, the power and function of worldly dharmas are inconceivable; they cannot be subjected to one-by-one challenges to force them into parity.

It is observed in the world that when one consumes madana fruits or other substances capable of inducing wind disorders (vāta-roga) in appropriate quantities and at the proper time, they serve as a cause for the elimination of those wind disorders rather than as a cause for disease.
The *karana* and other such factors are not like this; therefore, although things of different classes may produce one another, it is not the case that a single cause produces all effects.

Furthermore, the practice of the original vows is not inverted, for by being able to understand the true meaning of all phenomena and remaining without attachment to any phenomenon, it can serve as the generative cause for the unsurpassed, wondrous fruit.

Although they resolve their minds and initiate various sublime practices to seek the unsurpassed fruit for the benefit and happiness of sentient beings, they do so like a magician producing illusory phenomena, without any attachment whatsoever; therefore, this is not a state of perversion.
Furthermore, as before, one should ask:
"How do you definitively know that all phenomena possess an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), and on the basis of that nature, why do you cling to the existence of a real time?
If they should answer:

Because one gives rise to a mind of direct perception in accordance with the intrinsic nature of phenomena, and subsequently, through repeated investigation, is able to cognize for oneself: "I previously experienced such an object.
If there were no intrinsic nature of phenomena, one would not be able to investigate in this way at a later time; therefore, it is certain that all phenomena possess an intrinsic nature.
Furthermore, one should ask him:
"When you examine it closely, is there any substantial entity (dharmasvabhāva) that can be perceived?
He replies:
"No. Why is this? Because as soon as it arises, it ceases."
At this time, he has a vision of that which is not seen—that is, a vision arises regarding that which is not seen.
Furthermore, one should ask him:
"When you reflect back upon it, can the mind that previously perceived it recall, 'I saw such an object'?"
He replied: "No. Why is that?"
Past phenomena cannot be turned back; therefore, there is no turning back of the mind.
That is to say, there is no capacity to turn a past mind back to the present. If this were so, by what means could one now examine and definitively know that phenomena possess intrinsic nature?
He said: "By means of mindfulness. Why is that?"

It is claimed that recollection can only occur subsequent to direct perception, and that there can be no direct perception of a non-existent entity; therefore, it is definitively known that all phenomena possess an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
This is merely words without any actual meaning.

Why is this so? All recollections arise by taking as their object that which has a name but lacks a real referent. Since these recollections take only false objects as their conditions, they are therefore merely designated as conventional, provisional recollections.
This refers to clearly remembering, as if before one's eyes, an unreal and false object that does not exist; therefore, it is called "recollection" (*smṛti*).
Because its substance is actually non-existent yet an inverted appearance manifests, it is termed an "unreal and false object."
Therefore, one should not follow false views by conceptualizing all phenomena as having a real intrinsic nature.

Furthermore, as for your previous statement that recollection can only occur subsequent to direct perception, and that there is no direct perception of a phenomenon that lacks an intrinsic nature—this too is incorrect.
This has already been briefly explained above:

because seeing is not real, both the object seen and the subject that sees are non-existent. Therefore, one cannot use the manifestation of seeing as proof that the dharmas possess substantial reality.
Although this was briefly explained previously, it has not yet been extensively analyzed.
How can one definitively know that all phenomena do not exist?
Briefly stated, there are two kinds of existence as they are grasped by others:
First is the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) and second is the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).
The unconditioned is eternal, as has already been extensively refuted.
That is to say, if it possessed a function capable of producing various phenomena, it would necessarily be of the nature of the conditioned and not the unconditioned.
If that which lacks utility cannot produce a phenomenon, its essence must be non-existent, like a rabbit's horn.
There are two types of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*):
namely, those of the past and future, as well as those of the present.
The past and future have already been explained as above:
that which has existed or will exist does not possess an existing entity; if it possessed an existing entity, it would have to be called the present.
If one were to say that they are not the present because they lack utility, [that is incorrect].
Since it already exists as a substantial entity, how can it be without function?

If you argue that its function is not eternally present because it must depend upon conditions, then while the function may be impermanent, the entity—which does not depend on conditions—should be eternally abiding.
If one says that this essence can give rise to its function, then because the function is impermanent, the essence must also be impermanent.
Thus, since this essence can give rise to a function that exists only momentarily, the essence itself cannot exist eternally.

Furthermore, if conditioned phenomena possess an essence that is eternally existent and yet are capable of initiating activity, they cannot be unconditioned. Since you also admit that the essence of space and so forth is eternally existent, why do they not initiate activity and thus be designated as conditioned?
The unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) exists eternally yet does not give rise to activity; how could the conditioned (saṃskṛta), which gives rise to activity, exist eternally?
Furthermore, the substance of the past is certainly not presently existent, because it is designated as "already ceased" and is subsumed under the past, just like the activity of the past.
The essence of the future world is likewise not presently existent, because it is designated as "unborn" and is subsumed under the category of the future, just like the activity of the future.

If one were to argue that although the essences of the past and future exist, they are not called "presently existent" because they are not the present, then the formal inference (prayoga) you have established would be proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*).
This reasoning is incorrect.

You establish the substantiality of the three time periods as being neither "originally non-existent but now existent" nor "originally existent but now non-existent," but rather as existing at all times; thus, because it is like the emptiness you cling to, it is called "presently existent. It is not called "presently existent" by virtue of being subsumed within the present time period.
I now refute and dismantle the claim that [past and future entities] exist as manifest presence; therefore, this inference does not establish what is already established.

If you do not admit that the substance of the two periods of past and future exists as a real entity, then it follows that their substance must be non-existent, just as the prior and posterior states of an activity are non-existent.

Thus, all conditioned phenomena—whether in their essence or their function—depend upon a multitude of conditions; they were originally non-existent and now exist, or were originally existent and now cease to be. This would cause you to lose your own tenet that the substance of dharmas is eternally present.
If it is argued that the essence of the past and future exists in the present because they are subsumed within time, just like the present,
this reasoning is also untenable.

Since you admit that the activity of the past and future does not exist in the present yet is subsumed within time, your formal argument (prayoga) suffers from the fallacy of inconclusiveness (anaikāntika).
If it is argued that the essence of the past and future is substantially existent because they are included within the [three] time periods, just like the present, this reasoning is also incorrect.
If one relies on the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), even the present is not substantially existent according to our own school; thus, there would be no corroborative example (*dṛṣṭānta*).

If, according to conventional usage, things such as jars and basins are included within the worldly realm and are not substantially existent, then the formal argument (*pramāṇa*) you have established suffers from the fallacy of inconclusiveness (*anaikāntika*).

If, however, you claim that the substance of the past and future is substantially existent because it is not included among those things that are not substantially existent—just like those real dharmas known to common consensus—[then this is untenable].
This is also not the case.

If it is based on the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), there is no similar instance (*sapakṣa*); if it is based on the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti*), it establishes what is already established (*siddhasādhana*), for our own school also maintains that the past and future exist as real entities (*dravyasat*).

Furthermore, just as it is commonly known that conventional phenomena are real while other things are not, because they are not included among those that truly exist, the past and future should likewise not have the nature of existing as real entities; there are many such contradictions of this kind.

Furthermore, the essence of the past and future does not exist as a reality, because they are not subsumed under other truly existent phenomena, just like those phenomena commonly known to be non-existent.

There are infinite such types of inference (*anumāna*); therefore, the past and future do not possess an existing essence, but are merely established by way of conventional designation (*prajñapti*) based upon the present.

This means that when the present mind takes past or future phenomena as its object, they appear with a semblance of those [phenomena], and thus one conventionally designates them as "past" or "future. In reality, however, they are not [substantially] past or future.

For this reason, the phenomena commonly accepted as past and future do not exist as separate substantial entities apart from the present, because they are included within the time periods as admitted by our own school.

If, as you claim, past and future entities exist substantially just as present ones do, this is identical to the calculation of the Sāṃkhya heretics, who maintain that the substance of *prakṛti* (self-nature) is eternal and yet undergoes arising and passing away.
Since that [position] is flawed, this one should likewise be so.
Therefore, those who call themselves disciples of the Buddha should abandon this attachment.
Although present phenomena exist conventionally, they do not exist in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*).
Why is this so? If something existed in the ultimate sense, it would not depend upon conditions.
Since it arises in dependence on conditions—just like a magical illusion—how can it be said to exist as a reality?
Furthermore, present phenomena possess arising and ceasing, being like magical illusions; how could they be substantially real?
If present phenomena were substantially real, they would—like the nature of space as you conceive it—be without arising or ceasing; how then could they be called "present"?

Furthermore, present phenomena are composed of two parts: that which has already arisen and that which has not yet ceased. That which has already arisen depends upon the future, and that which has not yet ceased depends upon the past; because they are established through mutual dependence, they lack a real substantial entity. They are like coarse and subtle [qualities], which are formed by the aggregation of unreal dharmas, or like forests and the like.
How can they be substantially real?
Furthermore, since each individual phenomenon in the present possesses multiple natures, how could it be substantially real?

That is to say, every single phenomenon possesses the nature of aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*); it possesses the natures of being with outflows (*sāsrava*) or without outflows (*anāsrava*), mundane or supramundane, matter (*rūpa*) or mind (*citta*), and so forth—natures of infinite variety. Among these various natures, one cannot say which are real and which are provisional; such natures are distinctions in meaning that all depend upon a single essence.
Apart from these various natures (*svabhāva*), what other essence (*tattva*) could there be?
Nor can it be said that one nature is the essence while the remaining natures are its meanings; for they are all equally termed "natures" and possess no distinction.
How can it be that one is the essence while the others are all its meanings?
This too cannot be said; such natures as these are called "distinctions," yet their meaning is one.
If that were so, distinct modes of cognition (*ākāra*) would not arise;

nor can it be said that these distinct modes of cognition take only the names as their objects, for various modes of cognition such as suffering and impermanence all take the actual referents (*artha*) as their objects. Therefore, the substance of each conditioned phenomenon (*saṃskṛtadharma*) is composed of an immeasurable number of natures and characteristics. Like a house or a forest, it does not exist as a true reality, but exists as a substantial entity only by way of conventional designation (*saṃvṛti*).

If it is argued that all natures are merely common characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) because they can be described— just as armies, forests, and the like are conceptual constructs rather than real entities and are obtained through inference (*anumāna*),
whereas self-characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) are real and obtained through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
Since it is said to be real, what are its characteristics?
How can that which is apprehended by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) be described?
If it cannot be described, how can it be called real?
If it could be said that the intrinsic characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) is real, then it should be expressible; why, then, is it said to be inexpressible?

If you claim that the intrinsic characteristic is designated as "real" only by way of conventional designation and is not truly real, then everything—whether conventional or real—is established based upon worldly conceptual designations. Why, then, do you insist that all phenomena possess a substantial entity (*dravya*)?

If all phenomena are not substantially real, how is it that they are clearly visible before one? For instance, reflections in a mirror, the moon in water, the city of the Gandharvas, dream-objects, magical illusions, and a second moon are all clearly visible.
How could these truly exist?
Everything perceived in the world lacks reality; how then can one take what is seen as proof that the dharmas are real?

All that is seen during the waking state is not real; it is an object of consciousness, like what is seen in a dream. What is seen by the dreaming mind is certainly not real, being an object of a deluded consciousness, like a second moon.

Thus, although there is no real ontological essence, it can serve as an object and give rise to a mind that perceives it directly; based on this, recollection is subsequently produced. Since both the preceding and succeeding moments take as their objects what is not truly existent, one cannot use the arising of recollection to prove that a phenomenon is real.
Since phenomena are not real, how can time be real?
If inverted views arise due to false objects, then while the objects may be illusory, the views should be real.
But since the objects are illusory, how can the views be real?
Just as in a dream one thinks that visual and other consciousnesses perceive objects such as forms, yet upon waking one knows that both of these things are non-existent;
so too it is with delusive objects and inverted minds: the foolish claim they exist, while the noble ones know them to be non-existent.
The two types—the distorted mind and its objects—are both false; the non-distorted object and mind should both be real.
While this may be the case for the conventional level (*saṃvṛti*), it is not so for the ultimate level (*paramārtha*), because in the ultimate sense, all discourse regarding the mind ceases.
If, in the ultimate sense, the mind transcends all verbal expression, how can it be repeatedly stated that the mind and its objects are empty?
They are said to be empty merely to refute the grasping at reality;
once that grasping at reality is eliminated, even "emptiness" no longer exists.
Whether real or unreal, all are intended to dispel grasping.
This is spoken according to conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) and not from the perspective of ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
Even the expression "ultimate truth" is a provisional designation, established to overturn the conventional and to indicate that there is no fixed, definitive description.
If it can be said that the mind and its objects perceived in the present are non-existent, how could the mind and its objects remembered in recollection not exist?
If even what is presently perceived does not exist, how could what is remembered possibly exist?
If all phenomena were entirely without real existence, how could the world currently perform wholesome or unwholesome deeds?
If there were neither good nor evil, there would likewise be no suffering or pleasure; this would then be to deny all causes and effects.
To deny cause and effect constitutes a false view (mithyādṛṣṭi); do you not fear the retribution for such a false view?
How strange that the world is so deluded as to be difficult to awaken! People know only to fear sin, yet they do not recognize the causes of sin.
All phenomena of good and evil, suffering and happiness, are existents within the conventional realm, but they do not exist within the ultimate sense.
Since I rely on the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya) and state that [entities] are unfindable, I do not negate the conventional (saṃvṛti); how, then, could this constitute a false view?
To hold that things exist ultimately within the context of the conventional, when they do not accord with correct reasoning, is what constitutes a false view.
Now, within this context, in order to refute the attachment to time, I shall briefly explain that all phenomena exist conventionally but are non-existent ultimately.
As for investigating the reality or unreality of their meaning and determining what is right or wrong, these matters shall be analyzed in detail in a later chapter.

Having thus briefly established the true meaning of the Middle Way that avoids the two extremes, those who are wise and delight in the ultimate truth should diligently practice and study it; namely, they should understand how the erroneous attachments to the two extremes of permanence and impermanence are refuted in their respective order.
The Commentary on the Extensive Hundred Stanzas on the Mahāyāna, Fascicle Five.
The Commentary on the Extensive Hundred Stanzas on the Mahāyāna, Fascicle Six.
Composed by Āryadeva Bodhisattva; explained by Dharmapāla Bodhisattva.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree.

Chapter Four: Refuting Views Furthermore, if it is as you say—that the nature and characteristics of all phenomena exist conventionally while being empty in terms of ultimate principle, and that the Tathāgata possesses unimpeded wisdom and vision therein, his speech and eloquence clearly discerning and skillfully awakening the minds of others—then why is it that the world is still infatuated with various false views and mired in such turbulent disputes?
This is because the listener possesses faults.
What are the faults of the listener? They are:
attachment to one's own views, a lack of seeking for resolute conviction, and an inability to discern between well-spoken and ill-spoken teachings.
If one is free from these three kinds of faults, such a person is called a vessel for hearing the true Dharma.
To clarify this meaning, it is said in verse:
"One who is receptive, harmonious, and seeks supreme wisdom— Know that such a person is a vessel for the Dharma."
"Otherwise, there would be no teacher or disciple, and one could not obtain the supreme benefit without a cause.
The commentary says:
One must possess three qualities to be called a vessel for the Dharma.
First, they are naturally gentle and harmonious, free from partiality; they constantly examine themselves and do not cling to their own views.
Second, they always aspire toward superior understanding and seek the Dharma without weariness, never remaining complacent with their own limited capacity.
Third, they are by nature intelligent and wise, capable of correctly discerning the distinctions between virtue and fault in both wholesome and unwholesome speech.
If these three qualities as described are absent, then despite the existence of teacher and disciple, there will ultimately be no benefit.
What is called "benefit" refers, respectively, to the teacher’s and the disciple’s awakening and realization.

Just as those six teachers and other non-Buddhists, though they heard the true Dharma, attained no realization, it was not that the Buddha lacked a compassionate mind to rescue them, nor was it that the holy teaching did not contain the correct principle; rather, among those in the world who were destined for deliverance, all have already been delivered by hearing the Buddha’s holy teaching.
To clarify this meaning, the following verse says:
"The existence [of things] and their causes, Purity and the means to purity—
Since the world does not understand these for itself, How could the fault lie with the Muni?"
The treatise says:

The unimpeded wisdom and vision of all Buddhas and Tathāgatas perceive that the activities for the benefit of others do not exceed four kinds, namely: that which is relinquished, that which is realized, and the two causes of these.
Since both their substance and meaning are true and their designations are not erroneous, they are subsumed within the Noble Teaching of the Four Truths.
Although the Buddha has taught extensively, those beings do not understand; the fault lies with the world, not with the Sage’s failing.
Because the wisdom of the various non-Buddhists is dull and feeble, and because they lack correct cultivation, they are unable to understand it.
It is like the blazing sun emitting a thousand rays of light; that the blind do not see the sun is no fault of the sun itself.

Furthermore, those non-Buddhists are certainly bound by the fetters of ignorance, negligence, and torpor, which shroud their consciousness; thus they are unable to place faith in or rely upon what they themselves profess. Why is this so?
Therefore, the following verse says:
"Renouncing all existence for nirvāṇa is what all heterodox schools agree upon;
Since true emptiness destroys everything, why would they not rejoice in it?"
The Commentary states:

All non-Buddhist schools claim that by abandoning all things belonging to the self, only the self alone remains; being far removed from the entanglements of affliction, it is a state of solitary liberation, unconditioned and tranquil, which they call *nirvāṇa*. It is a true emptiness devoid of characteristics, transcending all delusive objects, and free from the discriminating mind that clings to existence and so forth.

Contemplating this can eliminate all states of mind and lead directly to the unsurpassed Great Parinirvāṇa; since it does not contradict the liberation you seek, why do you feel aversion and turn away from it instead of feeling joy?
In our nirvāṇa, we exclude only that which belongs to the self; since emptiness also negates the self, what is there to rejoice in?
If there were a self within your nirvāṇa, it would necessarily not be free from objects of attachment; how, then, could it constitute nirvāṇa?
I have already refuted this previously; you should not persist in clinging to it again. Therefore, you ought to rejoice in this emptiness of self, which is free from [the notion of] a self.
That which exists can be eliminated, whereas emptiness itself cannot be dispelled.

Clinging to existence gives rise to faults, while contemplating emptiness eliminates them. Since the merits and defects of these two paths—existence and emptiness—are as vastly different as heaven and earth, why do you and your followers side with existence and revile emptiness?

Pitiable are these misguided followers, deluded and ignorant, who cannot believe in or accept the beneficial true emptiness; they constantly delight in seeking the useless and the falsely existent, and instead give rise to resentment and envy toward the orthodox teaching.

Just as that wicked son, his mind deluded by lustful disorder, indulging in forms and sounds, acting recklessly and devoid of propriety, fails to know how to respectfully follow his mother’s compassionate instructions; instead, following his own wickedness and obstinacy, he turns against her with resentment and harm.
Furthermore, if one is separated from true emptiness (*śūnyatā*), there is ultimately no other means for relinquishing [defilements] or realizing [the fruit].
Therefore, the next verse says:
"Without knowing the cause of relinquishment and realization, there is no way to be able to relinquish or realize."
"Therefore, the Muni has said: 'There is nothing else that is cool [peaceful].
The commentary states:

Although those non-Buddhists resolve to seek the realization of nirvāṇa and the abandonment of saṃsāra, because they do not properly understand the means for abandoning and realizing, they will ultimately fail to accomplish what is to be abandoned and realized."

Because one loathes and turns away from true emptiness while being attached to false existence, one is said to have "improper knowledge" regarding skillful means; for apart from the contemplation of true emptiness, there is no other skillful means for abandoning birth-and-death and realizing nirvana.
Those who crave and seek after the views of non-Buddhist outsiders will ultimately never attain the supramundane state of coolness.
What is called "coolness" is the ultimate stillness of all suffering and its causes.
