Only the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*) is the cause for realization, as there is no other expedient means apart from this.

Such a contemplation of emptiness exists within the Buddha-dharma, whereas it is entirely absent from the heterodox treatises of all non-Buddhists; therefore, the Muni taught that the four fruits of the śramaṇa exist within my dharma, while they certainly do not exist in other systems.
Because the various non-Buddhists cling to their own views and revile the contemplation of emptiness, they do not realize nirvāṇa.
How should we understand that what we ourselves grasp is certainly not the correct means for relinquishing [defilements] and realizing [nirvāṇa]?

As has already been fully explained, when one posits the existence of a real entity based on the conceptualization of permanent categories, there are faults in all such cases; these shall be extensively refuted later.
Since you maintain [the reality of] the sense faculties, objects, and so forth, it is clear that your adherence is not a correct means.

Furthermore, the various non-Buddhists are truly unable to abandon views such as "mine" regarding the state of nirvāṇa; yet they claim that within that state there exists an internal self, and that liberation from what belongs to the self is called nirvāṇa.
Why is this? Because "I" and "mine" are ultimately devoid of any sense of separation.
You cannot claim that dharmas such as suffering and pleasure are remote from "I" within the state of nirvāṇa, for you yourself have established them as belonging to "mine."
Regarding the self-substance (*ātman*) as you conceive it, one cannot say that the self-substance does not belong to the self; thus, the supporting example lacks a probans (*hetu*).
Let it not be that the self-substance you conceive is without essence, for then it would be like a flower in the sky, which would entail the fault of contradicting your own tenet.

Therefore, that which is clung to by you non-Buddhists cannot ultimately bring about the abandonment of birth and death, nor can it realize ultimate nirvana; from this, one should know that it is not the correct means.

Furthermore, although the treatises composed by various non-Buddhists contain some elements of truth in their expositions— such as stating that giving and so forth are projecting causes capable of inviting rebirth in happy realms and other superior pleasures,
and that killing and so forth are projecting causes capable of inviting rebirth in miserable realms and other severe sufferings— [they remain incomplete].
However, that treatise is internally contradictory; it both permits such acts as killing and asserts that they can give rise to various evil views, while also being produced from such views.
It is like a blind person who encounters a path leading to the right way, yet at times becomes lost and instead treads upon a deviant path.
The treatises of non-Buddhist schools are likewise: some contain truth and others falsehood, and thus they cannot be relied upon or trusted.

If that were so, then among the noble teachings of the Tathāgata’s Tripiṭaka, there would be certain statements that are difficult to believe and understand; consequently, it would follow as an excessive fault that none of the scriptures—whether internal or external—could be trusted.
Why is this? Within the Buddha’s sūtras, various inconceivable supernormal transformations are described, as well as profound and ultimate principles that sentient beings are unable to fathom.

Furthermore, it is said that the functional activity of the Tathāgata’s three karmas is such that it cannot be known by those of the Śrāvaka vehicle and others; namely, through effortless exertion, throughout the infinite and boundless worlds of the ten directions, he is able to manifest sublime form-bodies at a single moment according to the inclinations of each and every sentient being—according to their immeasurable and innumerable varieties of individual faculties—to bring inexhaustible benefit.

Although he has severed all discursive thoughts, investigations, and conceptualizations, he is nevertheless able to proclaim for those immeasurable sentient beings the boundless, profound, vast, true, exquisite, and inexhaustible sound of the Dharma; in a single moment of thought, he can eliminate the defilements of the immeasurable and boundless mental activities of sentient beings.

Although this mind has no real arising or real ceasing, and lacks all subject-object duality, in a single instant it perceives all objects of knowledge universally and exhaustively; yet at the time of such perception, it remains free from all conceptualization and deliberation regarding seer and seen.

Although he has severed all latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) and fetters (*paryavasthāna*), he manifests birth and death within the three realms of existence; although he has long been free from desire, he is born in the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*); and though he dwells in the cramped prison of the household life, he amasses various kinds of wealth, grain, and rare treasures, and supports his wife, children, kinsmen, and servants.
Matters such as these are all difficult to believe and understand; therefore, I harbor deep hesitation regarding them.
If a matter were merely existent, it would be reasonable to give rise to doubt; yet, that matter is also empty.
Therefore, the following verse says:
"If one conceives doubt regarding the profound matters taught by the Buddha,
one should rely upon signless emptiness and give rise to resolute faith."
The commentary states:
The meaning of this verse is that the Tathāgata, in order to frighten the deer-like followers of external paths, let out a great lion’s roar to manifest true emptiness (*śūnyatā*).
This true emptiness is of definitive meaning, established clearly by both principle and scripture.
All those who possess wisdom take this as their definitive standard; though they may apply sharp challenges and refined contemplation, none can transcend it.
By following the principle of emptiness and practicing diligently without error, one is adorned by manifold virtues and achieves the unsurpassed fruit.
In this regard, one should give rise to a resolute faith and understanding that emptiness alone is the reality and all else is not true;
it is merely that the Tathāgata, in accordance with the capacities and inclinations of sentient beings, has skillfully manifested and proclaimed these through expedient means.
Furthermore, although the words spoken by the Buddha are immeasurable, they are briefly of only two kinds: namely, emptiness and non-emptiness.
If one has doubts regarding that which is non-empty, one should rely on the principle of emptiness to infer and thereby understand it.
Since all phenomena are empty, how can they be perceived?
It is because the existence of objects as denoted by words is not established.
Briefly, there are two kinds of essential characteristics of phenomena: that which is cognized by consciousness and that which is expressed by words.

When multiple consciousnesses arise simultaneously toward a single object, their perceived aspects differ according to the distinctions in what is seen; thus, this consciousness should not be said to arise in accordance with an external object.

Since a single objective entity cannot possess multiple aspects, it is known that the object of cognition is definitely non-existent. To say it exists is merely a conventional designation (*prajñapti*) that expresses only a common characteristic (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*); all common characteristics are unreal because they are composed of multiple factors, like an army or a forest.

Furthermore, all general characteristics (sāmānyalakṣaṇa) depend upon particular phenomena (bhinnadharma), and the number of these underlying particulars is infinite; those with limited vision cannot perceive them all.

Since they do not perceive the particulars, they cannot perceive the general characteristic, just as the nature of duality depends upon two distinct entities, and if the substrata are not seen, the [dual] nature can certainly not be seen.
Since such common characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) are not actually perceived, how can they serve as the basis for establishing expressive designations?
Therefore, common characteristics are merely conceptual constructs (*prajñapti*); they do not exist substantially (*dravyasat*) such that they could serve as the referents of verbal expressions.
Furthermore, if common characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) were substantially existent, it would be impossible for them to exist either entirely or partially within each individual phenomenon.
If they existed entirely within each individual phenomenon, then, like distinct phenomena, common characteristics could not be established.

If [the universal] were to exist as a distinct portion within each individual phenomenon, it would follow that it consists of multiple portions rather than being a single common characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*).

Furthermore, there is no separate entity existing over and above "substance" (*dravya*) and so forth, because the universal nature of substance and the like is the object of the cognition [that apprehends them], just as [there is no separate entity] over and above non-substance and the like.

The general nature (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) is precisely the common characteristic (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) of all phenomena; therefore, this common characteristic lacks any substantial reality and is merely a conventional designation established by worldly consensus.

Thus, whether these phenomena are objects of cognition or objects of verbal expression, both modes of investigation reveal them to be devoid of real existence. Since there is no distinct phenomenon apart from these two types of objects, one should accordingly believe and understand that all phenomena are empty.

Based on this sūtra, it is stated as follows: "The true nature of all phenomena is without demonstration and without opposition; they are all of one single characteristic, namely, the characteristic of being without characteristics (*animitta*).
The nature and characteristics of phenomena are not within the range of speech; because speech cannot express them, they are called 'without demonstration' (*anidarśana*)."

Because it is not an object traversed by mind or mental factors, and because it cannot be confronted by that which possesses resistance (*sapratigha*), it is called "without resistance" (*apratigha*).
Because there is no other characteristic existing apart from the two types of characteristics of the traversed objects, it is called "without characteristics" (*animitta*).
The characteristic of emptiness is non-dual, and is therefore called the "single characteristic.
Because it is not damaged by the poisonous arrows of false attachments such as greed, the true emptiness realized therein is clearly discernible; thus, it is called a "characteristic."
Furthermore, the principle of true emptiness is free from all dharmic characteristics such as existence and non-existence;
therefore, it is called "signless" (animitta). Being signless, it is non-dual, and is thus said to be "one.
It takes this very signlessness as its characteristic, and is therefore called a "characteristic," yet there is no separate characteristic apart from it.
Furthermore, those non-Buddhists speak as follows:
"The teachings of the Buddhas are briefly of two kinds, namely emptiness and non-emptiness.
If the word 'emptiness' is true, then the other teachings must be false."
If even one part of what the Buddha says is true, then the other parts must likewise not be false.
Our own words should be understood in the same way; why then do you categorically reject them, saying they are not to be trusted?
Since you outsiders possess errors regarding manifest phenomena, you are not to be relied upon or trusted. Why is this?
Therefore, the next verse says:
"Observing the present, there is still delusion; knowing the future, it is certainly unreal.
The commentary states:

Those heterodox practitioners have minds confounded by false perceptions; if they still possess such inversions regarding shallow and mundane matters, how could they possibly be free from error concerning the principles of cause and effect in the future life, which are profound, distant, and difficult to know?
Therefore, what has been stated cannot be relied upon or believed.
In what superficial matter do I hold a misconception? It is this:

the Vaiśeṣikas maintain that categories such as "sameness" and "difference" are objects of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), while the Sāṃkhyas maintain that sensations such as suffering and pleasure are objects of direct perception.
Such matters as these are infinite in number, and all involve inversion.
Why is this so? For example, the Vaiśeṣika school maintains that categories such as "sameness" and "difference" are objects of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), yet their reasoning is untenable.

The conceptualizing mental consciousness that discriminates the nature of oxen, horses, and so forth, is a provisional designation applied to phenomena such as form; it transcends the sense faculties and their objects and is not obtained through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), because it is undifferentiated across all its bases, like a composite entity.

They postulate a sixth category of meaning, "conjunction" (*saṃyoga*), whose essence is a single entity pervading all its substrates; it transcends both sense faculties and objects and is not apprehended by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
The same applies to the natures of "identity" (*sāmānya*) and so forth. How, then, can these be maintained to be the objects of direct perception?
Furthermore, that treatise asserts that the category of "substance" (dravya-padārtha) is an object of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
This reasoning is also incorrect. Why is this so?

Objects such as jars and garments are merely provisionally designated by the conceptualizing consciousness upon the basis of dharmas such as color and so forth; how then can they be grasped as objects of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*)?

Yet, that treatise states that because objects such as jars and garments possess qualities (*guṇa*), actions (*karman*), substances (*dravya*), and real identity (*sāmānya*) and difference (*viśeṣa*), as well as inherence (*samavāya*), they are seen by the eye and touched by the body; therefore, they are known through the sense bases (*indriya*) as objects of direct perception.
This is certainly not the case.

First, it is clarified that the real cognition (vastujñāna) induced by qualities (guṇa) is not subsumed under direct perception (pratyakṣa). That is to say, the real cognition induced by various qualities such as blue or warmth is definitely not subsumed under the direct perceptions of seeing or touching. This is because it is produced based on the conjunction with other characteristics, rather than being produced by the real entity (dravya) itself—such as karma or its specific difference (sāmānyaviśeṣa)—just like the real cognition induced by fragrance or taste.
The same applies to the real cognition induced by karma: it should be refuted through inference as appropriate.

That is to say, the real cognition induced by various karmas is likewise not subsumed under direct perception (pratyakṣa) such as seeing or touching, because it is produced based on and following other characteristics, being induced by a real entity that is neither identical nor different [from its cause], just like the real cognition induced by odors or tastes.
Real cognition is produced by means of real entities, just as one perceives a jar and knows it to be an ox and so forth.

Since the various categories of real entities such as jars have already been refuted as being neither seen nor touched, the real cognition they induce has likewise been refuted; for the cognition of jars and the like can only arise based on qualities (*guṇa*) and activities (*karman*), both of which have already been refuted previously. Therefore, such cognition is also not subsumed under direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).

The knowledge of reality (bhūtajñāna) induced by the nature of identity and difference is likewise not subsumed under direct perception (pratyakṣa) through seeing or touching, because it arises in dependence upon the conjunction with other characteristics. For example, all cognitions such as "non-reality" are called non-real cognitions; regarding qualities (guṇa), actions (karman), and so forth, the statement "this is not real" arises in dependence upon the conjunction with other characteristics, and therefore it is certainly not subsumed under direct perception through seeing or touching.
The same applies to other types of cognition.

From this, one should understand that all cognitions produced through the conventional conjunction of words and meanings are not true direct perceptions (*pratyakṣa*) of their objects. That is to say, a cognition that takes a real entity as its object is not itself real, because it is a direct perception of a real entity produced through conventional conjunction, just like the cognition of qualities (*guṇa*) and so forth.

In this way, even the cognition of the conjunction of conditions is not ultimately real, because it arises from the provisional aggregation of those conditions, like the cognition of reality (*yathābhūta-jñāna*).

Therefore, one should not maintain that among the six categories (*ṣaṭpadārtha*) there exists an object of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). Consequently, the Vaiśeṣika school is mistaken even regarding immediate and mundane matters of the present.

Furthermore, those Sāṃkhyas maintain that dharmas such as form are composed of the three *guṇas*, and that these are real rather than conventional, being apprehended by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
This reasoning is also incorrect, because they are composed of multiple factors, like an army or a forest.
Form and the other [aggregates] should be merely conventional; how then can they be said to be real?
Furthermore, because the three—pleasure and so forth—differ in their intrinsic natures, they should not become one, just as they do not in their untransformed state.
Moreover, if dharmas such as form were substantially existent, they should not be composed of the three, just like pleasure and the others.
Furthermore, since the three—pleasure and the others—each have distinct characteristics, how could they be combined to form a single characteristic?
It is impossible for them to transform into a single characteristic at the time of their conjunction, because their essence is no different from what it was before they were conjoined.

Furthermore, since the three natures—pleasure and so forth—are each distinct, their characteristics should not be identical; for you maintain that nature and characteristic are definitively one, it follows that the nature should be identical to the characteristic, and the characteristic should be as distinct as the nature.

Furthermore, pleasure and so forth are particulars, while form and so forth are the general; since you maintain that the general and the particular are definitely one, it follows that the general should be threefold and not one, just like the particulars, or the particulars should be one and not three, just like the general. How then can three particulars constitute one general?

Furthermore, at the time of transformation, if the three qualities—pleasure and the others—do not combine to form a single characteristic, then their characteristics would remain distinct as they were prior to transformation, and it should not be perceived that a single object, such as color, exists.

If the three [qualities] were to combine to form a single characteristic, they would lose their distinct characteristics as pleasure and so forth; nor can it be said that each of the three qualities—pleasure and the rest—possesses two characteristics:
one general and one particular.
Why is this? If the general characteristic were one, it could not be three;
if the general characteristic were three, one could not perceive it as one.

If it is argued that each [feeling], such as pleasure and so forth, possesses the three characteristics of pleasure and so forth, and because they are mutually blended with their common characteristics, they are difficult to discern—therefore one perceives only one—this too is not correct.
Since each [of the three natures] possesses three characteristics, one should likewise perceive all three; how then can one perceive only a single one?
Furthermore, how can it be known that pleasure and the others are distinct?
Moreover, if each individual [atom] possessed all three characteristics, why would they need to aggregate together to constitute form and so forth?
Consequently, each [quality] should be able to individually constitute the distinct sense organs and objects, such as form and so forth, for my enjoyment.
Furthermore, since these three qualities each possess three characteristics that differ from one another, how could form and the others have a single characteristic?

Furthermore, if each [quality] such as pleasure were able to constitute each phenomenon such as form, and if the essence of each phenomenon were composed of the three [qualities], then all phenomena—whether in terms of their intrinsic nature or their associations—would be indistinguishable, because they would all equally be constituted by the three qualities and the three characteristics.

If that were so, all causes and effects such as the great elements (mahābhūta) and so forth—consisting merely of the dimensions of the great elements and the various sense organs—would fail to account for anything perceived by the world, whether sentient or insentient, pure or impure, and other such entities.
Direct perception, inference, and other means of valid cognition would likewise lack any distinction, which contradicts what is currently perceived by the world and results in a great fallacy.
Although there are many such tenets held by non-Buddhist false teachers, none are reasonable; for who could possibly stir up a heap of excrement?
Within my Buddha-dharma, there are many generals of the Dharma who have already crushed those enemies; therefore, I need not trouble myself with further words.

Thus, when it comes to shallow and mundane matters, even on a level path in broad daylight, these non-Buddhists still stumble and fall—how much less could they possibly avoid error when confronted with the profound and remote, the perilous and impassable thickets of the great night of deep darkness?
Who among those with discernment would believe such false words and cease their return [to the truth]?
Therefore, it is said again in verse:
"Those who rely on his teachings and practice them Will be deceived without end."
The commentary states:

If sentient beings follow the teachings and practices of those non-Buddhists who possess obscured vision and perverted attachments, they are sustained by the habitual tendencies of false views resulting from the power of evil friends and heterodox teachings; consequently, they slander the Dharma realized by the Tathāgata, thereby incurring immeasurable and boundless karmic offenses.
Due to these causes and conditions, one falls into the various evil destinies and undergoes great sorrow and suffering with no prospect of escape.

Therefore, the wise should not follow the example of fools who deceive themselves by following the conduct of evil companions; rather, they should follow the true, faultless, and holy teachings of the Buddhas that swiftly lead to liberation and practice accordingly.
Furthermore, as stated above, the Buddha’s sūtras speak of various inconceivable supernormal transformations and also explain the profound and true principles of reality.
Sentient beings are unable to fathom them, and so forth, as explained at length.
That such matters as these are difficult to believe and understand is indeed as you have said.

Because the principles explained regarding the merits of all Buddhas are exceedingly profound, they are difficult to believe and understand. You, being foolish, of meager merit and little wisdom, seeking only your own benefit and unwilling to save others, have not yet drunk the nectar-like flavor of the Dharma of Great Compassion; how then could you believe and comprehend such a Dharma-gate?

Only those who possess the light of wisdom that shatters the darkness of ignorance, who with deep-seated compassion pity all sentient beings, and who seek the Bodhi of the Buddha while possessing vast merit, are able to believe in and understand such a Dharma-gate.

It is said that throughout immeasurable kalpas in the past, the Tathāgatas perfumed their minds with the lineage of compassion and wisdom; for the sake of uprooting the great suffering of birth and death for sentient beings and for the sake of seeking unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, they reverently made offerings to all Buddhas, heard the true Dharma, and applied their mindfulness in contemplation. They cultivated and accumulated boundless practices in accordance with the Dharma—namely, generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom—as well as various other difficult-to-perform, subtle, and supreme practices. Having practiced these with earnest gravity and without interruption until they were perfected, they realized unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment and attained inconceivable, sovereign spiritual powers.
The wondrous functions induced by the original vow are inexhaustible; for what reason, then, do you not have faith and understanding in this?
We see in the world that mechanical devices and the like are moved and operated solely by the force of prior momentum.
Such are the Tathāgata’s sublime supernatural transformations, which are spontaneously performed as drawn forth by his original vows.
Furthermore, it is like a worldly practitioner of illusion who, having attained complete mastery, displays inconceivable and wondrous feats before a great multitude.
How much less can the Tathāgata’s long-cultivated supreme meditative concentration, his fully perfected excellence, and his miraculous powers be measured?

Therefore, you should give rise to faith and understanding toward the inconceivable deeds of the Tathāgatas; you should seek with a sincere heart the Buddha’s perfect virtues and sovereign supernormal powers, and never harbor negligence.
There are śrāvakas who, regarding the Buddha’s boundless and inconceivable power, know for themselves that they have no part in it; their lamentations and cries of grief shake the trichiliocosm.
How can you all slander and disbelieve this?
Furthermore, those who possess wisdom attain nirvāṇa by themselves, whereas those of dull consciousness, even if they encounter a teacher, are unable to follow and learn from them.
To clarify this meaning, a verse is spoken:
"The wise attain nirvāṇa by themselves; This is what makes possible that which is difficult to do."
"The fool encounters a virtuous guide, yet lacks the mind to follow him.
The Commentary says:
"The entanglements of afflictions have existed since beginningless time; through repeated habituation they have become firm, strong, and difficult to sever."
Nirvāṇa is empty, tranquil, signless, and nameless; its supreme virtues are boundless, lofty, profound, and difficult to realize.

Those who possess wisdom do not rely on the teachings of others, but can naturally cross the great ocean of birth and death and realize ultimate *parinirvāṇa*; such great men are capable of performing what is difficult to perform.

Fools have long been submerged in the mire of various desires; indulging in the flavors of pleasure and entertainment, they seek no liberation. They are like dogs greedily gnawing at a blood-stained, dried bone, which they refuse to let go even when coerced with a staff.
Fools are likewise; though they relish and cling to various desires, they do not feel weary of them even when rebuked by the words of the Sages.
Such wise ones, however, naturally awaken and realize great *nirvāṇa*; this is what is difficult to accomplish.
Fools are heedless and lack discernment; though they encounter the words of the Noble Ones, they do not aspire for quiescence.

Furthermore, since the suffering of saṃsāra is extreme and the bliss of nirvāṇa is ultimate—such that their respective faults and virtues are coarse, manifest, and easy to understand—how is it that sentient beings remain complacent and do not desire to turn away from saṃsāra and aspire toward nirvāṇa?

Because those fools possess fear— specifically, because they harbor self-love and hear that *nirvāṇa* is empty, they dread that upon realizing *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*, their "self" would be annihilated—
it is due to this fear that they do not wish to weary of or turn away from *saṃsāra*, nor do they aspire to proceed toward *nirvāṇa*.
Such fear arises from a lack of wisdom. Why is this?
Therefore, the following verse says:
"One who does not know has no fear; the same is true for one who knows all.
It is from knowing only a small portion that fear arises.
The commentary says:
If sentient beings were entirely devoid of discerning wisdom and lacked understanding of all phenomena, they would not give rise to fear regarding nirvāṇa.

However, those who thoroughly know the true principle of all phenomena realize both saṃsāra and nirvāṇa: that when saṃsāra arises, it is merely the arising of conventional suffering, and when saṃsāra ceases, it is merely the cessation of conventional suffering. Since there is fundamentally no self and all phenomena are empty, such individuals have no fear whatsoever of nirvāṇa.

If there are those who understand only that at the time of parinirvāṇa all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) cease and become utterly non-existent, yet do not know that the suffering inherent in conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*) ceases spontaneously of its own accord, lacking any substantial essence or function, and being devoid of self and what belongs to a self (*ātman* and *ātmīya*).
Sustained by the view of a self and by self-love, they hear that in *nirvāṇa* there is emptiness and nothingness; fearing the annihilation of the self, they give rise to dread.
Such dread arises from a lack of wisdom; therefore, those with wisdom should correctly eliminate and sever it.
Furthermore, fear does not arise because of a lack of familiarity. Why is this?
Therefore, the subsequent verse says:
"The dharmas that flow with the current of birth and death are constantly practiced by the foolish;
they have never cultivated the逆流 (counter-flow), and for this reason they give rise to fear.
The commentary says:

All ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*) are called "fools" (*bāla*); they are not devoid of the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) of the afflictions (*kleśa*), and they delight in birth, loathe death, and take no pleasure in *nirvāṇa*.

Since beginningless time, they have repeatedly experienced the desirable maturations (*vipāka*) of the path to higher rebirth (*abhyudaya-mārga*), yet they have never cultivated the path to definitive excellence (*niḥśreyasa-mārga*) or the path to higher rebirth.

The various fruits of karmic maturation (*vipāka*) serve as the basis for latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) such as craving; though they are constantly scorched by the fires of suffering, beings do not perceive this and instead indulge in joy and play. Because they habitually practice within the suffering of *saṃsāra*, they fail to recognize its faults and lack the mind of renunciation, remaining ignorant of the faultless flavor of bliss found in liberation.
Because they have never known nor delighted in practicing for realization, these foolish people take pleasure in the suffering of saṃsāra and lack any aspiration for the bliss of liberation—
just as a pig in a sty delights in filth and dung, finding no joy in cleanliness or fine food.
Because they have not practiced it habitually, upon hearing its name mentioned, they are unable to accept it with faith and instead give rise to fear.

All those who possess wisdom should, through the power of analytical discernment, correctly and diligently seek the bliss of liberation; let them not be like foolish people who perversely conceive aversion and fear.

Furthermore, for those who seek liberation through non-erroneous means—whether by nature virtuous or through the power of wisdom—and who are about to cultivate the expedient means for realizing true vision, if one creates obstacles therein, the measure of the karmic offense incurred will be boundless.
To clarify this meaning, a verse is spoken:
"Those foolish people who obstruct others' true vision Have no means to be born in the happy realms; How, then, could they realize nirvana?"
The Commentary states:
The vision of true emptiness is the cause for realizing perfect, unsurpassed wisdom, and it is also the expedient means for the eternal cessation of all that is meaningless—namely, nirvana.
This path of skillful means is the source from which inconceivable merit arises; by means of it, one progressively and swiftly realizes bodhi.

Abiding not in nirvāṇa, its benefit and joy are inexhaustible; according to the differing faculties and natures of the immeasurable sentient beings to be converted, it establishes seeds, brings them to maturity, and provides endless benefit and joy.

There are certain foolish people whose own eye of wisdom is shrouded by the darkness of ignorance, such that they do not perceive true emptiness; furthermore, through false teachings and other expedient means, they obstruct the cultivation of the aforementioned merits by others. The karmic offenses they incur are immeasurable and boundless, and only a Tathāgata can know their limit.

Because their minds have been defiled and corrupted by grave and evil karma, they are very far removed from rebirth in the happy realms; as the latent tendencies and fetters continue in a firm succession, various karmic causes act as heavy obstacles such that even skillful means and compliant patience cannot arise—how, then, could the right view of nirvana be realized?
Knowing that the karmic offenses for obstructing the True Dharma are profound, the wise should protect themselves and refrain from committing them.

Furthermore, those who obstruct others from practicing the True Dharma will later personally induce the arising of false views; the offense of such false views is greater than that of violating the precepts.
To clarify this meaning, the verse further states:
"It is better to violate the precepts than to damage right view.
The commentary says:
As stated in the sūtras: "It would be better to violate pure ethical discipline than to destroy right view.
What is the meaning of this?

One who violates pure ethical discipline harms only themselves; however, one who destroys right view harms both themselves and others, causing immeasurable beings to undergo the fruits of great suffering throughout countless lifetimes and causing them to lose immeasurable and boundless benefit and happiness.
Furthermore, those who violate the precepts, due to their transgression, constantly harbor shame and remorse, and loathe themselves.
Those who destroy right view lack both shame and remorse; they praise and promote false views and are perpetually self-conceited.

Furthermore, for one who violates the precepts, wrong views do not increase; however, if right view is destroyed, unarisen evils of breaking the precepts will arise, and once arisen, they will expand, become firm, and be difficult to destroy.
Furthermore, while violating the pure precepts merely obstructs rebirth in the heavens, destroying right view obstructs the bliss of nirvāṇa. Why is this so?
Therefore, the following verse says:
“Precepts lead to rebirth in happy realms; right view leads to nirvāṇa.
The commentary states:

Although violating the precepts and corrupting one’s views both equally damage the causes of virtue and obstruct the fruits of happiness, violating the precepts is a minor offense, whereas corrupting one’s views is extremely grave.
Why is this? Observing the precepts leads to rebirth in the heavens, which increases the fetters and results in the suffering of birth and death.
Right view enables one to realize the bodhi of the three vehicles and attain the bliss of nirvāṇa; therefore, the wise should not destroy right view.
Furthermore, what is the true principle of all phenomena?
It is the principle that all phenomena are empty and selfless.
If this is so, then this principle also possesses faults.

Why is this? It is because there are some who, upon hearing of emptiness and non-self, claim that all phenomena are non-existent; they thus repudiate the correct principles of cause and effect, even to the point of severing all roots of virtue.
This is a fault of one's own view, not a defect of emptiness or selflessness.

Because of grasping at emptiness wrongly, false views arise and various evil deeds are committed; yet the principle of emptiness and selflessness is beyond the reach of mind and speech, and is not something realized by such [wrongdoers].

When foolish people hear it said that all phenomena are empty, they do not understand the intention of the Noble Ones; they then dismiss even worldly cause and effect as non-existent and destroy all wholesome dharmas.
Is this not the fault of [misunderstanding] emptiness and selflessness?
What is the intent behind the Noble One’s teaching on emptiness?
It is to dispel the clinging to all things as being truly existent.
If that is so, one should likewise teach that all phenomena exist, in order to dispel the false attachment to the emptiness of phenomena.
Indeed, if there are those who cling to the emptiness of all phenomena, the Tathāgata also says that all phenomena exist.
Since he speaks of both existence and emptiness in order to dispel such clinging, is the true reality of all phenomena empty or existent?
The true reality of all phenomena is neither existent nor empty; it cannot be reached by conceptual discrimination or frivolous proliferation.
For what reason, then, do the Noble Ones say it is not false?
It is not false because it serves to eliminate erroneous attachments.
Both the teachings of emptiness and existence are capable of removing attachment; why, then, did the Tathāgata predominantly teach the doctrine of emptiness?

It is because sentient beings for the most part cling to existence, and birth-and-death for the most part arises from this clinging to existence. Therefore, in order to eliminate clinging to existence and extinguish the suffering of birth-and-death, the Tathāgata predominantly taught the doctrine of emptiness.
Whether it be emptiness or existence, both are pedagogical gateways. Why, then, was emptiness previously described as the ultimate truth?
This is not contradictory, for it is a provisional designation employed as a skillful means.

Furthermore, this term "emptiness" is a negation rather than an affirmation; it is not merely the negation of existence, but is itself empty of emptiness. It universally dispels the mind of attachment, leading one to realize the ultimate truth of all phenomena—that they are neither existent nor empty.
The true reality of all phenomena is not emptiness; it is designated as "empty" because emptiness serves as its gateway.
If true reality were not empty, yet emptiness served as its gateway, then true reality would not be existent, and existence should instead serve as the gateway.
There is no fault in speaking of "existence" (or "being") as a provisional gateway;

however, the meaning of this gateway ultimately conforms to emptiness (*śūnyatā*). While notions such as "existence," "non-existence," and so forth all accord with a mind of grasping, notions such as "emptiness of emptiness" and "the emptiness of emptiness" contradict false attachments. Therefore, when a wise person hears the teaching of emptiness, they should abandon all attachments to existence, non-existence, and the like, realize that the true principle of phenomena is neither existent nor non-existent, and refrain from giving rise to the conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) of dualistic distinctions between existence and non-existence.
Furthermore, one should not rashly expound the principles of emptiness and selflessness before those of inferior intelligence, as this would increase their wrong views. Why is this?
Therefore, the next verse says:
"It is better that they give rise to the grasping of a self, rather than the view of emptiness and selflessness;
for the latter leads subsequently to the evil realms, while the former merely turns away from nirvāṇa.
The commentary says:

Those of inferior intelligence in the world claim that the grasping at a self (*ātma-grāha*) is itself the view of a transitory collection (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), and that the view of "mine" (*mamakāra-dṛṣṭi*) is also accompanied by the grasping at a self; therefore, the term "grasping at a self" also includes that latter view.
Although the grasping at a self does not accord with correct reasoning, it is better that it arise, for its faults are light.

Although the view of emptiness and selflessness accords with correct reasoning, they are unable to realize things as they truly are; because of this, they may denigrate and negate all phenomena, and since these faults are grave, it is better that such a view does not arise.
What is the relative gravity of these two faults?

It is said that the former, the attachment to a self, merely turns one away from *nirvāṇa*, whereas the latter, the wrong grasp of emptiness (*durgṛhīta-śūnyatā*), leads toward the evil destinies as well.
Those of inferior wisdom, when wrongly grasping emptiness, even become weary of their own roots of virtue, let alone [feeling compassion for] all sentient beings.

Because he turns his back on the wholesome and the mundane, severing his roots of virtue and harming sentient beings, he not only abandons the coolness of nirvāṇa, but also carries his own body into the fires of hell.
For one who gives rise to the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*), such things do not exist. Why is this?

Because they crave their own pleasure and desire to be free from suffering, they refrain from committing various evils and extensively cultivate all manner of merit; thus they escape the evil realms and do not lose the states of humans and devas. Yet, they only fear *nirvāṇa* and do not realize liberation.

Therefore, the Sūtra says: "It would be better to conceive a view of self as large as Mount Sumeru than to be one who misapprehends emptiness through overweening pride. If this were so, then the principle that all phenomena are empty and selfless would be perilously close to a ruinous state, and the Noble Ones should not have taught it.
It should truly not be spoken before those of inferior wisdom; however, because those of superior wisdom attain great benefit by practicing accordingly, it must be taught to them. Why is this so?
Therefore, the subsequent verse says:
"The sublime principle of emptiness and selflessness, The true realm of all Buddhas,
Able to terrify all evil views, The non-dual gate to nirvāṇa."
The Commentary says:
For one seeking liberation, there is no other expedient means capable of realizing nirvāṇa apart from the sublime contemplation of emptiness.
For a wise person wishing to remove the defilement of various false views, there is no superior expedient means other than this.

Because those who possess views cling to the existence of an objective referent, like other proponents of views who do not realize nirvāṇa, they are likewise unable to remove the defilements of various wrong views.

Those who cultivate this practice of emptiness to its ultimate conclusion can realize the supreme fruit of unsurpassed bodhi; they then skillfully reveal it to all sentient beings, further enabling them to perfectly realize the sublime fruit they seek.

For those who are able to accomplish the benefit and happiness of both themselves and others, the contemplation of emptiness and selflessness is the supreme cause; therefore, one should skillfully understand the faculties and natures of sentient beings and employ expedient means to reveal and teach [the Dharma] so that they may awaken and enter [it].
Furthermore, the Tathāgata, in order to eliminate the demons of evil views, has preached the *agada* medicine of emptiness and non-self.
Why is this so? When those with evil views hear the name of "emptiness," they all give rise to fear; through this, they are gradually tamed and naturally find relief.
To clarify this meaning, a verse is spoken:
"When fools hear the name of the Dharma of emptiness, They all give rise to great fear;
Like seeing one of great power, The timid and weak all flee."
The Commentary states:
The foolish say that evil views damage and obscure the eye of wisdom; yet when they hear the name of emptiness, the life-force of all their evil views is naturally destroyed.

Although emptiness has no intention to harm evil views, its power is so great that upon hearing its name, they perish of their own accord—just as a coward loses his wits upon hearing the name of a tiger.

Furthermore, it is like a well-trained elephant-king in the world whose temples glisten with sweat; although he has no intention to harm living beings, because of the elephant’s great majesty and power, those who see or hear him flee in terror.

The principle of emptiness is likewise; because its power is great, it causes those with wrong views to be struck with terror upon hearing its name, whereby their [wrong views] are naturally diminished and extinguished.
The principle of emptiness is without intention and does not act to harm things; yet for one who realizes the principle of emptiness, it should result in the harming of others.
If one realizes true emptiness, the mind becomes tranquil, equanimous, and non-dual; how could such a person wish to harm others?

Nevertheless, for the sake of benefiting and bringing happiness to all sentient beings, they employ skillful means to reveal the principles of emptiness and selflessness, so that those harboring evil views may extinguish them upon hearing this.
To clarify this meaning, the following verse says:
"Although the Buddhas have no [deliberate] mind, They teach the Dharma that crushes the arguments of others;
Yet those arguments collapse of their own accord, Like wild fire consuming kindling."
The Commentary states:

The Buddhas have no intention to refute the arguments of others; rather, for the sake of benefiting and bringing happiness to those beings to be converted, they reveal the broad path traversed by all Buddhas since time immemorial—namely, that the nature and characteristics of all phenomena are empty.
All Tathāgatas of the past and future have traversed this path, leading the deluded multitudes from cause to fruition.
Upon hearing this teaching of emptiness, the heterodox followers and their various evil views will naturally collapse and perish.

It is like a wildfire raging in the mountains and forests: when damp firewood and stacked timber have been dried by the scorching sun, even though no one brings fire to them, the wood draws near the flames as if it were igniting itself.
The various treatises of those with evil views and heterodox followers are likewise; they collapse of their own accord through the power of the teaching of emptiness.
Furthermore, since all the schools of the non-Buddhists assert false existence, the teaching of true emptiness is proclaimed in order to cause them to abandon such views.
Why is this so? Therefore, the subsequent verse says:
"Those who have awakened to the True Dharma will certainly not delight in heterodox doctrines."
"To eliminate other false gates, I shall thus reveal the meaning of true emptiness.
The Commentary states:

Those with wisdom can naturally distinguish the true from the false; encountering this True Dharma, they take no pleasure in heterodox schools. This is like a person who recognizes precious gems: having obtained a priceless jewel, they will never again take pleasure in ordinary crystal beads.

The systems of all non-Buddhist schools establish that which is falsely existent; they are as remote from the True Dharma as a gateway of deception, deluding sentient beings and causing them to lose great benefit.
Therefore, I manifest the Buddhist teaching of true emptiness, so that those heterodox followers may turn toward the truth and turn their backs on the false.
Furthermore, for what reason do non-Buddhists delight in their own heterodox tenets and feel aversion toward the Noble Teaching? It is due to the power of the view of a self (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*).
If they knew there were no self, they would certainly have neither delight nor aversion.
Why is this so? Therefore, the subsequent verse says:
"If one knows the principle of true emptiness and non-self as taught by the Buddha,"
"Following [favorable conditions], one does not give rise to delight; encountering adversity, one has no aversion or fear.
The commentary states:

If one understands the Buddhist teaching on the principle of emptiness and non-self, one severs the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) arising from the view of a self (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*). One observes the world as being like an empty house, and views the cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*) of all false conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) such that there is no delight in prosperity and no aversion toward decline; free from sorrow and joy, and without fear, one remains serene.

If one possesses the view of a self and thinks in terms of "I" being benefited or harmed, then when decline or prosperity arise, sorrow and joy will immediately follow; because of this, there will be endless fear.
Therefore, a person of wisdom should eliminate the grasping at a self.

Furthermore, because the various non-Buddhist groups are attached to the grasping at a self (*ātma-grāha*), they are able to bind themselves and also bind sentient beings; since the harm they cause is so great, they are deeply pitiable.
To clarify this meaning, a verse is spoken:
"Behold the various non-Buddhist groups, Who act as causes for much that is meaningless."
"Who would not feel profound compassion for sentient beings who delight in the True Dharma?
The commentary states:

The various non-Buddhist groups are gripped by craving and self-clinging, which cause both themselves and others to commit immeasurable transgressions, for the view of a personal identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) is the root from which all evils arise.
As it has been said, all evil and unwholesome dharmas arise with the view of a personal identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) as their root.

Among those who cherish wholesome dharmas within the realms of existence, though they lack fixed attachments and follow external conditions, they are nonetheless deluded by the false words of those heterodox outsiders; thus, through craving for the view of a self, they give rise to immeasurable transgressions.
Thus, these non-Buddhists cause both themselves and others to give rise to various kinds of firm fetters; what person of wisdom would not feel compassion for them?

Therefore, sentient beings who delight in the True Dharma and possess pure intentions should give rise to a mind of benefit and happiness and feel deep compassion, diligently teaching them the emptiness of selflessness so that they may cultivate right view and become free from all bonds.
Furthermore, the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas abide eternally in the world, truly possessing a pure mind that seeks to benefit and bring happiness to others.

Why is this? Because there still exist in the world immeasurable sentient beings who believe in heterodoxy, hold perverted views, and slander the Dharma, due to the fact that the objects and wisdom taught by the Buddha are profoundly deep, subtle, and difficult to realize.
The non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) are not so. Why is this?
Therefore, the following verse says:
“The Brahmins, the Nirgranthas, and the three objects of the Tathāgata’s veneration can be known through the eye, the ear, and the mind; therefore, the Buddha-dharma is profound and subtle.
The commentary says:
The various Brahmins merely habitually practice the recitation of empty words as their path; this can be known by the auditory consciousness, yet it is not profound or subtle.

The Nirgrantha heretics merely take the exposure of the body, its foul odors, and various forms of intense self-mortification as their path; this can be known by the visual consciousness, yet it is likewise not profound or subtle.

The holy teaching of the Tathāgata employs the sword of untainted wisdom that realizes true emptiness to forever sever all internal thieves of affliction, thereby attaining unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment to benefit and bring peace and happiness to all sentient beings; its principles, teachings, and underlying intentions are profoundly deep and subtle.

Those who have realized the principle of reality as it truly is may or may not understand the Buddha’s holy teaching; because the principles and teachings of the Buddha are most profound and subtle, outsiders and the ignorant are unable to enter into them.
They place their faith in the coarse and shallow, heterodox teachings of outsiders, while having little faith in the profound and subtle holy teachings of the Tathāgata.

In this world, many place their faith in the Brahmins because the Brahmins frequently practice deception: they recite mantras, offer fire sacrifices, and inflict self-mortification to expiate faults; they falsely contrive auspicious signs and delusively proclaim fortune and calamity. For the sake of a livelihood, they employ various expedients to deceive women, Śūdras, and others, causing them to conceive a sense of rare wonder toward them, providing for all their needs and exalting them as noble and venerable.
In ancient times, the wise Brahmins secretly composed the *Vedas*, claiming they existed naturally; they permitted only themselves to recite them and forbade others from viewing them.
They praised the Brahmins as the most noble and held the Kṣatriyas and others to be lowly and base, asserting that by providing for their needs, one would obtain immeasurable merit.
Fools lacking wisdom are unable to fathom this; they regard it as a true field of merit and offer it worship with faith and reverence.
However, those clearly written [scriptures] do not exist spontaneously, for because they convey specific meanings, they are like conventional worldly speech.
Furthermore, those illuminated scriptures do not fully accord with reason, for they are not the teachings of the Noble Ones and are thus like deceptive speech.

The Brahmin caste is not truly noble nor a genuine field of merit, as they constantly practice begging to support their wives and children; being like impoverished lepers, the wise should not place their faith in them.
Since the Dharma of the Brahmins is already full of deception and fraud, what can be said of the teachings of the Nirgrantha heretics?
The teachings they study mostly conform to ignorance. Why is this so?
Therefore, the subsequent verse says:
"The doctrines revered by the Brahmins mostly incite deceit and fraud;
the teachings of the Nirgrantha heretics for the most part conform to ignorance."
The Commentary states:
The Nirgrantha outsiders do not know the truth at all; they merely crave future pleasure while currently undergoing intense suffering.
Whatever they say is mostly irrational; being of a foolish nature, they gather in groups and are thus trusted and followed by the ignorant of the world.
How can one know for certain that they are foolish?
Because they expose their bodies without shame, they are like madmen, like animals, or like infants.
If the Brahmins were not truly noble and honorable, for what reason would those of high status and excellence also revere and serve them?
Because they habitually recite various *vidyā* treatises, these Brahmins truly possess no knowledge;
yet, for the sake of their livelihood, they recite those *vidyā* treatises at all times, falsely manifesting extraordinary appearances to stir the hearts of others.
Those of noble and superior standing in the world do not examine carefully, yet they honor and serve someone because they believe that person possesses virtue.

Furthermore, although there is no ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) within the treatises on worldly conduct (*loka-śāstra*), they contain some degree of conventional etiquette; because those of noble and superior standing wish to practice and learn these, they extend honor and service even to one who lacks virtue.

As for those others who do not recite the various *vidyā* treatises, they follow the worldly tradition because of their commonality; thus, they neither examine critically nor do they practice with reverence.
How is it that the *Nirgrantha* outsiders, being different from them, are also widely revered by the world?

Because they possess a superficial knowledge of astronomy, the movements of celestial bodies, the interpretation of birds' cries, the deciphering of dreams, and the divination of good and ill fortune, the common and ignorant masses frequently offer them respect and service.

Furthermore, because the Brahmins recite various *vidyā* treatises that are difficult to master, the world collectively honors them; and because the Nirgrantha heretics practice asceticism, the world collectively regards them with compassion.
None of these can bring liberation from birth and death; those who possess wisdom should correctly understand this and not follow such views.
Therefore, the next verse says:
"Out of respect for the Brahmins, They recite various mantras."
"Out of compassion for those who have left the bonds [of worldly life], he torments his own body.
The commentary says:
According to the Dharma of the Brahmins, they diligently recite the various Vedas; because this is considered difficult by the world, they are collectively revered.
However, the various *vidyā* treatises are not causes for liberation, as they consist merely of empty words devoid of actual meaning.
Even the extreme bodily mortifications of the Nirgrantha outsiders are considered difficult to achieve, such that the world collectively regards them with compassion.
Why is self-mortification not a cause for liberation?
Because it is a result of maturation (*vipāka-phala*) and not a wholesome dharma (*kuśala-dharma*).

The physical suffering produced by such acts as plucking out one's hair is summoned by unwholesome conduct in past lives; since it is a karmic maturation and not a wholesome dharma, it is like a pleasant maturation, which is not a cause for liberation.
If it is argued that this suffering arises from present effort and that the cause for it not being a maturation fruit (*vipākaphala*) is thus unestablished, this is also incorrect.

The suffering experienced by that [being] is indeed a maturation fruit, because it is devoid of benefit and is a suffering that arises simultaneously with the material sense faculties (*rūpindriya*) and consciousness, just like the bodily suffering experienced in the hells.
Even within our own school, there are those who do not accept that this suffering is a maturation (*vipāka*); one should resolve this matter by means of the following reasoning:

Any bodily suffering that is not a maturation cannot be the direct cause for realizing liberation, because it is a contaminated (*sāsrava*) physical experience produced by present conditions, just like the pleasure of sexual desire.
Furthermore, that self-inflicted suffering is not a cause for liberation because it contradicts the holy teaching (*āgama*), just like the suffering of self-harm.
The doctrine taught by those teachers is not the holy teaching, because it was not spoken in common by the Tathāgatas and others, just like erotic literature and the like.

Therefore, their self-inflicted suffering is merely summoned by the unwholesome deeds of previous lives and arises from the delusion of the present; it is certainly not a cause capable of realizing true liberation.
Furthermore, some say:
liberation is attained by relying on a superior body; since the Brahmins are the most superior in the world, only Brahmins can realize liberation, and no other classes of beings can attain nirvana.
This argument is incorrect; therefore, the following verse says:
"Just as that which is produced by the karma of suffering Is not the cause of true liberation;
So too, that which is born from superior physical karma Is likewise not the realization of liberation."
The commentary states:
Just as the physical suffering experienced by the followers of the Nirgrantha school is not a cause for liberation because it is the maturation (*vipāka*) of karma,
so too, even if the body of a Brahmin were granted to be noble and superior, it would still be produced by karma and thus not a cause for liberation.
Although this body cannot personally realize liberation, the wholesome states within the body are the causes of liberation.
If that is so, the same applies to the wholesome states of other bodies; why then do you speak only of the Brahmin?

Furthermore, regarding the faculties, objects, and other phenomena of the Brahmins, they are in every respect identical to those of all other classes; how then can they claim that their own are superior and others inferior?
Therefore, such assertions merely deceive the foolish; no person of wisdom should accept them.
However, the Brahmins are not superior to other classes of people on this continent, just like the Śūdras;
nor are the Śūdras and others inferior to that caste, because they are inhabitants of this same continent, just like the Brahmins.
Since it has been stated that all that is taught by non-Buddhists is false, one may wonder what reality exists within the Dharma of the Tathāgata.
To dispel this doubt, a verse is spoken:
"Briefly stated, that which the Buddha has taught Possesses two [features] that distinguish it from other schools."
"By not harming living beings, one attains the realms of humans and devas; by contemplating emptiness, one realizes liberation.
The Commentary states:
Among the immeasurable, profound, and wondrous Dharma-gates taught by the Buddha, the essentials for bringing benefit and happiness to sentient beings are of only two kinds:
First, non-harming can cause one to be reborn among gods and humans;
second, contemplating emptiness can lead to the realization of liberation.

The intention to harm or afflict others, along with the physical and verbal actions arising therefrom, is collectively termed "harming. To sever such harmful factors as described and to cultivate various virtuous causes is called "non-harming," which refers to the ten wholesome courses of action, the four means of integration—generosity, kind speech, beneficial conduct, and cooperation—as well as the meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*) and formless absorptions (*ārūpyasamāpatti*).
By means of this, one attains rebirth in the auspicious realms of humans and devas, experiencing various sublime and stainless karmic fruits.
Relying upon this, one is able to eliminate all afflictions and cultivate immeasurable roots of goodness.

Suchness and the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi) are called "emptiness" because they are free from characteristics. By correctly contemplating this emptiness, one realizes the bliss of nirvāṇa—the principle of emptiness and non-self—and within all phenomena, there are no marks and no names; all are of a single flavor, quiescent and peaceful. This is precisely nirvāṇa, for it must necessarily be realized through the contemplation of emptiness.
Thus, these two causes for rebirth in the happy realms and liberation can be found in their entirety only within the Buddha's teaching.
Although non-Buddhists speak of limited causes such as generosity that lead to birth among humans or devas, they are not complete.

Why is this? It is because those non-Buddhists lack the wisdom that analytically discerns cause and effect; they do not state that mental volition produces superior merit; and they possess no dharma of the distinct discipline of liberation (*prātimokṣa-saṃvara*).
If one does not even fully understand the coarse karma that leads to the happy realms, how much more so would the sublime cause for nirvāṇa be beyond one's reach?
Since the principles and teachings spoken by the Tathāgata are complete and perfect, why would the followers of external paths not take delight in them?
Because the Buddha’s true teaching contradicts their false tenets and opposes what they originally craved, they do not rejoice in it.
To clarify this meaning, a verse is spoken:
"Worldly people are attached to their own schools, Just as one loves one's native land."
"The True Dharma can utterly destroy them, / And the faction of the heterodox finds no joy.
The Commentary says:
Just as one may find that one's native land is not fertile or rich, yet having dwelt within it for a long time, one does not wish to leave.

One's own school is likewise; although it contradicts reason, one cannot abandon it because of its ancestral lineage. One does not even desire to take pleasure in the doctrines of other non-Buddhist schools, much less aspire to the nectar-like holy teachings of the Tathāgata.

The fire of wisdom regarding the profound reality of true emptiness can burn away the accumulated fuel of the heterodox attachments of non-Buddhists; because these contradict their own fundamental nature, they find no joy therein.
All who possess wisdom should reflect well upon this, lest they become defiled by heterodox schools and thereby contravene the True Dharma.
Furthermore, the Buddha-dharma shines universally like the full orb of the sun; those who seek supreme wisdom should have faith in it.
To clarify this meaning, a verse is spoken:
"The wise who seek supreme virtue Should believe and accept the True Doctrine."
"The True Dharma is like the orb of the sun; Those with eyes are able to see it because of this.
The Commentary says:
This passage demonstrates that one must possess two qualities to be able to have faith in the Mahāyāna:
First, there is knowledge;
second, there is the aspiration for sublime qualities.

The Mahāyāna can extinguish all heterodox systems and, by conforming to the Mahāyāna, brings great benefit: namely, that one can personally realize unsurpassed nirvāṇa and cause other sentient beings to likewise emerge from birth and death.

The True Dharma of the Mahāyāna is like that orb of the sun, universally dispelling the darkness of ignorance for the sake of the world. Those who possess the eye of wisdom, by means of the light of this Dharma, clearly perceive the true and the false; turning away from the heterodox and following the orthodox, avoiding peril and seeking peace, they accomplish the benefit and happiness of both themselves and others without exception.

All those who possess wisdom should have faith in the Mahāyāna; they must not heed heterodox schools that revile the True Dharma, thereby sinking themselves into the mire of saṃsāra and deluding sentient beings so that they lose their great benefit.
The wise differ from the foolish in that they discern right from wrong; let the wise not resemble the foolish by failing to distinguish the true from the false.

If you possess a sincere mind intent on benefiting and bringing happiness to others, you should employ the Mahāyāna to subvert the heterodox and establish the orthodox, diligently cultivate the contemplation of emptiness to swiftly realize Bodhi, and bring benefit and happiness to sentient beings until the end of the future.
The Commentary on the Extensive Hundred Verses of the Mahāyāna, Fascicle Six.
The Commentary on the Extensive Hundred Verses of the Mahāyāna, Fascicle Seven.
Composed by Āryadeva Bodhisattva; explained by Dharmapāla Bodhisattva.

Chapter Five: Refuting the Sense Organs and Their Objects. Furthermore, regarding what was stated above—that the sense organs, objects, and so forth shall later be extensively refuted—I shall now explain that.

The sense faculties (*indriya*) are the bases for the discernment of objects; wishing now to refute the faculties, one first eliminates their objects. Once the objects have been eliminated, the faculties likewise perish along with them.
The Kāpila says:
"Objects such as jars and garments are composed solely of color and other [sensory qualities]; the entities that are the domains of the faculties are substantially real."
To refute this view, a verse is spoken:
"Among the various parts of a jar, only form is visible;
to say that the entire jar is visible— how can such a claim lead to the realization of reality?"
The Commentary says:

According to your own school’s doctrine, the various faculties such as the eye each apprehend their respective objects without confusion; the eye perceives only color-form (*rūpa*), whereas a jar pertains to all four sense-objects (*catur-viṣaya*). How could one perceive the entire substance of a jar at the very moment of perceiving its color-form?
This demonstrates that the substance of the jar is not visible to the eye because it is not merely color (*rūpa*), just like sound and so forth. [Objection:
Is it not the case that the substance of the jar is also color?

[Response: I do not say that the substance of the jar is *not* color; rather, I say that the substance of the jar is not established by color alone. Therefore, the reason (*hetu*) I have posited does not suffer from the fallacy of being unestablished (*asiddha*).
Since you already contradict manifest reality, how can your claim to have realized the truth be believed?
It is just as when the eye perceives only color and not a jar; the same applies to odors and so forth.
Therefore, the subsequent verse says:
"All those of superior wisdom, following the meaning previously explained,
should likewise negate all categories of odor, flavor, and tactile objects."
The Commentary states:

Since the objects of the olfactory, gustatory, and tactile faculties each differ, the claim that they collectively apprehend the substance of a jar is also untenable; a jar is not an object apprehended by these three faculties.

Each of these inferences should be understood as previously explained. Since sound is not eternal, it is not mentioned here; by analogy with form and the other [sensory objects], the same should apply to sound.

Thus, all such things as jars, clothing, and carts are not objects apprehended by the material sense-faculties (*rūpīndriya*); they are not necessarily apprehended by the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) as external objects, for that must follow the lead of the material sense-faculties.
Since objects such as vases are not the domain of the sensory faculties, the mental faculty (*manas*) should likewise be so.
If this were not the case, then those who are blind or deaf would also be able to cognize external objects such as visible forms.
Thus, objects such as jars are not within the range of the sense faculties; they all arise from the conceptual construction of one's own mind.

If it is argued that because the substance of a jar and so forth is no different from the substance of dharmas such as color, the various faculties—such as the eye—would likewise apprehend jars and the like just as they apprehend their respective objects, and therefore the faculties could also gradually apprehend objects such as jars; [this is not so].

If that were so, then jars and the like would be objects of all the sense faculties, which contradicts the principle that each faculty perceives its own specific object; or else, the substance of a single jar and such would have to become manifold.
Perhaps the sense faculties do not apprehend the jar and so forth, because only the entities of color and so on constitute the objects of the faculties.
Since color and the other [sensory qualities] are individually not the jar, how could they, when combined, constitute the real entity of a jar?

If it is argued that since jars and the like are composites of many parts, one speaks of "seeing the jar" when seeing a single part—just as seeing a part of a city is called "seeing the city"—this is also not the case.
For a city is not real; its substance is merely conventional, being a composite of many parts. When only one part is seen, it cannot be called seeing the whole.
If jars and the like are thus merely conventional and not real, how can you maintain that they are substantially visible?
Furthermore, it is logically untenable to say they are visible based on seeing only a single part; therefore, the next verse says:
"If one sees only the color of the jar, And yet claims to see the jar itself;..."
"Since one does not see the fragrance and so forth, it should be called 'not seeing the jar.
The treatise says:

If there are many constituent parts within a composite whole, and the whole receives its name based on one part—such as saying "one sees the jar" because one sees the color-part within a single jar—then since the remaining parts such as fragrance are not seen, one should say "one does not see the jar" based on those many parts. Furthermore, one should not claim that the substance of color is superior [to other parts], because it is merely one part of the jar, just like fragrance and the rest.
Since form (*rūpa*) and so forth possess neither superiority nor inferiority relative to the jar, they ought to be designated as "invisible" based on their fragrance and other qualities.

In worldly nomenclature, names are established either according to what is predominant or according to what is most excellent. Since form possesses none [of these] while fragrance and the others possess at least one, jars and such should be designated as "invisible" based on their fragrance and other qualities.

In that case, external matter (bāhyarūpa) would also not be real, because it is of a visible nature and is subsumed under a portion of non-visible phenomena such as jars and garments, just like odors and so forth.
The world commonly knows that the color of a jar is visible; how, then, can it be established as invisible?

What is known in the world conforms to the transformations of one's own mind; it is conventionally described as "visible," yet it is not an external, real color. Now, by negating that there is anything truly visible existing outside the mind, there is no contradiction with the doctrine of invisibility, for such [external] things do not exist at all.
It should be said that it is ineffable. Why is this?
Because the visible does not exist, it is called "invisible. Since a non-existent dharma is utterly non-existent, how can it be described?
It may be argued that visible phenomena can be explained to others because they possess substantial reality;
however, this is not the case.
Even phenomena lacking substantial reality serve as grounds for explanation; were it otherwise, the term "visible" would necessarily be non-existent.
Furthermore, one sees that form provides no benefit whatsoever; for what reason, then, is form said to be "visible"?
It is not that it is invisible. Why is this so?

It is not by virtue of being seen or not being seen that form becomes different; why then is form said to be "visible" on account of being seen, rather than being said to be "invisible" on account of not being seen?

Just as a jar is said to be visible because the color upon it is visible, so too should the jar be said to be invisible because its fragrance and other qualities are invisible; for the reasoning is the same.
Furthermore, when the eye sees it, one says that form is visible; when the eye does not see it, one should likewise say that form is invisible, for the logic is the same in both cases.
Since there is already the sense of visibility and invisibility regarding both the jar and its form, why do you now specifically refute visibility and establish invisibility?
What is visible gives rise to grasping; because this [grasping] is negated by what is "invisible," it is called invisible, but this does not establish the color of the jar as being invisible.
Furthermore, color is not entirely visible in its totality; how, then, can one speak of seeing the jar on account of its color?
Why is this so? Therefore, the subsequent verse says:
"As for obstructive forms, their substance is not entirely visible."
"Those parts and the space between them are separated by these very parts.
The treatise says:
"Obstructed matter is not entirely visible; those parts and the intervening space are separated by these [other] parts, as in the case of a wall and so forth."
Regarding all forms (*rūpa*), although one part may be seen while the rest is not, they should therefore be called "invisible," just like a jar.
Among these various parts, this particular part is not superior, while the other parts are more numerous; thus, it should be called "invisible" according to the majority.

As coarse matter is gradually analyzed, it always possesses multiple parts until one reaches the ultimate atom (*paramāṇu*); yet when it reaches the state of an ultimate atom, it is no longer an object of the physical sense faculties. Therefore, all material forms are invisible.
Is it not the case that the outer surfaces of atoms are spread out laterally without any obstruction between them, such that they abide in immediate proximity and could be seen in their entirety?

Since the collective characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) of the multitude of atoms is provisional and not real, and each individual particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) is not an object of the sensory faculties, how can one establish that material phenomena (*rūpadharma*) exist substantially as wholes that are visible in their entirety, given that atoms which possess resistance have spatial distinctions of "this side" and "that side"?

Although the general characteristics of atoms as a whole are provisional, and each individual atom dwelling in isolation cannot be perceived, yet when atoms aggregate and assist one another such that they cannot be analyzed apart, they possess spatial orientations of "this side" and "that side"; therefore, each individual atom possesses a real substantial entity whose entirety can be perceived.
This is also not the case.
Therefore, the subsequent verse says:
"Whether atoms possess parts or not, one should examine and investigate this with careful scrutiny."
"The citation does not constitute proof; the argument can ultimately not be established.
The treatise says:

Since atoms also combine with other things, they should—like gross objects—possess parts and be conventional. It has already been demonstrated in the "Refutation of Permanence" that atoms possess parts and are not real.
Since individual atoms (*paramāṇu*) cannot be seen, how can they be seen when combined and assisting one another?
If, while assisting one another, they do not relinquish their original characteristics, they should not be able to assist;

if they relinquish their original characteristics, they would no longer be atoms. For if they were as subtle as before at the time of mutual assistance, there would be no capacity for assistance, and they should remain invisible.
If they were transformed into something coarse, they would no longer be atoms (*paramāṇu*); they would be conventional designations rather than real entities.
