Furthermore, if both the substance and function were non-existent at the time of arising, the conjunction of causes and conditions would have nothing to effect.
As has been stated previously, that which exists does not arise from non-existence; therefore, the state of the time of arising is existent and not non-existent.
Since that which has already arisen possesses no further distinct state, one should not establish a separate "time of arising.
Furthermore, it is logically sound to accept that there is no such thing as a distinct time of arising.
The fool remains stubbornly persistent; let us briefly further investigate: at the time of arising, is it non-existent or existent?
If it exists, it has already arisen; if it is non-existent, it has not yet arisen. Apart from these two, what could constitute the essential substance of the state of "arising"?
To clarify this principle, he further spoke in verse:
"When it exists, it is called 'already arisen'; When it does not exist, it is called 'not yet originated.
Apart from these positions of existence and non-existence, Who else could be said to be in the process of arising?"
The treatise says:
When examining the nature of that which you maintain arises, it does not exceed two possibilities—namely, existence and non-existence.

Since it is subsumed within these two states of existence and non-existence, there is no separate "time of arising" in between; for what reason do you irrationally and arbitrarily cling to such a notion?
This [point] is extremely coarse and shallow, yet you are still deluded by it; how much more so, then, could you conceive of or fathom that which is profound and subtle?
Therefore, you should believe and accept that there is no distinct time of arising.
Since the time of arising does not exist, how can arising itself exist?
Therefore, all phenomena are in reality without arising.
Since arising is truly non-existent, abiding and cessation are likewise so.
Because arising must precede them, the principle that they do not exist is established; thus, one does not separately designate the two characteristics of abiding and cessation.

Furthermore, having already refuted in detail the prior existence or non-existence of the effect, the following verse is stated at the end of this chapter to provide a general summary that negates the prior existence of the effect and so forth:
“For those who maintain that there is no distinct result produced apart from its cause,
the processes of arising and ceasing cannot logically be established.”
The Commentary states:
According to the tenets of the Sāṃkhya school, the effect is not separate from its cause.
The effect is identical to its cause, and its substance is substantially existent by nature.
In this way, the arising and ceasing of the essence of the fruit are not established; for the fruit is not separate from the cause, as it would share the permanence of the cause.

Since there is no principle of distinction between the essences of cause and fruit, and the nature of all phenomena is permanent—neither increasing nor decreasing—then any effort exerted would be in vain. To accomplish even the slightest effect would contradict your own treatise.

That which exists cannot be extinguished, and that which does not exist cannot arise; therefore, the "Great One" (*mahat*) and other principles should likewise lack the meaning of arising and ceasing, because they are self-natures (*svabhāva*), just like pleasure, pain, and delusion.
Furthermore, the Great One should not arise from its own self-nature; for a thing to produce itself contradicts what is observed in the world.
In that case, all that is directly perceived in the world—causality, arising and ceasing, and functional activity—would be entirely non-existent.
If you disparage even what is known through worldly perception, how could you possibly believe in or accept profound and hidden meanings?

Observing in this way, one sees that arising is not at all substantially real; because arising lacks reality, cessation is likewise non-existent in reality. It is only in accordance with worldly convention that we speak of arising and cessation.

What is spoken of according to worldly convention is conventional and not ultimate; within the principle of the supreme truth (*paramārtha*), there is neither arising nor cessation, and the nature of all phenomena (*dharmatā*) is neither annihilated nor eternal.
Since arising and ceasing are non-existent, dharmas should be eternally abiding; yet, as extensively refuted previously, the nature of permanence does not truly exist.
If that were so, there would be no nature of any dharma whatsoever.
This is not the case, for I maintain that conventional dharmas are not non-existent.

Is it not the case that our school teaches a single self-nature which, through the power of transformation, can accomplish anything; and although it accomplishes all things, it is free from faults such as arising and ceasing, or annihilation and permanence?
Why is this so? When a fruit arises, it does not come into being anew, for its nature has already been transformed;
when a fruit passes away, it is not annihilated, for it returns to its original nature.
The nature of the fruit is not eternal, because it undergoes transformation and ceases previously;
the nature of the fruit is not annihilated, because it undergoes transformation and arises subsequently.
Because its transformation is not constant, it is not definitively existent; because its intrinsic nature does not change, it is not definitively non-existent.
This is also not the case.
Since the principle of the arising and ceasing of all phenomena cannot be established, how could the transformation asserted by your school persist?

Furthermore, the arguments regarding "transformation," "intrinsic nature" (*svabhāva*), and so forth, have already been extensively refuted; it is not appropriate to persist in such attachments. Therefore, the reasoning of what you have stated is necessarily untenable.

Some say: "We, the Sautrāntikas and others, maintain that when causes and conditions harmonize, the effect arises without interval; once the effect has arisen, it repays the cause and is further able to produce a subsequent one. In this manner, through successive transmission from beginningless time, cause and effect are continuous and uninterrupted, free from such faults as arising and ceasing, or annihilation and permanence."
Why is this so? Because the continuity is beginningless, there is no arising;
because it has not yet attained its antidote and thus the continuity is not exhausted, there is no cessation.
Because it undergoes successive transformation, it is not eternal;
because it continues in an uninterrupted stream, it is not annihilated.
Since it does not possess a single, unchanging nature, it is also not subject to [substantial] transmutation.
This is also not the case.
If there were arising and ceasing, there could be continuity; since arising and ceasing do not exist, how can there be continuity?
The meaning of the non-existence of arising and ceasing has already been discussed at length above.
If the continuity has an end, it is then annihilation.
If the continuity is beginningless, it is then eternal.
If the essence of the continuity is one, there is then transformation.
Therefore, by establishing the theory of a continuous series (*saṃtāna*), the faults become even more numerous.
Some say: "I maintain that all dharmas exist eternally;

for all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*), from the very beginning, their intrinsic nature and characteristics are substantially real. As they respond to what precedes and give rise to what follows, flowing through the three periods of time, there are no such faults as annihilationism, eternalism, arising, or ceasing."
Why is this? Because its essence is eternally present, it is without arising and without cessation.
It is impermanent because it is conjoined with the characteristics of the conditioned.
The fruit arises to repay the cause, and for this reason it is not severed;
yet because each moment is distinct, it neither transforms nor continues.
This, too, is not the case.
The doctrine asserting that [things] are eternal has already been refuted.

If the essence of dharmas such as form were to exist eternally, they would resemble unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*) by being devoid of conditioned characteristics; thus, they would be identical to the Sāṃkhya position that everything is eternal, and one could not claim that their activity (*vṛtti*) undergoes arising and ceasing.

If activity were not separate from its essence, it would have to be eternal, identical to that essence; if the essence were not separate from activity, it would not be something that exists permanently.
If activity were originally present, it could not be called "arising";
if activity were originally absent, it could not be brought into being.
In the stage when the activity has not yet arisen, the activity of arising does not yet exist, so it cannot be called "arising.
In the stage when the activity has already arisen, the activity of arising has already ceased, so it also cannot be called "arising.
Apart from these two stages, there is no separate time for arising; as has been extensively explained previously, one must not cling to such a notion.
All phenomena arise through causal functioning; since arising itself is non-existent, cessation likewise does not exist.

Furthermore, if conditioned phenomena such as form are impermanent because they are conjoined with the characteristics of the conditioned, then these characteristics of the conditioned—being devoid of conjunction with other characteristics—should themselves not be impermanent.
If one says that this characteristic combines with other characteristics, then there would be an infinite regress.

If one says that conditioned phenomena possess characteristics of large and small, and that these characteristics of characteristics do not lead to an infinite regress, this is also not the case; for example, because dharmas such as form combine with other characteristics, they are not designated as "characteristics" (lakṣaṇa).
The same applies to birth and the other characteristics; when combined with others, they should not function as defining characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*).
Furthermore, just as the primary characteristics do not take the characterized phenomena, such as form (*rūpa*), as their own defining characteristics.
The same applies to the minor characteristics (*lakṣaṇāni*): the characterized phenomena, such as the great elements and so forth, should not be taken as the defining characteristics (*lakṣaṇas*).
If there were separate characteristics, it would lead to an infinite regress;
if there were no separate characteristics, they would have to be established as permanent.
Furthermore, conditioned characteristics (*saṃskṛta-nimitta*) are certainly not substantially existent; if they were substantially existent, it would contradict reason.
Why is this? Because they are like unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*).

If unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*) do not truly exist apart from their characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), this [case of conditioned phenomena] should likewise be so, for they share the same three characteristics.
That unconditioned phenomena are substantially existent has already been extensively refuted.
Furthermore, all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*) are not substantially existent either, because when analyzed by wisdom (*prajñā*), they resolve into emptiness.
Furthermore, conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) are established in contrast to the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). Since the unconditioned does not exist, the conditioned likewise does not exist.

If both the conditioned and the unconditioned arise from conditions, they are identical to illusory phenomena; if they do not depend on conditions, they are like flowers in the sky. Therefore, one should not cling to them as being substantially real.
As the sūtra says:
"The conditioned and the unconditioned are both conventional designations established through conceptual discrimination; their essence is entirely empty.
Apart from the conditioned and the unconditioned, there is no other dharma whatsoever.
Even if one were to say that they exist, it would be mere empty talk.
Conditioned and unconditioned phenomena encompass all dharmas; because these two are empty, all dharmas are empty.
Within emptiness there is no conceptual discrimination or frivolous proliferation (*prapañca*); this unhindered, pervasive penetration is the clarity of noble wisdom (*āryaprajñā*).
Therefore, the sūtra says:
"All dharmas are empty from the very beginning; emptiness is the absence of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*).

Because they lack intrinsic nature, they are the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), wherein not even the slightest dharma can be spoken of as arising or ceasing, as being annihilated or eternal, as being identical or different, or as coming or going."
O Lord of Devas, you should know that if any son or daughter of good family with pure faith can speak in this manner, they do not slander the Prajñāpāramitā.
"Those who speak otherwise are all said to be slandering [the truth].
If one were to say that permanence is empty, one would fall into the view of annihilationism; however, because the existence of permanence is negated, one does not fall into this extreme.
To cling to the notion that permanence is not empty would likewise lead to annihilationism, for that which is permanent and devoid of cause and effect is termed "annihilation."
All that I have taught is merely negation; "negation" refers to the refutation of others' attachments to arising, ceasing, and so forth.
That there is no arising does not mean there is cessation; it is solely for the purpose of negating arising.
That there is no cessation does not mean there is arising; it is simply for the purpose of negating cessation.
One should understand that [the categories of] non-interruption, permanence, and so forth are to be treated in this same manner.
Although at the time of *nirvāṇa* birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) is severed and extinguished, this is a provisional teaching (*upāya*) and is conventional rather than ultimate.

Just as it is said that there is permanence, bliss, and so forth within the celestial realms, such statements follow worldly convention and do not accord with reality; one should use the various phrases and expressions previously mentioned to dismantle all false attachments as appropriate.
All of us are deluded; who, then, could be considered true?

That which is called ultimate emptiness is where the paths of mind and speech are cut off, where conceptualization and frivolous proliferation cannot operate, and which is realized only by the internal wisdom of the noble sages.
Therefore, the wise should apply themselves with right diligence to realize this true emptiness and abandon those false attachments.
*The Commentary on the Extensive Hundred-Verse Treatise of the Mahāyāna*, Fascicle Nine.

Chapter Eight: Admonishing Disciples. Furthermore, once the correct doctrine has been established and the heterodox paths have been subdued, there still remains a slight lingering confusion regarding the profound meaning.
In order to further elucidate the True Doctrine through pure reasoning and instruction, and to dispel remaining doubts, he spoke these verses:
"Because of slight causes and conditions, One suspects that emptiness is not empty;
Based on the principles and teachings in the preceding chapters, These should now be further dispelled."
The Commentary states:

Although the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is empty, beginners are unable to see this; consequently, they cling to the false existence of things and fear the realization of profound emptiness, or fail to reach a definitive understanding due to other circumstances. Therefore, by means of correct reasoning and instruction, the preceding tenet is further elucidated so that they may eliminate their doubts and abandon their various inverted attachments.
Since the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is entirely empty, what could serve as their nature for those who have not yet realized this emptiness?
Furthermore, regarding the statement that "all phenomena are selfless," how is this to be understood?
It should be correctly explained as meaning they lack intrinsic nature; why resort to indirect or figurative expressions?
There is no basis for a definitive demonstration because they lack intrinsic substance; they can only be described through conventional designation.
Since all phenomena (dharmas) are without self and without an essence that can be grasped, they are called "empty.
As a sūtra says:
"It is said that all phenomena are empty, selfless, devoid of intrinsic nature, without grasping, and without appropriation.
Within the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), there is not even the slightest phenomenon that possesses a self or an intrinsic nature that could be described as "empty."
If that were so, the name "emptiness" should be inexpressible.
In truth, it is inexpressible; it is merely a conventional designation.
It is like speaking of "great space": although it lacks intrinsic nature and is truly inexpressible, one nevertheless establishes a name for it conventionally.

Since emptiness is already free from verbal expression, it should be said that it is both expressible and inexpressible; for, because it lacks any real essence, it is like saying that the true nature of all phenomena is entirely non-existent—within the principle of the absence of intrinsic nature, there is neither duality nor verbal expression.
If that is so, then since both the speaker and the spoken content are entirely empty, there should now be no speaking at all.
Yet, since there is indeed speaking, it follows that they cannot all be empty.
To clarify this doubt, the next verse says:
"If that which speaks and that which is spoken exist, then the principle of emptiness would be non-existent.
The Commentary states:

"That which speaks" refers to the person who speaks; "words" and "that which is spoken" are both termed "the spoken. These three collectively encompass all conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) phenomena.
This refers to the sense faculties such as the eye and their objects such as form. If these were substantially existent, what dharma would be empty?
To dispel this doubt, the verse further states:
"All dharmas are established through dependent conditions; therefore, the three factors do not exist."
The Commentary states:

The three factors—the speaker, the words, and the meaning—are empty of intrinsic nature because they are established by relying upon a multitude of conditions. Other schools also concede that names and expressions for all phenomena are merely conventional designations established by one's own mind in accordance with worldly usage.
Regarding this teaching, both the words and that which is expressed are non-existent in the ultimate sense (paramārtha) and exist only conventionally (saṃvṛti).
How, then, can these three things be said not to be empty?
And how can it be definitively known that these three things do not exist?
That which is established in dependence upon others is like a magical illusion; that which is not established in dependence upon others is like a rabbit's horn.
Therefore, the intrinsic nature of these three things is entirely empty, yet they are provisionally designated as existing for the benefit of the world through conventional discourse.
Furthermore, why do you raise doubts and difficulties regarding true emptiness?
My intention is still to establish the former view of existence;
you should abandon this intention.

Why is this so? It is not by refuting the tenets of another that one can establish one's own view; for example, merely refuting another's claim that [the self] is permanent because it is unimpeded does not itself establish that it possesses the nature of impermanence.
Even if such a principle were to exist, your position would still not be established. Why is this?
Therefore, the following verse says:
"If one merely states the fault of emptiness, the meaning of non-emptiness is thereby established;
since the fault of non-emptiness has already been clarified, the meaning of emptiness should first be established.
The treatise says:
If, by merely refuting emptiness, non-emptiness were established;
then since non-emptiness has already been refuted, the meaning of emptiness should be established.

In the preceding chapters, all the faults inherent in establishing the doctrine of non-emptiness have already been explained. If you wish to establish the doctrine of non-emptiness, you must first employ skillful means to eliminate those aforementioned faults.
If you do not eliminate your previous faults but merely speak of emptiness in vain, your own doctrine of non-emptiness will ultimately fail to be established.
Merely pointing out that others have faults and lack virtue cannot establish that one possesses virtue and is free from error oneself.
To establish one's own view, both capacities must be possessed: namely, establishing [one's position] and refuting [the opponent's].
Therefore, the subsequent verse says:
"Those who wish to destroy the tenets of others Must necessarily establish their own meaning."
"Why do you delight in speaking of others' faults while failing to establish your own position?
The treatise states:
"One must possess both establishment and refutation for one's own view to be fully realized."
Because the two capacities of establishing and refuting depend upon what is seen [as a basis].
To merely manifest the faults of others while failing to reveal one's own position is logically impossible for one’s own doctrine to be established.
For what reason do you people take pleasure only in refuting emptiness, yet fail to consider establishing your own doctrine of existence?
Therefore, one must be impartial toward both the establishment and the refutation [of a position] before one's own school’s tenet can be successfully established.
Since you lack the capacity to ultimately establish existence, the principle that all phenomena are empty is certain.
Is it not the case that this fault applies equally to the doctrine of emptiness?

To claim that you merely expose the errors of others without clarifying your own position is unreasonable; for the doctrine of emptiness and non-self has already been extensively elucidated in the preceding chapters.
However, since emptiness and selflessness dispel the notion of a self, your thesis is refuted and my own thesis is established.
If that were so, the discourse on emptiness would consist of nothing but empty words, for the names "emptiness" and "selflessness" would lack any actual referent.

It is so, it is so; it is exactly as you have said. The designations "emptiness" and "selflessness" are provisional and not ultimate; they are provisionally established to refute the attachments of others, and once those attachments are eliminated, the provisional positions themselves are likewise discarded.
To clarify this meaning, another verse is spoken:
"To refute the attachment to 'one' and so forth, The provisional establishment of 'negation' is set as the thesis;
When the other three attachments are thereby eliminated, One's own position follows as not being established."
The Commentary states:
First, "identity," "difference," and "neither" are termed the three attachments.
Since they are all equally [concerned with] identity and difference, they are not discussed separately.
The three categories of the three schools, when correctly examined, all return to the absence of intrinsic nature; not even the slightest thing remains. That nature is fundamentally empty;
it is not made empty by present negation. Therefore, a sūtra says:
"Kāśyapa, you should know that what is seen is fundamentally empty, not because it is negated by the present; those who cultivate emptiness realize the fundamental emptiness of intrinsic nature."
Therefore, all refutations are merely provisional expressions; likewise, all establishments should be understood as expedient devices rather than ultimate truths.
Since all phenomena are empty, upon what basis could a thesis be established?
It is precisely because we rely on what you yourself grasp that I establish my thesis.
Since that which is grasped does not exist, your thesis cannot be established.
Because you claim it exists, your thesis is not non-existent.
To preserve your own position, you must admit the existence of the other.
It is in order to dispel your attachment that we establish our own position.
If that which you grasp at does not exist, does our position not thereby become even more firmly established?
Nevertheless, it is improper to establish "emptiness" as a thesis, for we clearly perceive in the world the existence of things such as vases.

Although there are many forms of inference regarding emptiness and selflessness, they are subdued by the powerful force of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). Otherwise, things such as vases would not be known through direct perception. Why is this so?
Therefore, the following verse says:
"Granting that the jar is perceived through direct perception, The reason 'because it lacks causal capacity' is not established;
The reasons for direct perception accepted by other schools Are not admitted by this school."
The Commentary states:

If I were to concede that the jar is apprehended by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), then the reason [of the opponent] regarding emptiness could be said to lack probative force (*asāmarthya*) because it is an inference (*anumāna*).
However, since I maintain that the jar is not apprehended by direct perception, why should the reason for emptiness lack probative force?
Objects such as jars are not directly perceived; this has already been discussed in the various chapters refuting the sense organs and their objects.
One cannot maintain that a jar is directly perceived and establish it as a reason for proving [the existence of a whole] in opposition to this.
If what is perceived were identical, it could be cited as proof; since what is perceived differs, who would be willing to comply?
Therefore, the reason of emptiness does not contradict direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).

While one may establish that the nature and characteristics of all phenomena are empty, jars and other objects are directly perceived in the world. If one were to establish all such things as empty through inference (*anumāna*), then there would be no phenomenon in the world that is not empty, and thus emptiness could not be established as having a counter-correlate (*pratipakṣa*).
To raise this doubt, a verse is spoken:
"If the principle of non-emptiness does not exist, how can the principle of emptiness be established?
The treatise says:

Now, the principle of emptiness is established in opposition to non-emptiness; if non-emptiness does not exist, then emptiness likewise cannot exist. How, then, can it be established that all phenomena are empty?
To resolve this doubt, he further states in verse:
"Since you do not establish emptiness, Non-emptiness should likewise not be established."
The Commentary says:
The positing of "non-emptiness" is established in opposition to "emptiness. Since you do not believe in emptiness, how can non-emptiness be established?
How, then, can it be established that all phenomena are non-empty?
You do not believe in emptiness and yet seek to establish existence; I do not cling to existence, so why should I abandon the establishment of emptiness?
If you say that non-emptiness also has a counterpart—namely, mutual existence and non-existence, as well as the emptiness of absolute non-existence.

The emptiness of self (*pudgala-śūnyatā*) is likewise: it is established as "true emptiness" (*tathatā-śūnyatā*) in contrast to conventional existence (*saṃvṛti-sat*) in order to eliminate that false existence.
Furthermore, the emptiness thus established is intended solely for the purpose of dispelling attachment; it need not be posited only in relation to existence.

Just as the teaching of impermanence is proclaimed in order to dispel the notion of permanence—whereby impermanence is established even though permanence does not exist—you should not raise doubts or objections regarding this point.

This is because the negation applies to existence, not to emptiness. When there is a phenomenon, its opposite is non-existence; but since the principle of emptiness is itself non-existent, what could it oppose, and what would it negate?
If you argue that this is not the case because "emptiness" is the thesis (*pakṣa*), just as one establishes "the impermanence of form and so forth" as a thesis—
then since this thesis of impermanence is established as being existent, the thesis of emptiness must likewise necessarily not be non-existent.
This statement is not true, because the reason is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).
It is observed in the world that "non-existence" is also a thesis (*pakṣa*), and by logic it should be so as well.
Therefore, the next verse says:
"If the position of non-existence is admitted, then the position of existence can be established;
if the position of non-existence were not existent, the position of existence would not be established.
The treatise says:
If the absence of a thesis exists, it stands in opposition to the existence of a thesis;
if the absence of a thesis does not exist, what would the existence of a thesis oppose?
If you claim that the existence of a thesis is established without opposition, this contradicts your own previous assertion that emptiness exists in opposition to existence.
If all phenomena are without exception empty, and this true emptiness of non-self is of one single flavor, how is it that we currently perceive all phenomena as being different?
This is not so; for while they exist conventionally, they do not exist ultimately, and thus there is no contradiction in principle.
To clarify this meaning, it is said in verse:
"If all phenomena are empty, how can fire be called 'hot'?
This has already been fully refuted above; fire and heat are conventional, not ultimate."
The treatise says:
If the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is entirely empty, how can there be distinctions such as fire in the world?
Conventional things exist, and thus all phenomena are not identical.
In the ultimate sense, reality is empty and there is no distinction such as fire and so forth; therefore, your objection based on doubt is logically untenable.

Since fire and other phenomena have already been refuted—just as the senses and their objects were previously analyzed—and have been thoroughly examined as being conventional rather than ultimate, why do you raise this doubt and objection once again?
If phenomena do not exist, what would emptiness exclude?
Since emptiness has something to exclude, phenomena must exist.
If that were so, then the four philosophical systems, as they mutually exclude one another, would all be true; this would contradict your own intention.
To clarify this meaning, it is said in verse:
"If you claim that phenomena truly exist, And negate them by calling them 'empty,' Then all four philosophical systems should be true; Seeing what fault would you abandon them?"
The commentary states:

Because that which is to be negated (*pratiṣedhya*) must be established in order for the negator (*pratiṣedhaka*) to exist, if there were no object to be negated, how could the negator possibly exist?
It is like saying it is called "winter" because it is not raining; the time of winter is what is being negated, yet the time of rain must necessarily exist.
"Because emptiness excludes existence, existence must certainly not be non-existent.
This is also not the case, because the reason is inconclusive.

Since the four positions—such as "existence" and so forth—mutually exclude one another, they would all have to be true, for they are all that which is excluded. If being true entails being without fault, then all of them should be acceptable as tenets; what defect do you perceive in this?
Since you abandon three [theses] and maintain one, it cannot be said that there is actually something being negated.
If all that is negated were truly existent, your own words would be without fault.
Your fault would indeed be real; for if you deny emptiness, this emptiness ought to be real.
If the nature and characteristics of all phenomena were entirely non-existent, then the world would necessarily undergo total annihilation.
One does not even cling to existence, let alone cling to non-existence;
for clinging to either existence or non-existence results in error.
To clarify this meaning, a verse is spoken:
"If all phenomena were utterly non-existent, then birth and death would not exist;
how could the Buddhas ever have permitted the grasping of phenomena as definitively non-existent?"
The Commentary states:
If phenomena were entirely non-existent, there would be no birth and death.
Since the cycle of saṃsāra consists of the continuous succession of cause and effect, it cannot be established as a fixed non-existence; how, then, can this be raised as an objection?

I say that worldly cause and effect are not non-existent; yet the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, possess unimpeded wisdom and vision, and have never asserted them to be definitively existent or definitively non-existent.
As the Buddha told Kāśyapa in a sutra:
"The nature and characteristics of all phenomena are neither existent nor non-existent."
"Existence is one extreme; non-existence is the second—namely, permanence and annihilation.
Between these two, there is neither form nor visibility, neither abiding nor appearance; it cannot be indicated and cannot be designated."
This means that because they exist conventionally (*saṃvṛti*), the cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*) is established based upon them;
yet because they are empty in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), the nature and characteristics of all phenomena are neither existent nor non-existent, transcending the paths of mind and speech.
If all phenomena are truly free from existence and non-existence, by what further condition can one say they exist conventionally?
Although the ultimate is non-dual, how could the conventional be contradictory to it?
It should be that the conventional exists separately from the ultimate; though they are not separate, their meanings differ.
The conventional follows worldly conditions while the ultimate speaks of true principles; thus, while the ultimate is non-dual, the conventional has many paths.
Furthermore, all schools of thought admit that the ultimate is non-dual, yet they differ in their various categories and types. Therefore, one should not hastily give rise to doubts or objections.
To clarify this meaning, it is said in verse:
"If [you claim] that in truth there is neither existence nor non-existence, on what basis do you speak of conventional existence?
Your own fundamental position is likewise so; what purpose is served by raising such an objection?"
The Commentary states:
If phenomena such as form (*rūpa*) are truly free from both existence and non-existence, for what reason is it said that they exist conventionally?

Because cause and effect are uninterrupted within the cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*), they exist as provisional designations based on causes and conditions in accordance with worldly sentiment; yet when speaking of ultimate reality, they are neither existent nor non-existent.
Your own fundamental tenets all admit non-duality; why then do you raise objections whenever we speak of the existence of phenomena?
Why is this so? It is because the referents of various linguistic expressions are not themselves [identical to] existence, lest all phenomena be of the same essential nature.
Nor is it non-existent, lest all phenomena be devoid of essence.
Although neither existence nor non-existence pervades all phenomena, various propositions and meanings are established differently.
My teaching is likewise; why trouble yourself with such objections?
By this same principle, other difficulties are also resolved. Why is this so?
Therefore, the subsequent verse says:
"If all phenomena were entirely non-existent, Distinctions would not exist;
If one clings to the view that all phenomena exist, Distinctions likewise would not exist."
The Commentary states:

If the true nature (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena were entirely non-existent, then all the various distinctions between causes and effects in the world—namely, that visual consciousness and so forth arise from the eye and so forth—would all be non-existent, because there would be no distinction [between them].
This is explained as above: it means not clinging to non-existence, for both clinging to existence and clinging to non-existence are irrational.
Furthermore, if one clings to existence, the fault is likewise the same. Why is this so?

If all phenomena were identical in their nature of existence, then all worldly distinctions between cause and effect—such as the arising of visual consciousness from the eye and so forth—would necessarily not exist, because there would be no distinction between existence and non-existence.

It is by determining that although the secondary characteristics (*anulakṣaṇa*) within the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) differ, that the distinctions among all worldly phenomena (*lokadharma*) are established.
I am likewise: although [the ultimate] is empty because it is real, distinctions are established within conventional existence (*saṃvṛti*). Therefore, your objection is rendered futile.
A person of inferior intelligence may again raise this objection:
"If a phenomenon does not exist, it must necessarily be non-existent, which would destroy the cause that establishes existence.
This objection is irrational, because [the phenomenon] exists conventionally; thus, what you maintain is not non-existent.
If the establishing cause exists, why would that which is to be established not exist?
To clarify this point, another verse is spoken:
"If one claims that phenomena do not exist, There is no means to refute the existence of their causes."
"The refutation of the cause of existence has already been clarified; why then do you not establish your own thesis?
The treatise says:

If you claim that the nature and characteristics of all phenomena are non-existent, and thus the cause for refuting existence is also non-existent, this wisdom is extremely inferior, for it fails to comprehend even coarse and manifest phenomena before one's eyes.
The refutation of the existence of causes as encompassed by conventional reality has already been explained at length; what, then, is meant by "non-existence"?
You may not claim that what exists conventionally is not a cause, for in the context of ultimate truth, there is neither establishment nor refutation.
If you do not accept that there can be a reason for refutation, why then do you not establish a reason to prove the existence of your own position?
As I have explained at length, there is a reason for refutation;
yet you have never once presented a reason for existence. How, then, can you maintain that all phenomena are not empty?
Empty words are negation; by negating another, one establishes oneself.
Affirmative words are establishment; only by establishing oneself does one become complete.
Therefore, my emptiness requires no separate establishment, whereas the existence you cling to must have a separate reason established for it.
Since there is no other cause, on what basis do you know that it exists?
It is easy to refute a cause, but difficult to establish one; therefore, merely refuting the existence of a cause is not particularly remarkable.
If that is so, why does your own school not refute emptiness as well?
To refute their statement, a verse is spoken:
"To say that refuting causes is easy is but a conventional, empty word;
for what reason are you unable to refute the meaning of true emptiness?"
The Commentary states:
To claim that a reason for refutation is easily found is merely conventional, empty talk; for we have yet to see a reason that can refute true emptiness (*tathatā-śūnyatā*).

Although followers of the Hīnayāna and non-Buddhists may loathe true emptiness, they have not yet produced a reason that can refute its meaning; how, then, can it be said that a reason for refutation is easily found?
The emptiness of the nature of all phenomena is easy to establish and difficult to refute; the existence of the nature of all phenomena is difficult to establish and easy to overturn.

Since the truth and falsehood are as clear as the light of day, why do you remain so obstinate? You have been refuted by what was established and are trapped within a rigid web from which you cannot escape; thus, you fabricate such arguments.
Sound serves as the valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*) to indicate whether a phenomenon exists or not.
Since there is indeed sound, the phenomenon must necessarily exist;
if the phenomenon were non-existent, the sound would likewise be non-existent.
To refute this statement, a verse is spoken:
"The name 'existent' denotes that phenomena exist, meaning that phenomena are truly not non-existent;
the name 'non-existent' expresses that phenomena do not exist, and thus phenomena should truly not exist."
The commentary states:
They establish that all names have sound as their intrinsic nature, whereas we establish that names and so forth are not identical to sound; therefore, we cite only "name" to refute their attachment.

There is a sound that expresses existence; you maintain that the dharma expressed by it is truly not non-existent. There is a sound that signifies non-existence; one should therefore believe that the dharma expressed by it is truly not existent. Since the sound signifying non-existence is not a valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*), it would contradict your own tenet. Thus, what you have said does not serve as proof for existence.
These individuals of inferior wisdom, wishing to escape their own faults, labor in vain and ultimately cannot avoid them.

Based on phenomena that exist substantially, they establish names for what exists substantially; because of these names for what exists substantially, they give rise to conceptions of what exists substantially.
If phenomena did not exist, there would be no names for them.
If names did not exist, there would be no understanding.
Since there is indeed understanding, phenomena are not non-existent.
This is also not the case, because it is a conventional designation.
To clarify this meaning, a verse is spoken:
"Through names one understands that phenomena exist, And thus concludes that phenomena are not non-existent."
"Because it is said that one knows phenomena are non-existent, one should believe that phenomena are not existent.
The Commentary says:
If one hears that there is a name and gives rise to the understanding of existence, one consequently claims that all phenomena exist and are not non-existent.
Since one hears of "namelessness" and gives rise to the understanding of non-existence, one should believe that all phenomena are neither existent nor non-existent.
If this is not the case, how could that [other position] be so?
Understanding arises based on names; this is the very reason for realizing emptiness. To claim it is a cause for existence is necessarily contrary to reason.
If the essence of phenomena (*dharmas*) were existent, why would it depend upon a name?

Since the understanding of existence arises only by depending on a name, we know that the essence of all phenomena is in fact non-existent; they are merely provisionally established with names that circulate commonly in the world.
Names are definitively devoid of any real referent, for they are established based on conceptualization, just as one designates a person as "ox.
To claim that names can eliminate existence while simultaneously establishing it is no different from someone asserting that light is darkness.
If there were anything that could be described, it would be provisional and not real. Why is this so?
Therefore, the following verse says:
"All that can be spoken of in the world Is merely conventional and not real;
Apart from worldly designations and names, That alone is real and not conventional.
The commentary states:
All worldly discourse follows one's own mind; it is established through conventional designations for the sake of common transmission.
If a phenomenon can be expressed, it is provisional and not ultimate; that which is not provisional is ultimate and is definitively inexpressible.

All that can be expressed is conventional and not ultimate; this has already been extensively established in the preceding chapters. Therefore, that which is grasped as existing is merely provisional and not ultimate, because it can be described—just like a house or an army.
The four types of grasping at extremes have already been thoroughly refuted, and no other truly existent phenomena are established; thus, this treatise might fall into the extreme of nihilism.
To resolve this doubt, the following verse is spoken:
"To deny all phenomena as non-existent Is to fall into the view of nihilism."
"Only by eliminating all false attachments, how can one say that one falls into non-existence?
The Commentary says:
One may fall into the extreme of non-existence by slandering all existent phenomena; but if one merely dispels deluded perceptions, how could one fall into the attachment to non-existence?
In order to dismantle the clinging to existence, one provisionally establishes non-existence; once the clinging to existence is removed, non-existence is likewise dispelled.
Furthermore, since conventional existence has already been discussed at length previously, one should not say that this [position] falls into the clinging to non-existence.
If you grant that [things] exist conventionally, they must be non-existent ultimately;
if you do not grant that they are non-existent ultimately, you must grant that they exist truly.
This statement is irrational; therefore, the next verse says:
"Because existence is not truly existent, non-existence is also not truly nonexistent;
since there is no true non-existence, how can there be true existence?
The commentary says:
If true existence were present, then true non-existence could exist.
Since true existence is already absent, how could true non-existence exist?
Because there is no true non-existence, true existence is likewise non-existent.
That the ultimate truth (tattva) is neither existent nor non-existent has been repeatedly argued as before; how then can you again insist that the ultimate truth is either existent or non-existent?
If the ultimate truth is not non-existent, for what purpose do you frequently state that while the nature and characteristics of all phenomena exist conventionally, they are non-existent ultimately?
The meaning of this statement is as follows: only the conventional exists; because the ultimate lacks such existence, it is said that the ultimate is non-existent.
If this were so, then the ultimate and the conventional would have non-existence as their essence; otherwise, there would have to be a separate ultimate.
If there were a true reality existing apart [from the conventional], then existence would not be merely conventional.
Since existence is indeed merely conventional, the essence of truth must be non-existent.
If the essence of truth does not exist, what is there to rejoice in regarding its cultivation and realization?
Regarding this, one class of commentators explains the difficulty as follows:

"When I say that 'true non-existence' is a negation and not an affirmation, it means that while worldly people falsely perceive existence as real, I negate that 'real existence' rather than affirming a lack of essence."
However, its true essence is precisely conventional non-existence; it is not that there is a true essence existing separately from conventional non-existence.
When one speaks of "true non-existence," it means that the conventional is non-existent in its true nature; this negates its reality as something real, with no other referent to be expressed.
This does not yet exhaustively investigate the source of the meaning of words; who would say that "non-existence" truly has nothing else to indicate?

If a negation of other phenomena indicates something else as its referent, it is a word that both negates and affirms; having negated other phenomena, it indicates another common characteristic (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*), such as "not a sentient being," "not a eunuch," and so forth.

If the negation of other phenomena lacks a distinct referent, it is merely a negative statement; once the object of negation has been negated, its force is exhausted, as in such injunctions as "Do not eat meat" or "Do not drink alcohol."
This "truly wordless" merely negates that the true has any distinct referent; it does not mean that [the truth] can be fully known through words.
It is like the expression "not existent," which merely negates existence; it neither explains non-existence nor indicates anything else.
If it were to express its non-existence or indicate another phenomenon, then one should not say "this is not existent.
If the phrase "not existent" were to express existence, then the statement "not non-existent" should likewise express non-existence.
Such a negation is understood equally by both the foolish and the wise; since they have no doubt or objection regarding it, what is the purpose of stating it again?

The meaning of that objection is as follows: "If existence pertains only to the conventional, then the ultimate is non-existent. What, then, is there to be cultivated or realized? [The opponent claims: "To say merely that the ultimate is non-existent is a negation, not an affirmation," and so on at length. How could this possibly resolve the objection?
Furthermore, another explanation states:

when the cultivation of the contemplation of non-self reaches its ultimate perfection and one perceives true reality (*tattva*), all conventional existents (*saṃvṛti-sat*) fail to manifest; therefore, it is said that [conventional existence] is non-existent in truth.
This is also not the case, because the mental faculty is difficult to comprehend.
If that which is conventionally non-existent were called "ultimate," there would be nothing to be realized.
If there were a separate ultimate that constitutes the object of realization, one should not say that existence is merely conventional.
Furthermore, this contradicts the scriptural teaching that seeing nothing at all is called seeing the truth, whereas seeing even the slightest thing is not seeing the truth.
Therefore, this statement is also not a correct interpretation.
A commentator explaining it in this way should say: "Reality is neither existent nor non-existent, for it transcends both mind and speech.

To refute the attachment to existence, one conventionally speaks of 'non-existence'; to refute the attachment to non-existence, one conventionally speaks of 'existence. Both these dualistic assertions of existence and non-existence are merely conventional expressions; within the principle of the ultimate truth, both existence and non-existence are equally discarded."
That which is realized by noble wisdom is neither existent nor non-existent, yet it is both existent and non-existent; this shall be explained in detail later.
Someone might raise this objection:
"Is the cause for realizing the emptiness of phenomena existent or non-existent?"
If [emptiness] exists, then other phenomena must also exist; if it does not exist, one cannot realize the emptiness of all phenomena.
To raise this objection, the verse says:
"If there were a cause for realizing the emptiness of phenomena, then the emptiness of phenomena could not be established."
The Commentary states:
Emptiness must necessarily rely upon a reason (*hetu*) in order to be established; if it were not so, everything would be established [as empty].

Since the reason itself is not empty, the rest should likewise be so. If only things such as mirages were empty of the nature of water and so forth, then the thesis (*pakṣa*) being established would fail in every respect.
To resolve this difficulty, it is further stated in verse:
"Because the thesis and the reason are not distinct, the essence of the reason is in fact non-existent.
The commentary says:

For the Sāṃkhyas and others, there is no distinction between the general and the particular; thus, causes such as "being produced by volitional effort" and "being uninterrupted" are all identical to sound itself.
Consequently, just as the essence of sound does not extend to other things, the essence of these reasons cannot be established.
The Vaiśeṣikas and others maintain that the universal (sāmānya) and the particular (viśeṣa) are either different or not different.

As for their position that they are not different, the fault is the same as that previously [attributed] to the former masters; as for their position that they are different, it has already been refuted in the preceding chapters. Therefore, neither difference nor non-difference constitutes a valid reason.
For this reason it is said that the thesis (*pakṣa*) and the reason (*hetu*) are not distinct, and the essence of the reason does not truly exist.
Furthermore, if the essence of the established reason were truly existent, it would have to be either identical to or different from the essence of the thesis.

However, it cannot be said that the reason (*hetu*) and the essence of the thesis (*pakṣa*) are either identical or different; because they are neither identical nor different, they are like an army or a forest—conventional designations (*prajñapti*), not ultimate realities, and subsumed under the conventional (*saṃvṛti*).
In accordance with the false conceptualizations of the world, various theses (*pakṣa*) and reasons (*hetu*) are established differently in order to dispel all erroneous attachments.

Once these erroneous attachments are dispelled, the theses and reasons themselves also vanish; therefore, it cannot be said that phenomena exist in the same manner as their causes. Since theses and reasons are merely provisional designations, they are conventional and not ultimate.
Furthermore, there is an objection:
Is the analogy for realizing the emptiness of phenomena non-existent or existent?
If it is non-existent, one cannot realize the emptiness of all phenomena; if it is existent, then all phenomena must exist just as the analogy does.
This is also not the case; therefore, the subsequent verse says:
"To claim that because the analogy of emptiness is distinct, All phenomena are thereby not empty— Only the analogy itself would be established, While the internal self remains as black as a crow."
The Commentary states:
The example (*dṛṣṭānta*) is subsumed under one part of the reason (*hetu*). Since the reason exists conventionally, the example should likewise exist.

If it is claimed that the essence of the example exists separately from the reason, and that by means of this example all phenomena are established as existing and not empty, this is certainly not the case.
An example that is devoid of a reason can never prove the thesis to be established, because the thesis to be established is not itself subsumed under the reason.
If an example lacking a reason could establish a thesis, then it would follow that the internal self must be established as having the property of blackness, just like a crow.
Furthermore, all that is established would necessarily be proven, for it would be easy to find other instances where the lack of a reason is identical.
Therefore, the nature of the example must not be divorced from the reason; thus, the similarity to the reason cannot be raised as an objection.
If all phenomena are empty by their very nature, what superior benefit is there in realizing and seeing this emptiness?
To address this objection, it is said in verse:
"If phenomena are empty by nature, what benefit is there in seeing that emptiness?"
The Commentary says:
Within the conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) that are devoid of a self, one does not perceive even the slightest superior quality in the emptiness of a self; the same applies to all phenomena.
If their intrinsic nature is empty, what benefit is there in perceiving this emptiness?
If there were no benefit, why would one exert such toil to cultivate the practices capable of realizing emptiness and the immeasurables?
To resolve this difficulty, another verse is spoken:
"Bound by false discrimination, The vision of emptiness can remove it."
The Commentary states:

Although all phenomena and all conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*) are empty and devoid of self, foolish worldlings engage in false conceptualization (*vikalpa*), grasping at them as being identical or distinct and so forth. By the power of this false conceptualization, the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) of afflictions such as greed grow and flourish; following conditions, they give rise to various wholesome and unwholesome karmas. Thus, they sink into the ocean of the three realms of existence (*trai-dhātuka*) and continue in cyclic rebirth (*saṃsāra*), tormented by the three types of suffering and unable to escape on their own.

Diligently cultivating preparatory practices, one realizes the emptiness of selflessness and gradually eliminates false conceptualization; accordingly, one realizes the three types of enlightenment, such that the merit of benefiting oneself and others becomes inexhaustible.
What is the nature of this unreal conceptualization?
It refers to the minds and mental factors of the three realms.
Is it not the case that these phenomena are also empty by their very nature?

If form and so forth, as they are grasped by the foolish, were able to draw forth suffering and oppress sentient beings, then even though these are empty, they would still be able to draw forth suffering.
In that case, form and so forth would also possess this capacity; why then do you speak only of "false discrimination"?

Although form, mind, and so forth are all empty by their very nature, one must rely upon false conceptualization and discursive estimation to reckon that phenomena exist or do not exist; it is because of this that defilement and purity arise.
Because the defilement and purity of these conscious beings differ, it is therefore said that they are merely false conceptualizations (*abhūtaparikalpa*).
If phenomena were truly existent, this might be so;
but since phenomena are in fact non-existent, how can one engage in such speculative reckoning?

Because existence, non-existence, and so forth differ according to defilement and purity, just as in dreams and the like, although forms and other objects do not exist, various appearances manifest with clarity.
This analogy is incorrect; for in states such as dreaming, there is conceptual discrimination, and thus their functional activity is not non-existent.
It may be plausible that, with conceptual discrimination as their basis, various objects appear as images, giving rise to both defilement and purity;
however, since all things are now empty and lack substantial discrimination, who could initiate these differing functional activities?
That which lacks an essence yet possesses efficacy has never been observed.
If there were functional capacity despite the absence of an essence, then rabbit horns and tortoise hair should both possess utility.

Furthermore, if sentient beings could undergo defilement or purification without afflictions or without roots of goodness, then those who have already severed their afflictions would continue to transmigrate, and those who have not yet planted roots of goodness would attain eternal bliss.
Regarding this, one class of commentators explains the difficulty as follows:
"Since conventional reality is not non-existent, this fault does not arise.
One should then ask: Is conventional reality not [itself] true?
He replies that this is not so, because according to conventional measurement (*saṃvṛti-pramāṇa*), these are substantially existent and are thus also called "truths" (*satya*).
How can it be said that for a single phenomenon at one time, both existence and non-existence—which are contradictory—can simultaneously be called truths?

The same applies to arising and so forth: for a single phenomenon at a single time, there would be both arising and non-arising, cessation and non-cessation, abandonment and non-abandonment, permanence and impermanence, coming and non-coming, and going and non-going—and so on, as explained at length. Since these are mutually contradictory, how can it be said that they are all equally true and real?

He asserts this: that for a single phenomenon, at one and the same time, being without meaning is the ultimate (paramārtha) and having meaning is the conventional (saṃvṛti); because their meanings are distinct, they do not contradict one another.

It is just as in the world, where wholesome dharmas such as giving, because their nature is with outflows (sāsrava), receive the name "unwholesome," yet because they are associated with roots of virtue (kuśalamūla), they are also called "wholesome"; both are termed true and real without contradiction.

This reasoning is not tenable; while there may be no contradiction because wholesome dharmas such as giving differ in their mutual dependence, how can two truths—one existing and one non-existing—belong to a single dharma at a single time without any distinct basis for such dependence? How, then, could they be non-contradictory?
Why is this? Peace and harmony are called "wholesome" (*kuśala*).
There are two kinds of wholesomeness: namely, the mundane and the supramundane.

Supramundane wholesome dharmas can ultimately destroy the various entanglements of afflictions and are ultimately peaceful and harmonious; thus, they are called "wholesome in the ultimate sense" (*paramārtha-kuśala*).

Mundane wholesome dharmas possess efficacy only temporarily and lack it ultimately; because they can temporarily suppress the entanglements of afflictions, they are called "wholesome in the conventional sense" (*saṃvṛti-kuśala*). However, because they cannot permanently sever the entanglements of afflictions, they may also be termed "unwholesome in the ultimate sense."
These wholesome and unwholesome states do not contradict one another, because their capacities differ according to the distinction of time.

For example, a wholesome state such as giving is said to possess capacity while it abides for a single moment; once this moment has passed, it can no longer abide and is therefore said to lack capacity.
Although capacity and incapacity reside within a single dharma, they do not contradict one another because their temporal phases differ.
Since giving and so forth do not persist into the second moment and thus lack substantial existence, what could be called "incapacity"?
Because that essence lacks capacity, it is definitively non-existent; since the capacity is absent, it is termed "incapable.

Alternatively, there is no difference between the time of having capacity and the time of lacking capacity; rather, they differ only in terms of the respective objects expected, and thus there is no contradiction.

Why is this? Because it can temporarily suppress the entanglements (*paryavasthāna*) such as greed, it is said to possess capability; yet because it cannot eradicate the seeds (*bīja*) of greed and the like, it is said to lack capability—just as consuming medicinal ghee can eliminate wind-disorders (*vāta-vyādhi*) but does not expel phlegm (*kapha*).

Although the temporal periods of capability and incapability are identical, they do not contradict one another because there is a distinction between the objects from which they are respectively expected.
If a single dharma simultaneously possesses both existence and non-existence within the two truths without any distinction in their objective referents, how could there be no contradiction?
He further offers this defense:

"Just as a single moment of consciousness is conventionally called 'self' because it is the basis for the grasping of a self, yet is called 'selfless' from the perspective of ultimate truth—so too, the distinction between self and selflessness is not contradictory."
The same applies to the existence and non-existence of a single phenomenon at a single time; although there is no distinction in the object, they do not contradict one another.
This, too, is not the case, because the meanings of "self" and "non-self" are not mutually contradictory.
Why is this so? Because a single moment of mind lacks self-mastery, it is called "non-self" (anātman); yet that which serves as the basis for the grasping of a self is also called "self.
As a sūtra states:
"If consciousness were the self, it should possess sovereignty and not undergo transformation.
Yet, because foolish worldlings give rise to the grasping of a self based upon it, they designate it as "self."
The meaning of "lack of sovereignty" and the meaning of "basis for the grasping of a self," though belonging to the same single consciousness, are not mutually contradictory.
How could it be that a single phenomenon at one time possesses both the characteristics of existence and non-existence and is simultaneously designated as "truth" and "reality" without contradiction?

Now, regarding your attempt to establish that the two truths of existence and non-existence coexist within a single phenomenon without mutual contradiction, you may employ numerous worldly analogies and various skillful means, yet in the end, you will be unable to achieve your proof.
He further clarifies this by saying:
"Just as a single color, such as blue, exists from the perspective of its own nature but does not exist when viewed in relation to others, so it is with all phenomena.
Each and every dharma-nature exists according to conventional truth, yet does not exist when viewed from the perspective of ultimate truth."
This is also not the case. Blue and yellow have distinct natures; thus, one may rely on their own existence and regard them as non-existent from the perspective of the other.
But the conventional and the ultimate are not different in essence; if they exist from their own side, with respect to what could they be said to be non-existent?
Upon investigating its nature, the conventional is in fact the ultimate;
it is not that by examining the blue, it actually becomes yellow.
Therefore, what you have established is a case where the property of the subject and the example do not correspond.
Furthermore, the conventional and the true essence are not separate from one another; how, then, could the conventional essence be non-existent in relation to the true?
As the Buddha told Subhūti in a sūtra:
"The conventional and the ultimate do not have distinct essences."
"Conventional suchness is itself the ultimate; it is not that emptiness exists separately from form, and this is likewise true for the emptiness of consciousness up to the point of consciousness.
How can two meanings that are mutually contradictory both be called truths when one phenomenon does not have a separate object?

Consequently, the ancient masters and preceptors, differing in their perspectives on phenomena, established two truths: the conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya) uses language that closely reflects worldly conventions, while the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya) employs discourse that distantly points toward actual reality.
Although all worldly phenomena are designated according to conventional sentiment, their actual nature is empty; therefore, they are not ultimately real.

Furthermore, since direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) realizes that the dependent origination of form and mind cannot be fully expressed by language, they should not be considered conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
Therefore, the Sūtra states:
"Whatever is expressed by the names and phrases of the world is called conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
The intended meaning of this sūtra is that which is commonly known by the world.
The correspondence between the signifier and the signified, as well as the phenomena and meanings intended for expression, are not commonly known.

The scriptures and treatises concerning these phenomena and meanings are called conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*); however, the dependent origination of form and mind realized through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) is neither expressible by words nor is it conventional truth.

If it is argued that because they are what is expressed by conventionally established designations, this form and mind are also subsumed under conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), then ultimately the supreme ultimate (*paramārtha*) should likewise not be real, since it too is expressed and indicated by conventionally established designations.

In the ultimate sense, neither this form nor mind exists; since the truth is entirely non-existent while phenomena as entities do exist, these phenomena would not be subsumed under the two truths and thus would be non-existent, which contradicts what is established by worldly direct perception.
If one says that it exists but is not subsumed under the two truths, then a third truth—neither ultimate nor conventional—should be established.

If one says that although dependent origination consisting of form and mind exists and is apprehended by the direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) of worldly people, it is nevertheless not subsumed under the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*), and is therefore provisionally designated as being included within the conventional truth (*saṃvṛtisatya*), being merely a conventional designation established according to one's own whim.
If form and mind exist substantially, then there would be no dispute; for it is based upon this that the meanings of defilement and purification are established.
If you claim that form and mind exist conventionally, but do not exist nor arise from the perspective of ultimate truth—what meaning does such a statement convey?

If it is said that, like that non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*), its objective sphere is ultimately empty and non-existent, and is thus called "non-existent" because it does not exist in such a way;
then, since its objective sphere would be ultimately non-existent, non-conceptual wisdom should not be able to arise.
Even if one were to grant that such a cognition arises, it would not be true knowledge, because its object is non-existent, just like the cognition of other absences.

Since the cognition is not true, the object must be conventional; yet, although you claim that form and mind do not exist in that way, this actually further demonstrates that form and mind truly exist. Because you assert that their non-existence is ultimate non-existence, and because there is no difference in their characteristics, they must necessarily exist.
Since it is established that they exist, one must also admit that this matter and mind truly possess arising and so forth.
If you think that although matter and mind indeed exist and arise, they do not do so in the ultimate sense (paramārtha), [then...]
One should first carefully determine what the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) is, and only then can it be said that "this is not the ultimate truth.

If one claims that the ultimate truth is the absolute emptiness and non-existence that is the object of non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*), this has already been refuted; namely, because that which is its object is ultimately non-existent, non-conceptual wisdom would be unable to arise, and so forth, as explained at length.
Furthermore, this object of practice is not the true ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), because it does not exist, just like a rabbit's horn;
or because it is not existent, like a flower in the sky.
If one were to claim that the ultimate reality is something that can be investigated, this is also not the case, because there is no difference in the nature of the object.

Now, one who investigates thoroughly does not abandon the conventional; yet the conventional phenomena themselves cannot be investigated thoroughly. That which can be investigated thoroughly must transcend the conventional.

However, it is not the case that there is a separate ultimate truth apart from the conventional; therefore, it cannot be said that this [ultimate truth] can be investigated thoroughly. Consequently, what you have stated is not the characteristic of the ultimate truth.
If it is argued that the ultimate nature (paramārtha-lakṣaṇa) consists in the fact that the ultimate reality asserted by other schools does not exist at all, this is also incorrect.

For they define the ultimate as the nature of dependent origination, momentary abiding, and so forth; to now deny its existence would contradict both their own tenets and direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).

If it is claimed that being "truthful" (*tattva*) is the characteristic of the ultimate (*paramārtha*), then the conventional (*saṃvṛti*) would not be truthful; why was it previously stated that the conventional is truthful?
Even if one were to concede that only that which is neither existent nor produced is called "truthful," then existence and production would be merely conventional designations.

Since that which is established through false conceptualization is neither true nor real, how could mere conventional designations established by false conceptualization give rise to the functions of defilement and purification?

Therefore, their attempt to resolve this objection is logically untenable; it is not as if one can say that because "tortoise hair" is a name for something existent, it possesses a functional capacity to bind the world.
Furthermore, other masters explain this objection as follows:

"The substantial nature of phenomena as apprehended by conceptual construction is non-existent, whereas the substantial nature of phenomena produced from causes and conditions is existent. It is due to this that afflictions and latent tendencies are aroused, which bind the world to the cycle of rebirth within the three realms of existence;
yet, by practicing preparatory application and realizing the emptiness of selflessness, one attains supreme enlightenment and is liberated from the suffering of birth and death."
Although phenomena arising from causes and conditions pertain to both matter and mind, the mind is the source and is therefore emphasized here.
False discrimination binds the world; by wearying of this, one can cultivate the preparatory application for realizing emptiness.

Although there may be objective realms, if there is no mind, false conceptualization will ultimately not bind one; nor can one cultivate revulsion for the self through the realization of emptiness, thereby attaining the three types of enlightenment and transcending birth and death.
To prove this point, a sūtra is cited as follows:
“The thoroughly imagined is non-existent; The dependent nature exists.
Those who lose themselves through false discrimination Fall into the two extremes of superimposition and denial.”
Regarding this, one class of commentators explains the meaning as follows:
"The name is the thoroughly imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*), while the object is the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*).

Since the name does not exist in relation to its object, it is 'non-existent'; since the object is not non-existent according to worldly convention, it is 'existent. This cannot be cited as proof for the existence of the dependent nature."
This explanation is incorrect, for it contradicts the meaning.
If a name is non-existent because it does not exist in relation to its referent, how could the referent exist when it is likewise non-existent in relation to the name?
Furthermore, the linguistic designation established for that referent, being produced through causes and conditions, ought to exist just as the referent itself exists.

If the nature of the signifier, which is falsely grasped, does not exist, how could the nature of the signified, which is also falsely grasped, possibly exist? While you admit that names possess the capacity for expression as they exist conventionally, yet do not allow them to be of the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*); likewise, since meanings also possess the capacity for expression as they are conventionally and metaphorically designated, why do you not allow them to be of the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*)?
In conventional discourse, the designator and the designated are established as being either both non-existent or both existent; how then could a sutra state that one exists while the other does not?
Therefore, what you have said does not accord with the meaning of the sutras.
One should believe that the thoroughly imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) does not exist, for it is established by the false conceptualizations of worldly beings.
One should believe that the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) exists, for it arises from causes and conditions and is not a product of false conceptualization.
Having established his own position, he further cites a scriptural passage:
"By establishing such and such names, One expresses such and such phenomena;
Yet these are all non-existent by nature, For such is the nature of all phenomena."
This verse cannot prove that point.
The intent of the Sūtra is not to say that names do not exist in relation to objects; rather, it says that the *dharmatā* (the nature of phenomena) which is expressed is non-existent.

It clarifies that the *dharmatā* of all phenomena is inexpressible: that which is expressed by names and words is always a universal characteristic (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*), whereas the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of all phenomena transcends all names and words.

The specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) is not non-existent, and the universal characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) is not existent; herein it is briefly stated that the nature of the signified (*vācya*) is non-existent, but this does not mean that the nature of the signifier (*vācaka*) is substantially existent.
Therefore, the verse merely states that "it is not existent," for otherwise it would have had to say, "this nature is not existent."
To prove that this dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) does not exist, he further cites a brief verse spoken in the Sūtras:
"Not even the slightest dharma arises, nor does even the slightest dharma cease;
when viewing all dharmas with pure vision, they are neither existent nor non-existent."
This [verse] also cannot prove that the dependent nature (paratantra-svabhāva) is non-existent by its very essence. Why is this so?

The intent of this verse is to clarify that the specific characteristics of the imagined nature (parikalpita-svabhāva)—namely, the signifier and the signified—are both empty in essence, being neither produced nor extinguished.

Free from the attachment to pure views, one contemplates all worlds as produced by causes and conditions, being neither non-existent nor existent; therefore, this does not prove that the *paratantra-svabhāva* (dependent nature) is non-existent.
If the *paratantra* exists, for what reason does the Sūtra state, "The nature of all phenomena is such that there is nothing that is not empty"?
Furthermore, a sūtra states that the Buddha told Subhūti:
"The intrinsic nature of all phenomena, such as form and so forth, is entirely non-existent.
